## SUB 7 | Rajput Society, Warfare and Administration
[103:7:0] TABLE head: Term / feature | Meaning
  [103:7:0.0] Feudal structure | Land grants carried revenue, judicial and police rights
  [103:7:0.1] R.S. Sharma's "Indian feudalism" | Sub-infeudation, vishti (forced labour), closed village economy
  [103:7:0.2] Jauhar | Women's self-immolation to avoid capture (Rani Padmini, Chittor)
  [103:7:0.3] Sati | Also practised
  [103:7:0.4] Vinaya-sthiti-sthapaka | Keyed chief of the treasury (OPSC 2018); NextGen's official list reads "Vinaysthitisansthapaka: head of education department" (morals)
[103:7:1] - **Warfare:** **direct, face-to-face combat with emphasis on personal valour**; war treated as a sport; clan honour (maan) – not guerrilla, naval or gunpowder warfare.
[103:7:2] - Constant feuds among Rajput states prevented a combined opposition to the Turks.
[103:7:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.151; NextGen Indian History - APPSC 03 p.35 (officials list); testbook.com (OPSC key); app notes 1:103 (sub 2)

  x: Someshvara wrote Kirtikaumudi on Vastupala.

  Karnidan | *Dalpati Vijay | Dungar Singh | Jagnik
  x: Khuman Raso is by Dalpati Vijay, not Karnidan; Dungar Singh wrote Shatrusal Raso.
[g3c8259aa9aae] sub5
  Navasahasanka Charita of Padmagupta is a biography of which Paramara ruler?
  Bhoja | Munja | *Sindhuraja | Upendra
  x: Padmagupta (Parimala), court poet of the Paramaras, wrote Navasahasanka Charita about Sindhuraja, whose title was Navasahasanka.
[n184b3dc1466] sub6
  Which architectural feature is often associated with the Maru-Gurjara sub-style?

  x: The Maru-Gurjara style, associated with the Solanki tradition of Gujarat and Rajasthan, often includes a Kirti-torana.
[nb1973274c78] sub6
  Which one of the following descriptions correctly refers to the Latina or Rekha-prasada type of Nagara temple tower?
  A pyramidal tower with multiple terraces | A barrel-vaulted tower | A sloping, stepped roof | *A single curvilinear tower
  x: Latina, also called Rekha-prasada, is characterised by a single curvilinear tower. Phamsana has a sloping, stepped roof, while Valabhi is barrel-vaulted.
[n698130b455c] sub6
  With which dynasty is the Maru-Gurjara style of the 11th-13th centuries associated?
  Chandelas | Gahadavalas | Paramaras | *Solankis
  x: Maru-Gurjara is a Solanki-associated Nagara sub-style of Gujarat and Rajasthan, fusing Maha-Maru and Maha-Gurjara traditions.
[ne1c02876abd] sub7
  In R. S. Sharma's model of 'Indian feudalism', what does vishti mean?
  *forced labour | military levy | grant to temples | land tax
  x: Sharma's model includes sub-infeudation and vishti (forced labour), with closed village economies.
[nd21249d68db] sub7
  Which of the following statements regarding women and Rajput customs is correct?
  Sati was entirely unknown in Rajput society | Rani Padmini performed naval warfare against Alauddin Khalji | Jauhar meant the ritual coronation of a queen after victory | *Jauhar involved self-immolation to avoid capture
  x: Jauhar was self-immolation by women to avoid capture. Rani Padmini of Chittor is cited as an example in the conflict with Alauddin Khalji; sati was also practised.
[n475633c894f] sub7
  On which of the following did Rajput warfare generally place emphasis?
  guerrilla tactics and naval warfare | gunpowder artillery and trench warfare | *personal valour in direct combat | economic blockade and maritime raids
  x: Rajput warfare emphasised direct combat and personal valour, with chivalry and clan honour receiving great importance.
[f92508f374911] sub7

  *Alauddin Khalji | Muhammad Ghori | Mahmud of Ghazni | Mahmud Khalji of Malwa
  x: Rani Padmini's jauhar at Chittor is linked to Alauddin Khalji's attack.
[fc998e942c046] sub7
  Consider the following statements about Rajput society:
1. Land grants carried revenue, judicial and police rights.
2. Rajput warfare relied mainly on guerrilla tactics.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
  *1 only | 2 only | Both 1 and 2 | Neither 1 nor 2
  x: Land grants carried revenue, judicial and police rights; Rajput warfare was direct face-to-face combat, not guerrilla war.

=== NOTES 1:104 | Sources for Medieval India - Persian Chronicles, Inscriptions, Travellers' Accounts
## SUB 0 | Persian Chronicles and Their Authors
[104:0:0] - **Tawarikh** (singular **tarikh**): histories in **Persian**, the administrative language of the Sultans, written by secretaries, administrators, poets and courtiers.
[104:0:1] TABLE head: Work | Author | Subject / note
  [104:0:1.0] Taj-ul-Maasir | Hasan Nizami (UPPSC 1997) | First official chronicle of the Sultanate; patron Qutbuddin Aibak
  [104:0:1.1] Tabaqat-i-Nasiri | Minhaj-us-Siraj (State PSC) | Ghurids and early Sultans up to 1260; earliest account of Bakhtiyar Khalji's Bihar invasion (BPSC 2018); dedicated to Nasiruddin Mahmud
  [104:0:1.2] Khazain-ul-Futuh | Amir Khusrau | Alauddin's campaigns (Warangal 1310)
  [104:0:1.3] Futuh-us-Salatin | Abdul Malik Isami | Ghaznavids to Muhammad bin Tughlaq; written at the Bahmani court c. 1350
  [104:0:1.4] Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi | Ziauddin Barani; another by Shams-i-Siraj Afif | Balban to early Firuz; main account of Alauddin's market rules
  [104:0:1.5] Fatawa-i-Jahandari | Ziauddin Barani (UKPSC 2024) | Political theory of kingship – advice to Muslim rulers
  [104:0:1.6] Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi | Firuz Shah Tughlaq | The Sultan's own account and ordinances
  [104:0:1.7] Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi | Yahya bin Ahmad Sarhindi | Sayyid Sultan Mubarak Shah
  [104:0:1.8] Jawami-ul-Hikayat, Lubab-ul-Albab | Sadiduddin Muhammad Aufi | Earliest reference to the magnetic compass in Indian seas (JPSC 2016)
[104:0:2] - **Matches asked:** Futuh-us-Salatin – **Isami**; Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi – **Firuz Shah**; Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi – **Barani**; Khazain-ul-Futuh – **Khusrau** (UP RO/ARO 2023). Barani – Tarikh-i-Firuzshahi; Hasan Nizami – Taj-ul-Maasir; Minhaj – Tabaqat-i-Nasiri; Yahya – Tarikh-i-Mubarakshahi (UPPSC 1997).
[104:0:3] - **Periods covered, in order:** Taj-ul-Maasir → Tabaqat-i-Nasiri → Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi → Tabaqat-i-Akbari.
[104:0:4] - **Tabaqat-i-Nasiri:** **23 volumes** (tabaqat); English translation by **H.G. Raverty**.
[104:0:5] TABLE head: Later work | Author / note
  [104:0:5.0] Tabaqat-i-Akbari | Nizamuddin Ahmad (not Badauni)
  [104:0:5.1] Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh | Badauni
  [104:0:5.2] Fawaid-ul-Fawad | Amir Hasan Sijzi – conversations of Nizamuddin Auliya
  [104:0:5.3] Tarikh-i-Firishta (Gulshan-i-Ibrahimi) | Firishta; dedicated to Ibrahim Adil Shah of Bijapur; calls Telangana "Tilang"
  [104:0:5.4] Muntakhab-ul-Lubab | Khafi Khan – Aurangzeb's conquest of Golconda
  [104:0:5.5] Burhan-i-Maasir | Deccan history; Sadashivaraya's income 12 crore hons
[104:0:6] - **⚠ Not:** Kitab-ul-Hind ≠ Firdausi (Firdausi = Shahnama); Futuh-us-Salatin ≠ Khusrau.
[104:0:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 03 p.52; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.29-30; app notes 1:104 (sub 1)
## SUB 1 | Foreign Travellers – Origin, Ruler and Order of Arrival
[104:1:0] TABLE head: Traveller | Origin | Visited / ruler | Note
  [104:1:0.0] Al-Biruni | Khwarazm – present Uzbekistan | With Mahmud of Ghazni, 11th c. | Kitab-ul-Hind (Arabic)
  [104:1:0.1] Marco Polo | Venice (Italy) | Motupalli, 1292, Rudramadevi's reign | First foreign reference to a female ruler in India
  [104:1:0.2] Ibn Battuta | Morocco (born Tangier, 1304) | Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1333); made Qazi of Delhi, envoy to China | Rihla – Arabic, 14th c.; espionage, postal system, sati, slave markets
  [104:1:0.3] Nicolo Conti | Venice (Italy) | Vijayanagara c. 1420, Deva Raya I | Oil lamps at Diwali
  [104:1:0.4] Abdur Razzaq | Persia; envoy of Shah Rukh | Deva Raya II, 1443-44 | Rich city
  [104:1:0.5] Afanasy Nikitin | Russia (Tver), horse merchant | Bahmani kingdom under Muhammad Shah III (1469-74) | Vijayanagara then under Virupaksha Raya II
  [104:1:0.6] Duarte Barbosa | Portugal | Vijayanagara, Krishnadeva Raya | 
  [104:1:0.7] Domingo Paes | Portugal | c. 1520, Krishnadeva Raya | City as large as Rome
  [104:1:0.8] Nuniz | Portugal | Achyuta Deva Raya | 
  [104:1:0.9] Seydi Ali Reis | Turkey (Ottoman admiral) | Humayun, 1555 | 
  [104:1:0.10] Mahmud Wali Balkhi | Balkh – Afghanistan | 1620s | Lived like a sanyasi
  [104:1:0.11] Tavernier | France – jeweller (not Dutch) | Golconda, 17th c. (Abdullah Qutb Shah) | Diamond mines of Andhra
  [104:1:0.12] Mir Zainul Abidin | Persia | Muhammad Qutb Shah (1614) | 
  [104:1:0.13] Niccolao Manucci | Venice | Arrived 1656; artilleryman under Dara Shikoh | Storia do Mogor
[104:1:1] - **Match (APPSC G1 2017):** Al-Biruni – **Uzbekistan**; Ibn Battuta – **Morocco**; Mahmud Wali Balkhi – **Afghanistan**; Seydi Ali Reis – **Turkey**.
[104:1:2] - **Order of arrival (UPPSC 1997):** **Al-Biruni (c. 1017-30) → Ibn Battuta (1333) → Tavernier (from 1640) → Manucci (1656)**.
[104:1:3] - **"Greatest traveller of pre-modern times":** **Ibn Battuta** – about **30 years** on the road, about **44 modern countries**, about **73,000 miles** (far more than Marco Polo) (IAS 1993).
[104:1:4] - **Robert Sewell**, **A Forgotten Empire** – based on **Paes, Nuniz and Abdur Razzaq**.
[104:1:5] - **Other:** **Itsing** (China) saw students memorise Nagarjuna's Suhrllekha.
[104:1:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.29, p.47; app notes 1:104 (sub 2, 5); Britannica "Ibn Battuta"
## SUB 2 | Al-Biruni and Kitab-ul-Hind
[104:2:0] - **Came to India with Mahmud of Ghazni** (UKPSC 2010) – 11th century; native of **Khwarazm (Khiva)**, present **Uzbekistan**.
[104:2:1] - **Kitab-ul-Hind = Tahqiq-i-Hind** (Tahqiq ma li'l-Hind) – written in **Arabic**, c. **1030** (APPSC G2 2011).
[104:2:2] - **Learned Sanskrit**; studied Indian religion, philosophy, astronomy, caste – **first Muslim scholar to study the Puranas** (UP Lower 2002).
[104:2:3] - **Diwali** recorded on **Kartika Amavasya**.
[104:2:4] - Mahmud also patronised **Firdausi** (Shahnama) and **Utbi** (Kitab-ul-Yamini).
[104:2:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.29; app notes 1:104 (sub 2); Britannica "al-Biruni"
## SUB 3 | Regional and Sanskrit Sources
[104:3:0] TABLE head: Work | Author | Subject
  [104:3:0.0] Rajatarangini ("River of Kings") | Kalhana (APPSC FBO) | History of Kashmir (MPPSC 2012); 12th c., 8 tarangas; completed c. 1148-49 under King Jayasimha (Jaisingh) of Kashmir (UPPSC 2010)
  [104:3:0.1] Ramacharitam | Sandhyakara Nandi, 12th c. | Double-meaning poem: Ramayana + Pala king Ramapala; records the Kaivarta (Kaivartha) peasant revolt against the Pala prince (CDS 2003)
  [104:3:0.2] Prithviraja Vijaya | Jayanaka | Life of Prithviraj Chauhan
  [104:3:0.3] Prithviraj Raso | Chand Bardai | 
  [104:3:0.4] Chachnama | Muhammad Ali bin Abu Bakr Kufi | Arab conquest of Sindh (Persian)
  [104:3:0.5] Madhura Vijayam | Gangadevi | Kampana's conquest of Madurai; Madurai under Tughlaq (Madurai Sultanate) rule
  [104:3:0.6] Hadikat-us-Salatin | Ali bin Tahir Bustani | Qutb Shahis
  [104:3:0.7] Tarikh Muhammad Qutb Shah / Basatin-us-Salatin | Anonymous (1617) / Mirza Ibrahim Zuberi | Qutb Shahis
  [104:3:0.8] History of the Qutb Shahi Dynasty | H.K. Sherwani | Modern
[104:3:1] - **⚠ Pairs:** Prithviraj Raso = **Chand Bardai**; Prithviraja Vijaya = **Jayanaka**; Hasan Nizami = Taj-ul-Maasir, not Rajatarangini.
[104:3:2] ~~ Sources: app notes 1:104 (sub 4); Britannica "Rajatarangini", "Kalhana"
## SUB 4 | Calligraphy, Architecture and Painting as Sources
[104:4:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [104:4:0.0] Nastaliq | Persian (Perso-Arabic) script of medieval India – used for Persian texts (UPSC 1996) – not a raga, a cess or an ulema code
  [104:4:0.1] Naskh | Script for Quranic verses (Qutb Shahi Jami Masjid mihrab)
  [104:4:0.2] Trabeate → arcuate | Shift to true arch, dome, lime mortar
[104:4:1] - **Golconda painting:** founded by **Mir Hashimi**; manuscript "**Quliyat Quli**" has **14 miniatures**.
[104:4:2] - **Diwali evidence:** Al-Biruni, Nicolo Conti, Ain-i-Akbari.
[104:4:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture p.220; app notes 1:104 (sub 7)

  [104:6:0.3] Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri | Jahangir | Autobiography

## SUB 7 | Using the Sources – Bias and Cross-checking
[104:7:0] - **Foreign accounts supplement** Indian texts and must be **cross-verified** with inscriptions and archaeology.
[104:7:1] - **Court bias:** chroniclers wrote for rewards and glorified the patron; **Amir Khusrau** – court poet of Alauddin, went with **Malik Kafur's 1310** Warangal campaign.
[104:7:2] - **Barani:** orthodox **Sunni** view; theorised kingship.
[104:7:3] - Firishta's story of **Deva Raya kidnapping Nehal** – **rejected** by modern historians.
[104:7:4] TABLE head: Source group | Warangal invasions counted
  [104:7:4.0] Telugu (Pratapa Charitra, Vilasa, Kaluvacheru) | 8
  [104:7:4.1] Muslim (Amir Khusrau, Wassaf) | 5
[104:7:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 03 p.52; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.29; app notes 1:104 (sub 0, 8)

=== NOTES 1:106 | Khalji Dynasty - Jalaluddin, Alauddin's Conquests, Malik Kafur's Deccan Campaigns
## SUB 0 | Mongol Invasions – Kili, the Siege of Delhi and the Ravi Frontier
[106:0:0] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [106:0:0.0] 1221 | Chengiz Khan reached the Indus under Iltutmish, chasing Mangbarni – the first Mongol threat; he did not cross the Indus (CDS 2020)
  [106:0:0.1] Jalaluddin (1292) | Beat a Mongol force under Abdullah; converts settled as "New Mussalmans"
  [106:0:0.2] 1297-98 | Jalandhar – Mongols beaten (Ulugh Khan, Zafar Khan)
  [106:0:0.3] 1299 | Battle of Kili (third invasion of Alauddin's reign) – Mongols under Qutlugh Khwaja; Zafar Khan killed fighting them (BPSC 1996)
  [106:0:0.4] 1303 | Targhi besieged Delhi; Alauddin sheltered in Siri fort
  [106:0:0.5] 1305 | Amroha – Ali Beg and Tartaq (Khwaja Tash) beaten by Malik Kafur and Ghazi Malik
  [106:0:0.6] 1306 | Kabak beaten on the Ravi by Kafur and Ghazi Malik → Ravi = Sultanate–Mongol boundary after 1306 (UPPSC 2014)
[106:0:1] - **UPSC 2022:** "first Mongol invasion under Jalaluddin" – **false**; "a Mongol assault besieged Delhi under Alauddin" – **true**; "Muhammad bin Tughluq lost parts of the north-west to the Mongols" – **false** (he bought off Tarmashirin) → **B only**.
[106:0:2] - **Defence:** repaired and built north-west forts (completing **Balban's** policy); new capital **Siri**; **large standing army**; **Ghazi Malik** warden of the marches, said to have beaten the Mongols **29** times.
[106:0:3] - **Later:** **Timur** sacked Delhi in **1398** (Nasiruddin Mahmud Tughlaq).
[106:0:4] - **⚠** **Zafar Khan** died at **Kili**; **Nusrat Khan** died at **Ranthambore**.
[106:0:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.36-37, p.52 (UPSC 2022 answer "2 only"); NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 03 p.61; app notes 1:106 (sub 5)
## SUB 1 | Malik Kafur and the Deccan Campaigns
[106:1:0] - **Origin:** a eunuch slave seized at **Cambay** by **Nusrat Khan** in the **Gujarat campaign (1299)** and presented to Alauddin; called **Hazar Dinari** because his first master had **bought him for 1,000 dinars**; rose to **Malik Naib**.
[106:1:1] - **Commander** of all of Alauddin's **Deccan campaigns** (WBCS 2020).
[106:1:2] TABLE head: Year | Kingdom | Ruler | Result
  [106:1:2.0] 1307-08 | Devagiri (Yadava) | Ramachandra | Taken to Delhi; vassal, tribute
  [106:1:2.1] 1309-10 | Warangal (Kakatiya) | Prataparudra II | Treaty and annual tribute; loot on 1,000 camels
  [106:1:2.2] 1310-11 | Dwarasamudra (Hoysala) | Vira Ballala III | Submitted
  [106:1:2.3] 1311 | Madurai (Pandya) | Vira Pandya / Sundara Pandya | Sacked; Kakatiya troops aided Kafur
[106:1:3] - **Order:** **Devagiri → Warangal → Dwarasamudra → Madurai**.
[106:1:4] - **Pairs (UPPSC 2018):** Devagiri – Ramachandra; Hoysala – Vira Ballala; Madurai – Vira Pandya; **Warangal – Prataparudra II, not Shankar Dev** (Shankaradeva was Ramachandra's Yadava son).
[106:1:5] - **Aim:** **wealth and tribute, not annexation** – "financial ventures" (K.S. Lal); so in "A: financial ventures, R: wanted to annex" → **A true, R false** (UPPSC 1997). Annexation came only under **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**.
[106:1:6] - **Significance (CDS 2013):** boldness and spirit of adventure, **untold wealth** brought to Delhi, **fresh geographical knowledge** of the south, and Kafur's elevation as **Malik Naib**.
[106:1:7] - **Koh-i-Noor:** a later popular tradition only; no contemporary record.
[106:1:8] # AP Angle: Kakatiya–Delhi Relations
[106:1:9] - **1303:** first attack on Warangal by **Malik Fakhruddin Juna** (with Malik Chhajju) **failed at Upparapalli** – the **Kakatiya army defeated Alauddin's army** (UPPSC 2017); victors **Potuganti Maili** and **Recherla Venna**.
[106:1:10] - **1309-10:** **Kafur** with **Khwaja Haji** besieged Warangal; **Amir Khusrau** went along – Khazain-ul-Futuh: **double-walled fort** with a **moat**.
[106:1:11] - Tribute **stopped after 1316**; **third invasion (1318)** by **Khusrau Khan** under Mubarak Shah. Telugu sources count **8** invasions.
[106:1:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 03 p.60; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.38-39; app notes 1:106 (sub 4), 1:107 (sub 6); examrobot.com CDS-I 2013 Q34
## SUB 2 | Alauddin's Conquests in Order
[106:2:0] TABLE head: Year | Kingdom | Ruler | Note
  [106:2:0.0] 1299 | Gujarat (Vaghela) | Rai Karan (Karnadeva II) | Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan; Somnath plundered; queen Kamala Devi taken; Kafur acquired
  [106:2:0.1] c. 1299 | Jaisalmer | Bhatti Rajputs | Raided on the way to Gujarat (PMF)
  [106:2:0.2] 1301 | Ranthambore | Hammir Deva Chauhan (sheltered New Mussalmans) | First siege 1299 failed, Nusrat Khan killed; Alauddin took it in person
  [106:2:0.3] 1303 | Chittor (Mewar) | Rana Ratan Singh | Renamed Khizrabad
  [106:2:0.4] 1305 | Malwa | Mahlak Deva | Ain-ul-Mulk Multani; Ujjain, Mandu, Dhar, Chanderi
  [106:2:0.5] c. 1308-11 | Siwana, Jalore | Shital Deva (Siwana) | Rajputana completed
  [106:2:0.6] 1309-10 | Warangal | Prataparudra II | Malik Kafur
[106:2:1] - **Chronology asked:** **Gujarat → Ranthambore → Chittor → Warangal** (UPPSC 2022); **Jaisalmer → Ranthambore → Chittor → Warangal** (UPPSC 2025).
[106:2:2] - **Statements (AP paper):** conquests **began with Gujarat (1299)**; **Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan** sacked **Somnath**; **Ranthambore** was the first **main** target in Rajasthan.
[106:2:3] - **Events in order:** **Gujarat (1299) → Mongols under Ali Beg and Tartaq (1305) → Kafur sacks the Pandyas (1311) → Yadava kingdom annexed (1313 by Kafur; finally 1318)**.
[106:2:4] - **Policy:** **north annexed**; **south** – kings kept thrones and **paid tribute**.
[106:2:5] - **First Turkish invasion of the south:** Alauddin's **Devagiri** raid (**1296**) as governor of Kara.
[106:2:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 03 p.60-61; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.36, p.38, p.41; app notes 1:106 (sub 3)
## SUB 3 | Alauddin – Rise, Titles, Nobles and Kingship
[106:3:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [106:3:0.0] Ali Gurshasp | Earlier name
  [106:3:0.1] Amir-i-Tuzuk | Master of ceremonies (post under Jalaluddin)
  [106:3:0.2] Ariz-i-Mumalik | Army minister (post under Jalaluddin)
  [106:3:0.3] Sikandar-i-Sani | "Second Alexander", on his coins
[106:3:1] - **Nobles:** **Ulugh Khan, Nusrat Khan, Zafar Khan, Ain-ul-Mulk Multani, Malik Kafur, Ghazi Malik**; court poet **Amir Khusrau**. **Munim Khan** was **Akbar's** noble, not Alauddin's (CDS 2007).
[106:3:2] - **Ain-ul-Mulk Multani** served **Alauddin** (Malwa 1305) and later Sultans; he could **not** have served **Iltutmish** (d. 1236) (MPPSC 2017).
[106:3:3] - **Ambitions:** world conquest and a **new religion** – dropped on the advice of the **Kotwal Ala-ul-Mulk** (Barani's uncle).
[106:3:4] - **Kingship:** told **Qazi Mughisuddin of Bayana** he acted in the **interest of the state**, not by the ulema; revived **Balban's** harsh centralised rule without religious sanction.
[106:3:5] - **Barani** separated **Shariat** from **Zawabit** (state laws made by the ruler).
[106:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 03 p.59-61; app notes 1:106 (sub 2), 1:107 (sub 5)
## SUB 4 | Sultans' Reigns and the End of the Khaljis
[106:4:0] TABLE head: Sultan | Reign
  [106:4:0.0] Jalaluddin Khalji | 1290-1296
  [106:4:0.1] Alauddin Khalji | 1296-1316
  [106:4:0.2] Muhammad bin Tughlaq | 1325-1351 (exam option "1324-1351")
  [106:4:0.3] Khizr Khan (Sayyid) | 1414-1421
  [106:4:0.4] Bahlol Lodi | 1451-1489 (not 1491)
[106:4:1] - **⚠ Two Khizr Khans:** Alauddin's son (set aside 1316) ≠ the Sayyid Sultan.
[106:4:2] - **After 1316:** **Kafur** set aside Khizr Khan and enthroned minor **Shihabuddin Umar** → Kafur killed → **Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah** (1316-20, last Khalji) → murdered by **Khusrau Khan** (Nasiruddin Khusrau Shah).
[106:4:3] - **1320:** **Ghazi Malik**, Alauddin's general and governor of the Punjab, killed Khusrau Khan and became **Ghiyasuddin Tughluq** – **first Tughlaq Sultan** (UPPSC 1999).
[106:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 03 p.63; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.28-29, p.41; app notes 1:106 (sub 0, 7)
## SUB 5 | Jalaluddin Khalji (1290-1296)
[106:5:0] - Khalji of **Turkestan** stock; crowned himself at **Kilokhari (1290)** at about **70**.
[106:5:1] - **First Sultan with a benevolent attitude to Hindus**; lenient to rebels such as **Malik Chhajju**.
[106:5:2] - Married his daughter to **Ulugh Khan**, a descendant of **Chengiz Khan**; settled Mongol converts as **New Mussalmans**.
[106:5:3] - **Murdered at Kara (1296)** by his nephew and son-in-law **Alauddin**.
[106:5:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 03 p.58; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.35-36
## SUB 6 | Chittor and the Padmini Legend
[106:6:0] - **1303:** Alauddin defeated **Rana Ratan Singh**; **Rani Padmini**, his wife, and the Rajput women performed **jauhar** (State PSC).
[106:6:1] TABLE head: Book | Author | Year / language
  [106:6:1.0] Padmavat | Malik Muhammad Jayasi | 1540, Awadhi (early Hindi)
[106:6:2] - **CDS 2009:** "Jayasi wrote Padmavat in Hindi" – correct; "**Muhammad Shah (1719-48)** was the first Mughal ruler to patronise **Urdu**" – correct in the key → **both**.
[106:6:3] - **Debate:** written over two centuries later; many historians treat the Padmini motive as legend.
[106:6:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.38-39; app notes 1:106 (sub 6)

=== NOTES 1:113 | Sultanate Economy – Kharaj, Jizya, Zakat, Khams; Agriculture, Towns, Trade and Craft
## SUB 0 | Sharia Taxes and Cesses
[113:0:0] TABLE head: Tax | Nature | Payer
  [113:0:0.0] Kharaj | Land tax, usually 1/3 (up to 1/2) of produce | Non-Muslim cultivators
  [113:0:0.1] Ushr | Land tax, 1/10 (5-10%) of produce | Muslim landholders
  [113:0:0.2] Jizya | Poll / protection tax in place of military service | Non-Muslims
  [113:0:0.3] Zakat | Religious tax, about 2.5% of wealth | Muslims only
  [113:0:0.4] Khams (Khums) | State's 1/5 share of war booty (and treasure-troves) | Army booty
[113:0:1] - **Taxes on land produce:** kharaj, ushr (and other land levies) – **not khams**, which is war booty.
[113:0:2] - Khams: **Alauddin and MBT took 4/5** of booty; **Firoz restored the sharia 1/5**.
[113:0:3] - **Firoz Tughlaq** kept only the four sharia taxes – **kharaj, jizya, zakat, khams** – abolished about 24 cesses (incl. ghari, charai) and added **haq-i-sharb**.
[113:0:4] TABLE head: Cess | Nature | Sultan
  [113:0:4.0] Ghari | House tax (first levied) | Alauddin
  [113:0:4.1] Charai | Grazing tax on milch cattle | Alauddin
  [113:0:4.2] Haq-i-sharb (sharb) | Irrigation tax, 10% of yield, on the ulema's advice | Firoz
[113:0:5] - **Abwab** = **miscellaneous cesses** outside the sharia, such as house tax, grazing tax, irrigation tax.
[113:0:6] - **Jizya** under **Aurangzeb** reimposed in 1679 (Akbar had abolished it).
[113:0:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.60 (taxes table, jizya); NextGen Indian History - APPSC 05 p.12 (Firoz, Alauddin cesses); Rocket Indian History 01 p.82-83; app notes 1:113 (sub 0, 1)
## SUB 1 | Land Revenue Demand
[113:1:0] - Peasants usually paid **one-third**; **Alauddin Khalji raised it to one-half** of the produce (kharaj 50%), measured the land and collected directly.
[113:1:1] - **MBT** raised taxes in the **Doab** during a famine; neither Alauddin nor MBT took one-sixth – so "one-sixth" statements are **false** (CDS 2005).
[113:1:2] - **Alauddin** held a religious discourse with the Jain **Acharya Mahasena** (Jain tradition) – CDS 2005 statement I true.
[113:1:3] - **NDA 2002:** Alauddin **fixed grain prices**, **paid soldiers in cash** and **raised revenue to half** – all three correct.
[113:1:4] - **Land categories:** **khalisa** (crown), **iqta** (assigned in place of salary), **inam** (religious grants).
[113:1:5] - **MBT:** **taccavi (sondhar)** loans to extend cultivation; first Sultan to organise **famine relief** (loans, relief, Swargadwari camp).
[113:1:6] - Alauddin's price-control markets show that **military needs shaped economic policy**.
[113:1:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.59-60; Rocket Indian History 01 p.82 (Alauddin 50%); NextGen Indian History - APPSC 03 p.61, p.65; app notes 1:113 (sub 1, 2)
## SUB 2 | Coins of the Sultanate
[113:2:0] TABLE head: Coin | Metal | Sultan
  [113:2:0.0] Tanka | Silver, 175 grains (about 11 g) | Iltutmish
  [113:2:0.1] Jital | Copper (48 jitals = 1 tanka) | Iltutmish
  [113:2:0.2] Shashgani | Silver, worth 6 jitals | Tughlaqs
  [113:2:0.3] Dinar | Gold, popular after the South Indian loot | Alauddin
  [113:2:0.4] Token | Copper / brass (1329-30), at par with silver; failed through forgery | MBT
  [113:2:0.5] Bahloli | Copper | Bahlol Lodi
[113:2:1] - **Iltutmish:** first Sultan to issue a **regular standard currency** and to make **Delhi the capital**; he also set up the **iqtadari** system.
[113:2:2] - The **two basic Sultanate coins** = **silver tanka and copper jital**; **rupiya and dam** are Sher Shah's (Rupiya 178 grains, **173 pure silver**; 1 rupiya = **64 dams**).
[113:2:3] - **Dehliwal** = pre-Sultanate coin of the Tomaras and Chauhans. **Ghori**'s gold coins bore **Lakshmi**.
[113:2:4] - Sher Shah's revenue system was the model for **Todar Mal's bandobast**.
[113:2:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.62 (Iltutmish coins); NextGen Indian History - APPSC 03 p.56 (tanka); app notes 1:113 (sub 3)
## SUB 3 | Agriculture and Irrigation
[113:3:0] - **Araghatta** = **water-wheel for irrigation** – a large **wheel with earthen pots tied to the outer ends of its spokes** (ara = spokes, ghata = pot), **animal-driven**, lifting water from **open wells**; in the **Panchatantra** and **Rajatarangini**. Turks spread the **Persian wheel (saqiya)**.
[113:3:1] - Crops of the 13th-14th c.: wheat, barley, gram, rice, sugarcane, cotton, oilseeds; **maize was not grown** (brought later by the **Portuguese**), nor **tobacco**.
[113:3:2] - **Canals:** **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq** = first canal-builder; **Firoz Tughlaq** = **most canals** (longest Yamuna → **Hisar**).
[113:3:3] - **MBT:** Diwan-i-Kohi and taccavi; **Firoz:** 1,200 orchards near Delhi.
[113:3:4] - **AP angle:** Kakatiya **Maagani** = irrigated land, **Metta** = dry land; land tax **Ari**.
[113:3:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (Araghatta table); NextGen Indian History - APPSC 03 p.72 (Persian wheel); app notes 1:113 (sub 2)
## SUB 4 | Towns, Crafts and Trade
[113:4:0] - **Towns:** Lahore, Multan, Broach, Cambay grew; Siri (Alauddin), Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah (MBT), Hisar, Firozabad, Jaunpur (Firoz), **Agra (Sikandar Lodi, 1504; later a Mughal imperial centre)**. Firoz took about **1,300 Sanskrit manuscripts** from the Jawalamukhi temple, **Nagarkot**.
[113:4:1] - **Royal karkhanas:** Firoz ran about **36**, with thousands of slaves.
[113:4:2] - **Crafts:** textiles, **leather, metal-work, carpet-weaving**; Turkish gains – **paper** (record-keeping), glass, **spinning wheel**, Persian wheel, arch and dome mortar.
[113:4:3] - **Trade:** **Multanis and Khurasanis** – overseas trade and finance; **Gujaratis, Marwaris, Bohras** – inland trade; **Banjaras** carried grain on oxen.
[113:4:4] - **Imports:** horses, textiles, glassware from **West Asia**; silk and porcelain from **China**. Ibn Battuta: Malabar **pepper**.
[113:4:5] - **Amir Khusrau:** Warangal's wealth and **diamonds** drew the Delhi invasions.
[113:4:6] - **Society in brief:** ulema kept the religious law; **khuts and muqaddams** collected peasants' revenue; caste continued, **sati and purdah** spread; slave markets (Ibn Battuta), Firoz's slave department.
[113:4:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC 03 p.71-72; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.58; app notes 1:113 (sub 4, 5, 6)

=== NOTES 1:117 | Provincial Kingdoms – Bahmani Sultanate and Mahmud Gawan; Bengal, Gujarat, Malwa, Jaunpur, Kashmir
## SUB 0 | Jaunpur – the Sharqi Kingdom
[117:0:0] - **City:** founded by **Firoz Shah Tughlaq**, named after his cousin **Muhammad bin Tughlaq (Jauna Khan)**.
[117:0:1] - **Kingdom:** **Malik Sarwar** (Khwaja Jahan, title **Malik-us-Sharq**, "Lord of the East") made it independent in **1394**; **Jaunpur** was the Sharqi capital.
[117:0:2] - **Shiraz-i-Hind:** Jaunpur was called the "**Shiraz of India / of the East**" as a great **centre of learning**, at its height under **Ibrahim Shah Sharqi (1402–40)**.
[117:0:3] - **End:** last ruler **Hussain Shah Sharqi**; **Bahlul Lodi** conquered Jaunpur in **1479** – his main achievement.
[117:0:4] TABLE head: Monument | Builder
  [117:0:4.0] Atala Masjid (1408) | Begun under Firoz Tughlaq (1376), completed by Ibrahim Shah Sharqi – massive propylon
  [117:0:4.1] Jama Masjid, Jaunpur | Sharqi rulers
  [117:0:4.2] Lal Darwaza Mosque | Bibi Raje (Sharqi queen)
[117:0:5] - **Music:** the Sharqi court patronised **Khyal**; Sufi musician **Pir Bodhan** under **Husain Shah Sharqi** (not Ibrahim).
[117:0:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History Rocket Sheets #4, #16; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 3 p.235, p.237; PMF IAS Indian Art & Culture p.313; app notes 1:117 (sub 5)
## SUB 1 | Bahmani Sultanate and the Vijayanagara Wars
[117:1:0] - **Founder:** **Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah** (**Hasan Gangu**, Zafar Khan) revolted against **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** – **1347**; the **first independent Muslim kingdom of the Deccan**.
[117:1:1] - **Capitals:** **Gulbarga** (renamed **Hasanabad**) → **Bidar**, shifted by **Ahmad Shah I (Wali, 1422–36)** after annexing Warangal (not Muhammad Shah I, not Firoz).
[117:1:2] - **Muhammad Shah I (1358–75):** built the **Gulbarga Jama Masjid** (compared to Cordoba); fought Bukka I.
[117:1:3] - **Firuz Shah (1397–1422):** scholar-king, observatory near Daulatabad, Hindus in administration; defeated Deva Raya I.
[117:1:4] - **Last Sultan:** **Kalimullah**; kingdom ended **1527**.
[117:1:5] - **Bone of contention:** the **Raichur Doab** between the **Krishna and Tungabhadra**; also the **Krishna-Godavari delta** and Marathwada.
[117:1:6] - **Gunpowder:** the **first recorded use** of firearms in India was by the **Bahmanis (Muhammad Shah I) against Vijayanagara**, c. **1366–68**; Babur only popularised field artillery (1526).
[117:1:7] - **Bidriware** (Bidar): blackened **zinc alloy inlaid with silver**; under the **Bahmanis**, not Vijayanagara.
[117:1:8] ~~ Sources: PMF IAS Ancient & Medieval India 2nd ed. p.506, p.515-516; NextGen AP History - qutbshahis p.1; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunpowder_weapons_in_the_Bahmani_Sultanate; app notes 1:117 (sub 1)
## SUB 2 | Kashmir – Shah Mir Dynasty and Zain-ul-Abidin
[117:2:0] TABLE head: Ruler | Fact
  [117:2:0.0] Shamsuddin Shah | Founded the Shah Mir line (1339)
  [117:2:0.1] Sikandar (1389–1413) | "Butshikan" (idol-breaker); jizya imposed
  [117:2:0.2] Zain-ul-Abidin (1420–70) | Original name Shahi Khan (brother of Ali Shah); "Bud Shah" and "Akbar of Kashmir"
[117:2:1] - **Tolerance:** **first to abolish jizya** (before Akbar), **banned cow slaughter**, rebuilt temples, called back the Brahmins.
[117:2:2] - **Learning:** **Mahabharata** and **Rajatarangini** translated into Persian; **Jonaraja** continued Kalhana's Rajatarangini.
[117:2:3] - **Works:** **Zaina Lank** island in **Wular** lake; Zaina Kadal bridge.
[117:2:4] - **Jama Masjid, Srinagar** (completed by him): **turrets**, **pagoda-like roofs (Buddhist)** and **Persian style** → **I, II and III**.
[117:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History Rocket Sheets #32, #84; app notes 1:117 (sub 4)
## SUB 3 | Malwa – Mandu
[117:3:0] - **Founder:** **Dilawar Khan Ghuri** made Malwa independent in **1401** (capital **Dhar**); **Hoshang Shah** moved it to **Mandu**.
[117:3:1] - **Mandu** lies in **Dhar district**, MP; "Group of Monuments at Mandu" includes the **Hindola Mahal** (T-shape, sloping walls, "swinging palace") and the **Jahaz Mahal** (between two tanks).
[117:3:2] TABLE head: Ruler | Work
  [117:3:2.0] Hoshang Shah | Capital to Mandu; his tomb = India's first marble tomb; began the Jami Masjid
  [117:3:2.1] Mahmud Khalji (1436–69) | Founded the Khalji line; completed the Jami Masjid, Mandu; Ashrafi Mahal
  [117:3:2.2] Ghiyasuddin Khalji (1469–1500) | Jahaz Mahal and Hindola Mahal (not Hoshang Shah)
  [117:3:2.3] Baz Bahadur | Last Sultan; romance with Rupmati
[117:3:3] - **⚠ MPPSC 2017 "Jantar Mahal":** misprint of **Jahaz Mahal**; with Ghiyasuddin not offered, key **Mahmud Shah Khalji** (his father, in whose reign it was begun) – never Alauddin Khalji of Delhi.
[117:3:4] ~~ Sources: PMF IAS Indian Art & Culture p.313, p.581; https://prod.incredibleindia.gov.in/content/incredible-india-v2/en/destinations/states/madhya-pradesh/top-attraction-and-destinations/mandu-jahaz-mahal.html; app notes 1:117 (sub 6-7)
## SUB 4 | Gujarat Sultanate and the Portuguese

  [117:4:0.2] Mahmud Begarha (1458–1511) | Took Girnar and Champaner ("two forts"); joined Egypt against the Portuguese (Chaul 1508, lost at Diu 1509)
  [117:4:0.3] Bahadur Shah (1526–37) | Annexed Malwa (1531); pressed by Humayun, gave Diu to the Portuguese (1534–35); killed by them on board ship at Diu, 1537

## SUB 6 | Mahmud Gawan
[117:6:0] TABLE head: Angle | Fact
  [117:6:0.0] Office | Persian (Afaqi) noble; wazir of Muhammad Shah III (1463–82); kingdom at its height
  [117:6:0.1] Reform | Divided the 4 tarafs into 8 provinces, each under a tarafdar; forts under central commanders
  [117:6:0.2] Revenue | Nobles' salaries fixed (cash or jagir); land measured and tax fixed; a khalisa tract in every province set apart for the Sultan (not the tarafdar)
  [117:6:0.3] Military | Took Goa (1472); crushed Telangana revolts with Velama help
  [117:6:0.4] Madrasa, Bidar | Three storeys, glazed tiles; Persian (Herat/Samarkand) model
  [117:6:0.5] Letters | *Riyaz-ul-Insha*
  [117:6:0.6] End | Framed by rival nobles; executed 1481 → break-up

## SUB 7 | Bengal Sultanate
[117:7:0] - **Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah** unified Bengal in **1342** with **Pandua** as capital; **Sikandar Shah** built the **Adina Mosque (1373–75)**; **Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah** – **Eklakhi Tomb**.
[117:7:1] - **Hussain Shah (1493–1519)** and Nusrat Shah supported **Bengali Mahabharata** translations; **Chaitanya** lived in Hussain Shah's reign.
[117:7:2] - **Maladhar Basu**, author of *Sri Krishna Vijaya*, received the title **Gunaraj Khan** from the Bengal Sultan (Barbak Shah).
[117:7:3] - **Founding order:** **1342** Bengal – **1347** Bahmani – **1394** Sharqi – **1401** Malwa – **1407** Gujarat.
[117:7:4] ~~ Sources: https://en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Maladhar_Basu; app notes 1:117 (sub 0, 6-7)

2. His letters are collected in the Riyaz-us-Salatin.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
  *1 only | 2 only | Both 1 and 2 | Neither 1 nor 2
  x: Mahmud Gawan took Goa in 1472; his letters are the Riyaz-ul-Insha, while the Riyaz-us-Salatin is a history of Bengal.

  x: Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk founded the Imad Shahi state of Berar (1490), with its capital at Ellichpur.
[f978666d4ba45] sub8

=== NOTES 1:118 | The Five Deccan Sultanates – Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmednagar, Bidar, Berar; Golconda and Andhra
## SUB 0 | Kohinoor, Golconda Diamonds and the English at Machilipatnam
[118:0:0] # Kohinoor – the most-asked fact of this topic
[118:0:1] - **Mine:** the **Kohinoor** came from the **Kollur (Kolluru)** mine on the **Krishna** (Guntur / Palnadu) – APPSC G2 2011; AP History PYQ ×2. Not Paritala, Gollapalli, Malapalli, Panna or Hazaribagh.
[118:0:2] - **Kingdom:** Kollur lay in the **Golconda** kingdom, so "excavated from the mines of" = **Golconda** (SSC 2006) – not Bijapur, Odisha or Chota Nagpur.
[118:0:3] - **Found:** **1656** (NextGen); it is now in the British Crown Jewels.
[118:0:4] - **Presented to Shah Jahan by:** **Mir Jumla**, minister of **Abdullah Qutb Shah**, who went over to the Mughals (UPPSC 2015 ×2) – not Aurangzeb, Murad or Abul Hasan.
[118:0:5] - **⚠ Trap:** **Tavernier**, the **French** jeweller who visited the mines under **Abdullah Qutb Shah** and wrote *Six Travels*, only **recorded** the Kohinoor; he did not give it.
[118:0:6] - **Duarte Barbosa** (Portuguese, early 16th c.) also described the region's **diamond trade**; Tavernier gave the fullest account.
[118:0:7] # Golconda diamond mines and trade
[118:0:8] TABLE head: Mine | Region
  [118:0:8.0] Kollur | Krishna river, Guntur – the Kohinoor
  [118:0:8.1] Paritala | Krishna district
  [118:0:8.2] Ramalla Kota | Kurnool – 3 lakh pagodas a year
  [118:0:8.3] Vajra Karur | Anantapur
[118:0:9] - Diamonds were traded at **Moti Darwaza** (Golconda) and polished at **Karwan** (west of Charminar); mines were given on lease.
[118:0:10] - **Latest:** the **Golconda Blue** diamond (**23.24 ct**, fancy vivid blue, pear-shaped) was in the news in **May 2025**; Machilipatnam port works revive the old **Gilakaladindi** port.
[118:0:11] # Europeans at Machilipatnam
[118:0:12] TABLE head: Company | Machilipatnam factory
  [118:0:12.0] Dutch | 1605 – first European factory in Andhra, under Muhammad Quli
  [118:0:12.1] English | 1611 – Captain Hippon, ship Globe; permission of Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
[118:0:13] - **Who allowed the English factory (1611):** **Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah** (1580–1612) – APPSC G2 2008 ×2; 2023 screening; AP History PYQ ×2. Not Ibrahim (died 1580), Abdullah (from 1626), Sultan Muhammad or Jamshid.
[118:0:14] - **Golden Farman (Bangaru Farmana):** **Abdullah Qutb Shah** gave the English trading rights (1632 in the old notes; NextGen dates it 1636).
[118:0:15] - Machilipatnam was famous for **muslin and Kalamkari** and was the outlet for Golconda diamonds; **Narsapuram** (Godavari delta) was the chief **shipbuilding** port.
[118:0:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History - Qutb Shahis p.7-8, p.13-14; NextGen Rocket Sheets AP History; app notes 1:118 (sub 7)
## SUB 1 | Qutb Shahi Rulers – Founder to Tana Shah
[118:1:0] # Basics
[118:1:1] - **1518–1687**, **7 rulers**, **Shia**; **Qara Qoyunlu (Black Sheep) Turkmen** from **Hamadan**; official language **Persian**; capital **Golconda** (old name **Mankal**), from 1592 **Hyderabad**.
[118:1:2] - **"From where did the Qutb Shahis rule":** **Golconda** (G2-B 1991). **Golconda today** lies in **Hyderabad** (MPPSC 1990).
[118:1:3] # The seven rulers
[118:1:4] TABLE head: Ruler | Key facts
  [118:1:4.0] Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk (1518–43) | Founder (Bahmani Tarafdar of Golconda from 1496; title Qutb-ul-Mulk named the dynasty; independent 1518); 31 years counted from 1512; strengthened Golconda fort, built Golconda Jama Masjid; took Rachakonda, Devarakonda, Warangal (from Shitab Khan), Rajahmundry, Eluru, Kovilakonda; killed by son Jamsheed
  [118:1:4.1] Jamsheed (1543–50) | Patricide; won Battle of Koulan over Bidar (1544); created cabinet – Wakil, Peshwa, Mir Jumla; then minor son Subhan Quli
  [118:1:4.2] Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah (1550–80) | 7 years exile at Vijayanagara; title Malkibharama; chief Telugu patron; Talikota (1565) ally; Hussain Sagar (1562); first Qutb Shahi coins; high walls, 87 towers and 8 gates of Golconda; "Second Egypt"; gained Kondavidu after 1565
  [118:1:4.3] Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah (1580–1612) | Ascended 1580 at 14; founded Hyderabad (1591); Charminar, Dar-ul-Shifa (1595), Jama Masjid; Dakhni/Urdu poet "Maani" (*Kulliyat-e-Quli*); Dutch (1605) and English (1611) at Machilipatnam
  [118:1:4.4] Sultan Muhammad Qutb Shah (1612–26) | Nephew and son-in-law of Muhammad Quli; began Mecca Masjid (1614); pen name Zillullah
  [118:1:4.5] Abdullah Qutb Shah (1626–72) | Longest reign; with mother Hayat Bakshi Begum; Inqiyad Nama (1636) – accepted Mughal suzerainty; Bangaru Farmana to the English; Kshetrayya; Tavernier
  [118:1:4.6] Abul Hasan Tana Shah (1672–87) | Last ruler; Madanna–Akkanna; treaty with Shivaji (1677); Peshwa renamed Diwan
[118:1:5] - **Founder of the Golconda dynasty:** **(Sultan) Quli Qutb Shah** – not Jamshed, Subhan or Ibrahim.
[118:1:6] - **Malkibharama / Malikibharam:** **Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah** (G1 2002; G1 PYQ) – a title from his subjects for tolerant rule; coinage does not explain it.
[118:1:7] - **Last king:** **Abul Hasan Tana Shah** (G1 PYQ) – title "Tanisha" from Sufi saint Shah Raju Qattal.
[118:1:8] - **How long Quli Qutb Shah ruled:** **31 years** (1512–1543; Deputy EO screening). ⚠ From formal independence (1518) it is only 25 years.
[118:1:9] - **Built by Muhammad Quli:** **Hyderabad city, Charminar, Jama Masjid** – **not Golconda** fort, which was a Kakatiya fort (Mankal) rebuilt by Sultan Quli and Ibrahim (G1 2003).
[118:1:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History - Qutb Shahis p.1-9; Wikipedia, Sultanate of Golconda (1512–1543); app notes 1:118 (sub 1, 2)
## SUB 2 | Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur – Jagadguru and Kitab-i-Nauras
[118:2:0] # Ibrahim Adil Shah II (1580–1627)
[118:2:1] - **"Jagadguru":** hailed so by his subjects for his **mixed-faith (secular) outlook** and support of Hindu scholars (UPSC 2000 ×3) – not Zain-ul-Abidin (Kashmir), Husain Shah (Bengal) or Mahmud II.
[118:2:2] - ***Kitab-i-Nauras*** (Book of Nine Rasas): written by **Ibrahim Adil Shah II** in **Dakhni** – songs to **Saraswati, Ganesha** and Muslim saints; **59 songs, 17 couplets** (UPPSC 2020).
[118:2:3] - **UPSC 2003 statements:** Kitab-i-Nauras by Ibrahim Adil Shah II ✓; **Amir Khusrau** originated the early **Qawwali** in India ✓ → **both correct** (asked ×3).
[118:2:4] - Founded **Nauraspur**; **Firishta** dedicated his history to him; a painter of the **Deccan Ragamala**; married **Chand Sultana** (Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah's sister).
[118:2:5] - **Bangab Nama** ("Book of the Pot Smoker"), a Dakhni poem praising bhang, was written by **Mahmud Bahri** of Bijapur (G1 PYQ) – not either Ibrahim Adil Shah or Namdev.
[118:2:6] # Patrons – who supported what
[118:2:7] TABLE head: Patron | Supported
  [118:2:7.0] Ibrahim Adil Shah II | Arts, music, painting
  [118:2:7.1] Satavahanas | Prakrit; Buddhist architecture
  [118:2:7.2] Rudradaman I | Sanskrit (Junagadh inscription), not Telugu
  [118:2:7.3] Krishnadeva Raya | Telugu literature
  [118:2:7.4] Rana Kumbha | Music, literature, art
  [118:2:7.5] Zain-ul-Abidin | Translation
  [118:2:7.6] Jahangir | Painting; European and Persian arts
  [118:2:7.7] Sawant Singh | Kishangarh painting

## SUB 3 | Bijapur – Gol Gumbaz, Goa and the Adil Shahis
[118:3:0] # Gol Gumbaz
[118:3:1] - **Tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah** (17th c., 1656), who built it for himself (SSC 2008; UPPSC 2010) – not Yusuf or Ismail Adil Shah or Mahmud Gawan.
[118:3:2] - At **Bijapur** (Vijayapura, Karnataka) – SSC CGL 2019.
[118:3:3] - Its dome is **one of the largest in the world** (IAS 1995) – not Sher Shah's tomb, Jama Masjid or Ghiyasuddin Tughluq's tomb; famous **whispering gallery**.
[118:3:4] - **⚠ NOT true:** "there is **no mosque and no arches** near the tomb" – the complex has a **mosque** and arches (G2 2003; AP History PYQ).

  [118:3:6.2] Goa | Taken by Albuquerque (Portuguese) from the Sultan of Bijapur in 1510
  [118:3:6.3] Battle of Raichur (1520) | Ismail Adil Shah lost to Krishnadevaraya, who took the Raichur fort

## SUB 4 | Ahmednagar – End of the Nizam Shahis, Chand Bibi and Malik Ambar
[118:4:0] # How the Nizam Shahis ended (UPSC 2004 ×3)
[118:4:1] - **Shah Jahan** annexed **Ahmadnagar** (**1633**) and the last ruler **Husain Shah (Nizam Shah III)** was **imprisoned for life at Gwalior**.
[118:4:2] - **Mahawat Khan** won **Daulatabad** by bribing **Fath Khan** (10.5 lakh); **Shahji Bhonsle** then set up a puppet, **Murtaza Nizam Shah III** (1634), and held out till **1636**, when the last lands were split between the Mughals and Bijapur.
[118:4:3] - **⚠ Wrong options:** "Malik Ambar defeated in 1631 and the royal family killed" (Malik Ambar died in **1626**); "Fateh Khan usurped the throne".
[118:4:4] # Chand Bibi and Malik Ambar
[118:4:5] - **Chand Bibi** is linked with **Ahmadnagar** (CG Patwari 2019): daughter of **Hussain Nizam Shah I**; married **Ali Adil Shah** of Bijapur (anti-Vijayanagara alliance); defended Ahmadnagar against the **Mughals** (1595–96); died when it fell (**1600**).
[118:4:6] - **⚠ Chand Sultana** (wife of Ibrahim Adil Shah II) is **not** Chand Bibi.
[118:4:7] - **Malik Ambar:** **Abyssinian** regent of the Nizam Shahis; fought **Jahangir**; revenue on **Todar Mal's lines** – survey, fixed assessment, **no revenue farming**; founded **Khirki → Aurangabad**.
[118:4:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 4 p.77; app notes 1:118 (sub 9, 10)
## SUB 5 | Hyderabad, Charminar and Hussain Sagar
[118:5:0] TABLE head: Monument | Founder / feature
  [118:5:0.0] Hyderabad | Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, 1591; first called Bhagyanagar / Bagh Nagar after Bhagamati, later Hyderabad; capital moved from Golconda in 1592; planned on Isfahan lines by Peshwa Mir Momin Astarabadi
  [118:5:0.1] Charminar | Muhammad Quli, 1591–92, to commemorate the eradication of plague; architect Mir Momin; Char Kaman gateways
  [118:5:0.2] Hussain Sagar | Built 1562 in Ibrahim Qutb Shah's reign by his son-in-law Hazrat Hussain Shah Wali, after whom it is named; UNWTO "Heart of the World" (2012)
  [118:5:0.3] Mecca Masjid | Begun 1614 by Muhammad Qutb Shah; completed by Aurangzeb (1692–93)
  [118:5:0.4] Dar-ul-Shifa | Unani hospital, 1595, Muhammad Quli
  [118:5:0.5] Golconda fort | Old names Mankal / Mangalavaram; handclap at the gate heard at the Bala Hisar
  [118:5:0.6] Qutb Shahi tombs (Ibrahim Bagh) | Onion domes on square bases
[118:5:1] - **Bhagyanagar founded by:** **Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah** (G1 2012) – not Ibrahim, Muhammad or Abdullah Qutb Shah.
[118:5:2] - **Hyderabad built in:** **1591** (AMVI 2013). **Charminar:** end of **plague** – not victory over Vijayanagara or Hindu-Muslim unity.
[118:5:3] - **Hussain Sagar built by:** **Ibrahim Qutb Shah's** reign (2002 paper) – not Abul Hasan, Muhammad Quli or Qutb-ul-Mulk.
[118:5:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History - Qutb Shahis p.5-7, p.16-17; app notes 1:118 (sub 6)
## SUB 6 | Telugu Patronage, Tolerance and Bhadrachalam
[118:6:0] # Telugu poets under the Qutb Shahis
[118:6:1] TABLE head: Poet | Work | First / patron
  [118:6:1.0] Addanki Gangadhara | *Tapati Samvaranopakhyanamu* – dedicated to Ibrahim Qutb Shah | First Telugu kavya dedicated to a Muslim ruler (G1 1994)
  [118:6:1.1] Ponnaganti (Ponnekanti) Telaganarya | *Yayati Charitra* – for Amir Khan, Ibrahim's governor of Patancheru | First kavya in pure (achcha) Telugu
  [118:6:1.2] Kandukuri Rudrakavi | *Sugriva Vijayam*, Nirankusopakhyanam; got Rentachintala agraharam | First Telugu Yakshagana
  [118:6:1.3] Kshetrayya | Movva padams | Under Abdullah
  [118:6:1.4] Bhakta Ramadasu (Kancherla Gopanna) | Dasarathi Satakam | Under Abul Hasan
[118:6:2] - **NOT correct about the Qutb Shahis:** "followed **Roman** style of architecture" – their style is **Indo-Saracenic** (Persian + Hindu). They **were** tolerant, gave scholars **titles, jagirs and agraharas**, and **patronised Telugu**.
[118:6:3] # Madanna, Akkanna and Bhadrachalam
[118:6:4] TABLE head: Angle | Madanna | Akkanna
  [118:6:4.0] Office | Mir Jumla / Diwan (prime minister) | Sar Lashkar (army chief)
  [118:6:4.1] Title | Surya Prakasa Rao | –
[118:6:5] - **Pingali Brahmin** brothers from **Hanamkonda** (Warangal); **murdered 1686**.
[118:6:6] - Nephews: **Podili Linganna** – governor of the Karnatak; **Kancherla Gopanna** – tahsildar of **Palvancha / Bhadrachalam**.
[118:6:7] - **Bhadrachalam:** Gopanna built the Rama temple with state funds, was jailed in Golconda fort and released by **Abul Hasan Tana Shah**, who **donated Bhadrachalam, Shankaragiri and Palvancha** villages to the temple – so the contemporary and helper = **Abul Hasan** (Dy. EO 2008; AP History PYQ).
[118:6:8] # Andhra under Golconda – society
[118:6:9] - The Qutb Shahis united the Telugu lands for the **third time** (after the **Satavahanas** and **Kakatiyas**).
[118:6:10] - Hindus in high office: **Murari Rao, Jagadeva Rao, Madanna**.
[118:6:11] - Muharram was celebrated in Andhra as **Peerla Panduga**.
[118:6:12] - **Bonalu** began at the **Jagadamba Mahankali temple**, Golconda fort; roots in the **Kakatiya and Qutb Shahi** periods.

## SUB 7 | The Five Deccan Sultanates – Origin and Capitals
[118:7:0] - The **Bahmani** kingdom (Hasan Gangu, 1347, Gulbarga) split into **five** successor states – so Adil Shahi, Nizam Shahi and Qutb Shahi all came out of it (**all of the above**).
[118:7:1] TABLE head: Dynasty | Capital | Founder, year | End
  [118:7:1.0] Adil Shahi | Bijapur | Yusuf Adil Shah, 1489/90 (first to break away) | Aurangzeb, 1686
  [118:7:1.1] Nizam Shahi | Ahmadnagar | Malik Ahmad (Ahmad Nizam Shah), 1490 – founded Ahmadnagar city | Shah Jahan, 1633
  [118:7:1.2] Imad Shahi | Berar (capital Ellichpur / Achalpur) | Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk, 1490 | Annexed by Ahmadnagar, 1574
  [118:7:1.3] Barid Shahi | Bidar | Amir Ali Barid – "cunning fox of the Deccan" | Bijapur, 1619
  [118:7:1.4] Qutb Shahi | Golconda, later Hyderabad | Sultan Quli (Quli Qutb Shah), 1518 | Aurangzeb, 1687
[118:7:2] - **IAS 2008 match:** Adil Shahi–Bijapur, Barid Shahi–Bidar, Imad Shahi–Berar, Nizam Shahi–Ahmadnagar, Qutb Shahi–Golconda → **4 3 2 1 5**.
[118:7:3] - **Wrongly matched (UPPSC 2004):** **Yusuf Adil Shah – Ahmadnagar** (he founded Bijapur). Baz Bahadur–Malwa, Qutb Shah–Golconda, Muzaffar Shah–Gujarat are correct.
[118:7:4] - **Bijapur** = first to break away (1489); **Golconda** = last to break away (1518) and last to fall (1687). "Berar was founded by" = **Imad Shahis** (APPSC G2 2005).
[118:7:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 4 p.77; NextGen AP History - Qutb Shahis p.1; app notes 1:118 (sub 0)
## SUB 8 | Mughal Annexation of the Deccan and the Fall of Golconda
[118:8:0] - **Talikota (1565):** four of the five – **all except Berar** – combined to defeat Vijayanagara.
[118:8:1] TABLE head: Emperor | Action
  [118:8:1.0] Akbar | Ahmadnagar city (1600); Asirgarh / Khandesh (1601)
  [118:8:1.1] Shah Jahan | Ended the Nizam Shahis (1633); 1636 treaties with Bijapur and Golconda (Inqiyad Nama)
  [118:8:1.2] Aurangzeb | Attacked Golconda (1656) as subedar; annexed Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687)
[118:8:2] - **Aurangzeb's two Deccan conquests:** **Bijapur and Golconda** (UPPSC 2004) – Ahmadnagar was Shah Jahan's, Bidar went to Bijapur.
[118:8:3] - **Golconda fell in 1687** (Medical Officer 2021; Dy. EO 2008): on **21 September 1687** the traitor **Abdullah Khan Pani** opened the **Fateh Darwaza**; **Abdur Razzaq Lari** fought bravely; Golconda became the **21st Mughal Suba**.
[118:8:4] - **Abul Hasan** was imprisoned at Bidar, then **Daulatabad**; died **1699** (NextGen: 1700); buried at **Khuldabad**.
[118:8:5] - **Akkanna and Madanna** were murdered in **1686**, just before the fall.
[118:8:6] - Order: 1600 Ahmadnagar city → 1633 Nizam Shahis → 1686 Bijapur → 1687 Golconda.
[118:8:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History - Qutb Shahis p.8-9; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 4 p.77; app notes 1:118 (sub 10)
## SUB 9 | Qutb Shahi Administration and Revenue
[118:9:0] # Administration
[118:9:1] - Hierarchy: **Sultan → Taraf (Tarafdar) → Sarkar (Faujdar) → Pargana (Tahsildar) → Village**; Abdullah: **6 Tarafs**; Abul Hasan: **37 Sarkars, 517 Parganas**.
[118:9:2] TABLE head: Official | Duty
  [118:9:2.0] Peshwa / Wakil | Prime minister; renamed Diwan under Abul Hasan (held by Madanna)
  [118:9:2.1] Mir Jumla | Finance minister
  [118:9:2.2] Ain-ul-Mulk | Military department
  [118:9:2.3] Tarafdar | Governor of a Taraf: law and order, revenue, troops
  [118:9:2.4] Faujdar | Head of a Sarkar
  [118:9:2.5] Tahsildar / Deshmukh | Head of a Pargana
  [118:9:2.6] Mukaddam / Kulkarni | Village head / village accountant
  [118:9:2.7] Kotwal | City police; also ran the mint
  [118:9:2.8] Mahasibs / Mustasibs | In charge of public morals (like the Mughal Muhtasib)
  [118:9:2.9] Shahbandar | Chief port officer, customs
  [118:9:2.10] Majumdar / Dabir | Auditor / secretary
  [118:9:2.11] Kayastha | Scribes (record-keepers)
[118:9:3] - **Mahasibs / Mustasibs** (2023 screening) = **public morals** – not chief justice, Taraf head or civil cases.
[118:9:4] - **Kayastha** (AP History PYQ) = caste of **scribes** – not traders, physicians or professionals.
[118:9:5] - Justice: Sultan → **Shariat Panch** (chief justice) → **Qazi** → **Pargana Majlis**. **Sar Lashkar** = army chief (Akkanna).
[118:9:6] # Revenue
[118:9:7] - **Main source of income: land revenue** (2023 screening) – collected by **tax farming**, rights auctioned to the highest bidder; not tourism, customs or feudal levies.
[118:9:8] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [118:9:8.0] Mustajirs | Tax farmers (highest bidders, mostly Hindus)
  [118:9:8.1] Haveli | Crown lands
  [118:9:8.2] Dasabandhu lands | Paid only one-tenth
[118:9:9] - **Machilipatnam** was leased for **1,80,000 pagodas** a year.
[118:9:10] - Other sources: trade taxes, port customs, diamond-mine leases, taxes on courtesans and professions (military service did not replace taxes).
[118:9:11] - **State monopolies: salt, betel leaf, tobacco**.
[118:9:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History - Qutb Shahis p.10-13; NextGen AP History APPSC Part 7 (Kayastha); app notes 1:118 (sub 3, 4)

=== NOTES 1:119 | Foundation of Vijayanagara – Harihara and Bukka, Vidyaranya; the Sangama Dynasty
## SUB 0 | Founding of Vijayanagara (1336) – Harihara I and Bukka I
[119:0:0] - **Founders:** brothers **Harihara I and Bukka I (Bukkaraya I)**, sons of **Sangama** → **Sangama dynasty** (APPSC FBO, G2; UKPSC; Uttarakhand PCS 2004, 2024) – not Krishnadevaraya, Rama Raya, Achyuta Raya, Devaraya I/II, Pushyamitra or Bhadrabahu.
[119:0:1] - **Year:** **1336** (RPSC 2010; APPSC 2019) – not 1326, 1332, 1346 or 1035; **1346** = Sringeri visit after the Hoysala victory.
[119:0:2] - **First ruler:** **Harihara I** (1336-56) – Bukka I succeeded him (1356-77).
[119:0:3] - **River:** on the **southern bank of the Tungabhadra**, a tributary of the **Krishna** (APPSC ASO 2011; UPPSC 2011) – not the Krishna, Kaveri, Penna or Wainganga; ruins at **Hampi**.
[119:0:4] - **Agent of the deity (UPSC 2015 ×2):** **Harihara I** founded the new city and ruled as the agent of **Virupaksha**, to whom all land **south of the Krishna** belonged – not Amoghavarsha I, Ballala II or Prataparudra II.
[119:0:5] - **Story in brief:** subordinates at **Kampili** (under the Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra) → **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** took Kampili, captured the brothers, converted them in **Delhi** and sent them back → **Vidyaranya** of **Sringeri** reconverted them → independence declared at the **Virupaksha temple, Hampi**; crowned **18 April 1336**.
[119:0:6] - **"Treasurers of Warangal":** one tradition makes the brothers treasury officers of **Prataparudra (Kakatiya)**; the place they founded = **Vijayanagara** (APPSC Medical Officer 2021; dropped from the key for a wording error) – not Kadapa, Hyderabad or Tirupati.
[119:0:7] - **Capital:** first **Anegondi**, then the new city of **Vijayanagara** (completed **c. 1343**, under Bukka I's oversight).
[119:0:8] - **Name:** Vijayanagara = **"City of Victory"**; legend of a **hare turning on the hunting dogs** marked the site; emblem **Varaha (boar)**; Sangamas were **Shaiva**, the later dynasties **Vaishnava**.
[119:0:9] - **Largest Hindu kingdom** of medieval South India (APPSC) – not Rashtrakuta, Kakatiya or Satavahana.
[119:0:10] # Why the site (APPSC ATWO)
[119:0:11] TABLE head: Factor | Correct?
  [119:0:11.0] Rocky granite hills of Hampi – natural fortification (Giri Durga, seven stone ramparts) | ✓
  [119:0:11.1] Tungabhadra – water for farming and the city | ✓
  [119:0:11.2] Local granite for temples and forts | ✓
  [119:0:11.3] "Coastal location, trade with the Roman Empire" | ✗ inland; Rome long gone
  [119:0:11.4] "Godavari gold reserves for coins" | ✗
[119:0:12] - **Statements (APPSC JA, Huvina Hadagali news):** "founded in **1035**" ✗ (1336); **Krishnadevaraya** wrote the Telugu **Amuktamalyada** on statecraft ✓; "**Devaraya II** laid the foundation of the Virupaksha temple" ✗ (the shrine is older than Vijayanagara, c. 7th century; UNESCO lists the **Group of Monuments at Hampi**, 1986) → **only B**.
[119:0:13] - **Harihara I's title:** **Purva-Paschima Samudradhipati** (lord of the eastern and western seas; Badami inscription, 1340) – not Devaraya II, whose title is Gajabetekara; annexed the **Hoysala** kingdom (**1346**).
[119:0:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History - APPSC 13 p.4; NextGen Vijayanagara Kingdom p.1, p.8-9; NextGen previous papers p.33-34, p.42; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.65; app notes 1:119 (sub 0, 2)
## SUB 1 | The Four Dynasties of Vijayanagara
[119:1:0] TABLE head: Order | Dynasty | Span | Founder | Origin
  [119:1:0.0] 1 | Sangama | 1336-1485 | Harihara I and Bukka I | Andhra / Kannada (disputed)
  [119:1:0.1] 2 | Saluva | 1485-1505 | Saluva Narasimha – first usurpation | Kalyana (Karnataka); "Telugu people" (NextGen)
  [119:1:0.2] 3 | Tuluva | 1505-1570 | Vira Narasimha (son of Tuluva Narasa Nayaka) – second usurpation | Tuluva nadu
  [119:1:0.3] 4 | Aravidu | 1570-1646 | Tirumala Raya | Araviti (Kurnool), Andhra
[119:1:1] - **First dynasty:** **Sangama** (UKPSC 2011; Polytechnic 2020; APPSC) – not Hoysala, Saluva, Tuluva or Aravidu.
[119:1:2] - **Order:** **Sangama → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu** = C, A, B, D / C, A, D, B (Sachivalayam papers) – S-S-T-A.
[119:1:3] - **Last Hindu dynasty of Vijayanagara:** **Aravidu** (APPSC 2019 ×2).
[119:1:4] - **Ruled under Vijayanagara:** Sangamas, Saluvas, Tuluvas and Aravidus (Asst. Comm. 2017) – **Hoysalas, Yadavas of Devagiri and Poligars** were never Vijayanagara dynasties.
[119:1:5] - **Odd one out:** **Vishnukundins** (an older Andhra dynasty) against Saluva, Sangama, Tuluva (APPSC G1 ×2); **Kadamba** = the dynasty that never ruled Vijayanagara (APPSC 2019).
[119:1:6] - **Odd one (APPSC G2 2001):** **Kings of Vijayanagara** – Yadagirigutta, Simhachalam and Vemulawada are temple towns.
[119:1:7] - **Devaraya II** (1426 in the stem; reign 1422/26-46) belonged to the **Sangama** dynasty.
[119:1:8] - **Sangama:** longest-ruling dynasty; greatest king **Devaraya II**; last king **Praudha Raya** (removed 1485 by **Saluva Narasimha**, who succeeded him).
[119:1:9] - **Tuluva:** **Vira Narasimha** crowned **1505** after killing **Immadi Narasimha**; then **Krishnadevaraya** and **Achyutaraya** (Tuluvas).
[119:1:10] - **Aravidu:** capitals **Penukonda, Chandragiri, Vellore**; after Talikota the capital moved **Hampi → Penukonda → Chandragiri**; Anegondi was never an Aravidu capital.
[119:1:11] - **Andhra in origin:** only **Sangama and Aravidu** (app notes); the Kakatiyas were not a Vijayanagara dynasty.
[119:1:12] TABLE head: Ruler | Dynasty / fact
  [119:1:12.0] Krishnadevaraya (1509-29) | Tuluva; wrote Amuktamalyada; queens Tirumala Devi, Chinna Devi; founded Nagalapuram for his mother Nagala Devi; credited with the Vithala temple; contemporary of Purandara Dasa
  [119:1:12.1] Sadasivaraya | Tuluva; regent Rama Raya remitted the barbers' tax (at Kandoja's request)
[119:1:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Vijayanagara Kingdom p.1, p.3-6, p.14-17; NextGen AP History - APPSC 13 p.4-8; app notes 1:119 (sub 2, 3)
## SUB 2 | Devaraya II (1422/26-46) – the Greatest Sangama King
[119:2:0] - **Greatest king of the Sangama dynasty**; also called **Praudha Devaraya**.
[119:2:1] - **Title Gajabetekara** (Gajabetegara, "**hunter of elephants**") (RPSC 2010; APPSC) – it is a **title of Devaraya II**, not a coin, a king's name or a Jain monk; coins bearing it are his **Gajabetekara coins** – not Devaraya I, Bukka I or Mallikarjuna. **Andhra Bhoja** and **Dakshinapatha-swami** are Krishnadevaraya's titles.
[119:2:2] - **Army:** enlisted about **10,000 Muslim** soldiers (mounted archers) (APPSC G2 2011 ×3) – not Vira Narasimha, Bukka I or Virupaksha; gave them **jagirs** and a mosque; kept a **Quran before his throne** so they could salute it.
[119:2:3] - **First to enlist Muslims at all:** **Devaraya I** (NextGen; APPSC) – Devaraya II enlarged it to 10,000.
[119:2:4] - **Ceylon:** his general **Lakkanna** (Dakshina Samudradhipati) invaded **Sri Lanka** and collected **tribute** (IAS 2003) – not Harihara I/II or Bukka II.
[119:2:5] - **Abdur Razzaq**, Persian envoy of **Shah Rukh**, came in **1443** in **Devaraya II's** reign (BPSC 2018; APPSC JL 2004; UDA/LDA 2010) – not Devaraya I, Krishnadevaraya, Achyuta Raya or Vira Vijaya; described diamond bazaars, about **300 ports**, taxed **prostitution**.
[119:2:6] - **Literature:** wrote the Sanskrit **Mahanataka Sudhanidhi** (APPSC AE 2011) – not Devaraya I, Krishnadevaraya or Peddana; his literary hall = **Mutyala Sala** (APPSC G1) – **Bhuvana Vijayam** is Krishnadevaraya's.
[119:2:7] - **Srinatha** adorned his court (CGPSC 2019, 2020): **kanakabhishekam** after defeating **Dindima Bhatta** – not Harihara II, Devaraya I or Krishnadevaraya.
[119:2:8] - Other: took **Kondaveedu (1424)**; **Draksharama inscription (1444)** – pushed back the **Gajapatis**; Nicolo Conti also spent time at his court.
[119:2:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Vijayanagara Kingdom p.3, p.11-12; NextGen AP History - APPSC 13 p.6; NextGen previous papers p.36, p.42; app notes 1:119 (sub 5)
## SUB 3 | Bukka I (1356-77) – Madurai, Madhura Vijayam, Jains and Vaishnavas, China
[119:3:0] - **Kumara Kampana** (Kamparaya), son of Bukka I, conquered **Madurai** – destroyed the **Madurai (Ma'bar) Sultanate** (c. 1371) after overthrowing **Sambhuvaraya** (APPSC; G2-A 1989) – not Harihara II, Devaraya, Marappa or Sankula Nayaka.
[119:3:1] - **Madhura Vijayam** (Veera Kamparaya Charitam), Sanskrit, by his wife **Gangadevi (Gangamba)** (UPPCS 2000; APPSC G1 2010; G2 2000; G2-B 1989) – not Molla, Tirumalamba, Ramabhadramba, Madhuravani, Bharati or Polamamba.
[119:3:2] - **Gangadevi's gurus: Agastya and Vidyanatha** → "disciple of **Agastya**" (APPSC G2 2012) – not Vidyaranya, Sayana, Rameswara Pandita, Tikkana or Potana.
[119:3:3] - **Jains and Vaishnavas:** **Bukka I** settled their dispute in **1368** (**Shravanabelagola** inscription) and protected the Jains (APPSC G1 1994, G2 2003; ×4 in all) – not Harihara I, Devaraya I/II, Saluva Narasimha or Krishnadevaraya.
[119:3:4] - **China:** **Bukka I** sent an embassy to the **Ming** emperor (**1374**) (CGPSC 2008) → the south Indian power that sent an envoy to the Ming in the late 14th century = **Vijayanagara** (APPSC JA) – not Kakatiya, Pandya or Bahmani.
[119:3:5] - **Nachana Somana** (Uttara Harivamsam) = court poet of **Bukka I**, the first Telugu poet of the Vijayanagara court (APPSC 2011); granted **Penchikaladinne**.
[119:3:6] - **Succession:** Bukka I → his son **Harihara II** (APPSC 2019) – not Harihara I, Bukka II or Devaraya I.
[119:3:7] - Completed the capital; title **Vedamarga Pratishthapaka**; took **Srisailam** and **Dupadu** (near Markapur); general **Saluva Mangu** killed the Madurai Sultan → title **"Parapakshi Saluva"**.
[119:3:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History - APPSC 13 p.5; NextGen Vijayanagara Kingdom p.2, p.9-10; NextGen previous papers p.28 ("Gangadevi was the student of Agastya"), p.43 ("Bukka-I resolved the conflict between the Jainas and Vaishnavas"); app notes 1:119 (sub 4, 6)
## SUB 4 | Origin Theories and Sources – Sewell's 'A Forgotten Empire'
[119:4:0] - **'A Forgotten Empire (Vijayanagar)'** (1900) = **Robert Sewell** (APPSC G2 2011 ×2, G2 Mains 2017, JA 2012) – not Ferishta, B.A. Saletore, Burton Stein, James Fergusson, Father Heras, H.G. Wells, N. Venkataramanayya or K.A.N. Sastri; it carries the English translation of **Domingo Paes** and **Fernao Nuniz**, and covers 1336-1565.
[119:4:1] - Sewell recorded **seven** local traditions of the founding.
[119:4:2] TABLE head: Theory | What it says | Backed by
  [119:4:2.0] Kakatiya service | Brothers served Prataparudra of Warangal (treasurers); after 1323 taken to Delhi and converted | Local tradition
  [119:4:2.1] Kampili | Governed Kampili; captured by MBT, converted in Delhi, sent back as Sultanate governors | NextGen, PMF
  [119:4:2.2] Kannada / Hoysala | Officers of Veera Ballala III | Father Heras, S.K. Ayyangar, H. Krishna Sastri, P.B. Desai
  [119:4:2.3] Andhra | Brothers were Andhras | N. Venkataramanayya, Sewell, Nilakanta Sastri
[119:4:3] - **Sangama's lineage:** the inscriptions trace the family to the **Yadava** (lunar) race – "Sangama was **a Yadava**" (APPSC G2 2005); the Kakatiya link belongs to the brothers' service story, not to Sangama's descent.
[119:4:4] - **Delhi legend:** fall of Warangal → conversion in Delhi → sent against Deccan rebels → defeat → met **Vidyaranya** near **Pampa** → return to Hinduism → Anegondi in the name of Virupaksha.
[119:4:5] TABLE head: Work | Author
  [119:4:5.0] *Kampili and Vijayanagara* | Nelaturi Venkataramanayya (not Sewell)
  [119:4:5.1] *The Aravidu Dynasty of Vijayanagara* | Father H. Heras
  [119:4:5.2] *Peasant State and Society in Medieval South India* | Burton Stein – "segmentary state"
  [119:4:5.3] *Social and Political Life in the Vijayanagara Empire* | B.A. Saletore
  [119:4:5.4] *Rayavachakam* | Sthanapati
[119:4:6] - **Ferishta:** Persian chronicler – the **Bahmani** view of the wars.
[119:4:7] TABLE head: Traveller | Reign
  [119:4:7.0] Ibn Battuta | Harihara I (first foreign visitor)
  [119:4:7.1] Nicolo Conti (Italian) | Devaraya I (earliest European visitor)
  [119:4:7.2] Abdur Razzaq (Persia) | Devaraya II (1443)
  [119:4:7.3] Domingo Paes, Barbosa | Krishnadevaraya
  [119:4:7.4] Fernao Nuniz (Portuguese) | Achyutaraya
  [119:4:7.5] Cesare Federici (Italian) | Sadasivaraya
[119:4:8] - **Padikaval** = sale of police rights to individuals.
[119:4:9] - First record calling Harihara I king: **Nellore inscription**; Vidyaranya headed the **Sringeri Shankara Math**.
[119:4:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Vijayanagara Kingdom p.5, p.8; NextGen previous papers p.33; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.65 (legend of Kakatiya feudatories, Kampili); Epigraphia Indica (Yadava genealogy of Sangama); app notes 1:119 (sub 0, 1, 9)
## SUB 5 | Harihara II, Sayana and Devaraya I
[119:5:0] - **Sayana** (Vedic commentator, **Vedartha Prakasha**), brother of **Vidyaranya**, minister of **Harihara II** → "patronised by / flourished under the **Vijayanagara** rulers" (UPPCS 2008; Uttarakhand 2002) – not Paramaras, Satavahanas, Vakatakas, Cholas or Guptas.
[119:5:1] - **Vedic commentaries of Sayana and Madhava:** written in **Harihara II's** period (NextGen; APPSC) – the work was begun on **Bukka I's** order and finished under Harihara II.
[119:5:2] - **Harihara II (1377-1404):** longest-reigning Sangama king; titles **Rajavyasa, Rajavalmiki**; first Vijayanagara ruler to **attack Sri Lanka**; his general **Madhava** took **Goa** (with Belgaum, **1380**) – title **Bhuvanaikavira** → first ruler to capture Goa from the Bahmanis = **Harihara II** (BPSC 1995); minister **Irugappa** built the **Ganigitti Jain temple**, wrote **Navaratnamala**; rule over Kanara, Mysore, Kanchi, Trichinopoly; gave a daughter to **Kataya Vema's** son.
[119:5:3] - **Tungabhadra dam:** **Devaraya I** (c. **1410**) built a large dam and a canal-cum-aqueduct about **24 km** long to the capital (UPSC 2023 ×2) – not Mallikarjuna, Vira Vijaya or Virupaksha; in the Sachivalayam version the only option naming him is "**Bukka I and Devaraya I**".
[119:5:4] - **Devaraya I (1406-22):** first to **enlist Muslims** in the army; defeated at **Mudgal** in the **war of the goldsmith's daughter** (Nehal) with **Firuz Shah Bahmani** – gave his daughter and **Bankapur**; **Nicolo Conti** visited; fought the **Kandukuru Reddis**, allied with Kataya Vema and the Velamas; **Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam**; coronation copper plates with a **Vamana** seal (unveiled in Bengaluru, Apr 2025).
[119:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History - APPSC 13 p.5; NextGen Vijayanagara Kingdom p.2, p.10-11; Rocket Indian History 01 (Harihara-II Goa + Belgaum 1380); Wikipedia "Sayana" (prefaces name Bukka); app notes 1:119 (sub 4, 6)
## SUB 6 | Vijayanagara–Bahmani Conflict
[119:6:0] - **Main rival in the south:** the **Bahmani Sultans** (APPSC G1) – not Hoysala, Warangal or Madurai.
[119:6:1] - **Bone of contention:** the **Raichur Doab (Raichur Antarvedi)**, between the **Krishna and Tungabhadra** (APPSC G2 2000) – not Mathura, Warangal or Malabar.
[119:6:2] - **Conflict began under Harihara I:** the Bahmani kingdom was founded by **Hasan Gangu** at **Gulbarga in 1347**, in **Harihara I's** reign (Police Constable 2019; APPSC) – Mallikarjuna, Devaraya I and Virupaksha are later.
[119:6:3] - **First war:** under **Bukka I** against **Muhammad Shah I** (1362-67; Mudgal, Kautalam, Adoni) – where both Harihara I and Bukka I are offered for "the **war** started", key **Bukka I** (APPSC); treaty to spare civilians.
[119:6:4] TABLE head: War | Outcome
  [119:6:4.0] Mudgal (1367) | Bukka I; called the first Indian war with artillery
  [119:6:4.1] Goa, Belgaum (1380) | Taken by Harihara II's general Madhava
  [119:6:4.2] Goldsmith's daughter | Devaraya I vs Firuz Shah; Bankapur as dowry
  [119:6:4.3] Devaraya II | Two wars: Mudgal, Raichur, Bijapur
  [119:6:4.4] Goa lost (1472) | To the Bahmanis
  [119:6:4.5] Raichur (1520), Gulbarga (1523) | Krishnadevaraya
  [119:6:4.6] Talikota (1565) | Deccan Sultanates defeated Rama Raya
[119:6:5] - Order: Mudgal 1367 → Goa lost 1472 → Gulbarga 1523 → Talikota 1565.
[119:6:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Vijayanagara Kingdom p.1, p.9-11, p.14; Wikipedia "Bahmani–Vijayanagar War (1362–1367)"; app notes 1:119 (sub 8)
## SUB 7 | Saluva Narasimha and the Sangama Campaigns in Andhra
[119:7:0] - **Saluva Narasimha:** lord of **Chandragiri**; clan from Kalyana; removed **Praudha Raya** (1485) with **Tuluva Narasa Nayaka** – **first usurpation**.
[119:7:1] - **Court:** *Saluvabhyudayam* – **Rajanatha Dindima**; **Annamacharya** (contemporary, supported); **Pillalamarri Pina Veerabhadrudu** – *Jaimini Bharatam*, *Sringara Sakuntalam*.
[119:7:2] - **Vinukonda Vallabharaya**, governor of Vinukonda under Devaraya II, wrote ***Kridabhiramam*** – describes **Kakatiya Warangal**.
[119:7:3] - **Gangadevi** wrote Madhura Vijayam, **not** Jaimini Bharatam.
[119:7:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Vijayanagara Kingdom p.3, p.14-15; app notes 1:119 (sub 7)
