=== NOTES 1:129 | Akbar – Conquests, Rajput Policy, Religious Policy, Ibadat Khana, Din-i-ilahi, Sulh-i-kul
## SUB 0 | Religious Policy – Ibadat Khana, Mahzar, Din-i-Ilahi, Sulh-i-Kul
[129:0:0] # Measures in order
[129:0:1] TABLE head: Year | Measure
  [129:0:1.0] 1563 | Pilgrimage tax abolished – by Akbar (not Bahlul Lodi, Sher Shah or Humayun)
  [129:0:1.1] 1564 | Jizya abolished
  [129:0:1.2] 1575 | Ibadat Khana (House of Worship) built at Fatehpur Sikri – first for Ulemas, Sayyids, Shaikhs
  [129:0:1.3] 1576 | Haj caravans from the state treasury under a Mir Haj – Akbar was the first Indian ruler to organise the Haj at state expense (UPPSC 1998)
  [129:0:1.4] 1578 | Ibadat Khana opened to all religions – Hindus, Jains, Christians, Zoroastrians
  [129:0:1.5] 1579 | Mahzar – an attested statement of leading Ulemas making Akbar supreme arbiter in religious disputes; issued by Akbar, drafted by Shaikh Mubarak
  [129:0:1.6] 1582 | Din-i-Ilahi (Tauhid-i-Ilahi) launched
[129:0:2] - **Chronology:** **jizya 1564 → Ibadat Khana 1575 → Mahzar 1579 → Din-i-Ilahi 1582 = 1, 2, 3, 4** (UP UDA 2006).
[129:0:3] - **Ibadat Khana = the hall where Akbar held discussions with scholars of various religions** (UPSC 2014) – **built by Akbar (1575)**; not a royal mosque, a private prayer chamber or a nobles' room.
[129:0:4] - Guiding principle **Sulh-i-Kul** = "**peace with all**" (universal harmony) – **promulgated by Akbar** (not Nizamuddin Auliya, Zainul Abidin or Nasiruddin Chirag); the result of **political generosity, religious tolerance and a liberal cultural attitude – all three** (UPPCS 1998).
[129:0:5] - Coins with **Rama and Sita** and the Devanagari legend **"Rama-Siya"** – **Akbar** (UPPCS 2011), not Bhoja, Siddharaja or Zain-ul-Abidin.
[129:0:6] - Akbar is called **"an enlightened despot"** (UP Mains 2009).
[129:0:7] - Akbar's reign is known for **annexation, provincial administration, judicial administration – NOT religious intolerance** (1, 2, 3); his popularity rested on **mansabdari, religious policy, land revenue and social reforms – all** (UPPSC 1990).
[129:0:8] - He did **not** forsake Islam – that is the factor NOT conducive to calling him a nationalist (RAS 1994); unity in law, administration and culture and his religious policy were.
[129:0:9] - **Pilgrim tax at Banaras and Allahabad:** a deputation of Banaras pandits led by **Kavindracharya** (Sarasvati) persuaded **Shah Jahan** to end it (UPPCS 2000).
[129:0:10] # Taxes – who imposed or abolished
[129:0:11] TABLE head: Tax / measure | Ruler / meaning
  [129:0:11.0] Jizya, pilgrimage tax abolished | Akbar (1564 / 1563)
  [129:0:11.1] Jizya reimposed | Aurangzeb, 1679
  [129:0:11.2] Grain tax ended | Sikandar Lodi (not Akbar)
  [129:0:11.3] Jizya and cow slaughter ended | Zain-ul-Abidin of Kashmir
  [129:0:11.4] Privileges of Khuts, Muqaddams, Chaudharis ended | Alauddin Khalji
  [129:0:11.5] Ushr | Land tax on Muslims
  [129:0:11.6] Zakat | Alms tax on Muslims
  [129:0:11.7] Khums | One-fifth of war booty
  [129:0:11.8] Haqq-e-Sharb | Irrigation tax
[129:0:12] # Din-i-Ilahi (1582)
[129:0:13] - **Promoted / promulgated by Akbar** (MPPSC 1998; State PSC); **launched 1582** (CGPSC 2011).
[129:0:14] - Features: **one God**, greeting "Allah-hu-Akbar", reverence for **sun and fire**, avoiding meat; piety, prudence, kindness.
[129:0:15] - **Never forced** – a voluntary small circle of about **18**, not a mass religion; **Abul Fazl** its chief exponent; **Birbal the only Hindu**; it **ended with Akbar's death**.
[129:0:16] - **Why it failed (SSC 2009):** not patronised after Akbar, rejected by orthodox Muslims, never projected to the masses – **all of the above**.
[129:0:17] - Debate: an ideology based on **Sufi pantheism**, not a religion; **Mohsin Fani** (Jahangir's time) called it a religion in **Dabistan-i-Mazahib** – none of **Abul Fazl, Badauni, Nizamuddin** (UPPCS 2000: "none of these").
[129:0:18] - Orthodox critics: **Badauni** and **Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi** (Naqshbandi, "Mujaddid Alf-i-Sani").
[129:0:19] # Jesuits, Jains and others at court
[129:0:20] TABLE head: Group | Person | Title / grant / year
  [129:0:20.0] Jesuits (Goa) | Rudolf Acquaviva, Antonio Monserrate | 1580 – first mission, Fatehpur Sikri
  [129:0:20.1] Jesuits (Goa) | – | 1591 – second mission
  [129:0:20.2] Jesuits (Goa) | Jerome Xavier, Pinheiro, Bento de Goes | 1595 – third mission, met Akbar at Lahore
  [129:0:20.3] Jains | Hiravijaya Suri | "Jagat Guru" (CGPSC 2024; UPPSC 2012)
  [129:0:20.4] Jains | Jinachandra Suri | "Yuga Pradhan"
  [129:0:20.5] Sikhs | Guru Ram Das | Land granted – Amritsar grew
  [129:0:20.6] Parsis | Dastur Meherji Rana | Land grant
[129:0:21] - **CGPSC 2022:** the 1595 mission was the **third** and met Akbar at **Lahore**; **Monserrate** belonged to the **first** (1580) – so (i) and (ii) only.
[129:0:22] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History Part 4 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-04.txt) p.27; NextGen Indian History Part 5 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.16 (Ibadat Khana); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian History Part 1 (src/indian-history/rocket-indian-history-01.txt) p.114, p.125; app notes 1:129 (sub 3, 4, 5)
## SUB 1 | Court, Navratnas and Translations – Abul Fazl, Faizi, Tansen
[129:1:0] TABLE head: Figure | Field | Fate / note
  [129:1:0.0] Abul Fazl | Akbarnama, Ain-i-Akbari; Panchatantra as Ayar-i-Danish; chief exponent of Din-i-Ilahi | Murdered 1602 by Bir (Vir) Singh Bundela of Orchha on Prince Salim's orders; the killer was rewarded by Jahangir
  [129:1:0.1] Faizi (Abul Faizi) | Poet laureate, Abul Fazl's brother; Persian Lilavati; supervised the translation department – incl. the Persian Mahabharata | Died 1595
  [129:1:0.2] Birbal (Mahesh Das) | Wit, adviser; only Hindu in Din-i-Ilahi | Killed 1586 fighting the Yusufzai
  [129:1:0.3] Todar Mal | Revenue minister; earlier served Sher Shah | Died 1589
  [129:1:0.4] Tansen | Original name Ramtanu Pandey; Miyan ki Malhar, Miyan ki Todi; first patron Raja Ramchandra Singh of Rewa (Bhata); Akbar gave the title "Miyan" | Navaratna
  [129:1:0.5] Man Singh I | General (Kachhwaha of Amber) | Led the Mughals at Haldighati
  [129:1:0.6] Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan | Son of Bairam Khan; Hindi dohas; Baburnama into Persian | –
[129:1:1] - **Ata Ali Khan** – the name of **Abul Faizi** (CGPSC 2014 key).
[129:1:2] - **Abul Fazl's death** was caused by **Prince Salim** (Jharkhand 2013); actual killer **Bir Singh Deo Bundela** (MPSC 2009) – not Hemu, Bairam Khan or Udai Singh.
[129:1:3] - **Abul Fazl** is the medieval writer who **refers to the discovery of America** ("alam-i-nau", the New World) (UPSC 1997 ×2) – not Jayasi, Amir Khusrau or Raskhan.
[129:1:4] - Abul Fazl **shaped, represented and articulated the ideas of Akbar's reign**; his qualities made Akbar choose him as **adviser and spokesperson** – statement II explains I (NDA 2019; NCERT Themes II).
[129:1:5] - **Sheikh Mubarak** – father of Abul Fazl and Faizi. Death order: **Sheikh Mubarak (1593) → Faizi (1595) → Abul Fazl (1602) → Prince Daniyal (1605)** = 2, 3, 1, 4 (UPPSC 2024).
[129:1:6] - **Persian Mahabharata (Razmnama)** – translated by Naqib Khan, Badauni and others **under the supervision of Faizi** (RAS 1999) – not Utbi, Naziri or Abul Fazl.
[129:1:7] - Akbar **learnt Hindu music from Lala Kalavant** (UPPSC 2016); Dhrupad under Akbar: Tansen and **Swami Haridas**; **Vilas Khan** – Jahangir's court.
[129:1:8] # Maktab Khana and translations
[129:1:9] - **Maktab Khana** ("House of Translation") at **Fatehpur Sikri**, set up around **1574**.
[129:1:10] - **Razmnama** = Persian **Mahabharata**; Atharvaveda, Rajatarangini and the Baburnama also translated; **Nizamuddin Panipati** – Persian **Yogavasistha**.
[129:1:11] - **Buland Darwaza** at Fatehpur Sikri commemorates the **Gujarat conquest (1572-73)**.
[129:1:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History Part 4 p.9 (Razm Namah); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian History Part 1 p.58, p.114, p.115; NCERT Class 12 Themes II ch.9 (Abul Fazl); app notes 1:129 (sub 6)
## SUB 2 | Accession, Bairam Khan's Regency and Conquests
[129:2:0] # Accession and regency
[129:2:1] - Born **15 October 1542** at **Amarkot**; enthroned **14 February 1556** at **Kalanaur (Gurdaspur, Punjab)** on news of Humayun's death (CGPSC 2015) – not Kabul, Lahore or Sirhind – by **Bairam Khan**.
[129:2:2] - **Age at coronation:** books and keys say **fourteen** ("only fourteen years old", NextGen); strictly **13 years 4 months** ("under 14", Rocket).
[129:2:3] - **Panipat II – 5 November 1556**: Hemu hit in the eye by an arrow; Afghan power ended.
[129:2:4] TABLE head: Phase | Years | Who dominated
  [129:2:4.0] Bairam Khan's regency | 1556-60 (JPSC 2010) | Bairam Khan – made Wakil/Wazir and given the title Khan-i-Khanan by Akbar at that time; dismissed 1560; killed 1561 on the way to Mecca
  [129:2:4.1] Petticoat government | 1560-64 | Maham Anaga and her son Adham Khan
[129:2:5] - **Adham Khan** was **personally killed by Akbar (1562)** for murdering the minister **Atagh (Atka) Khan** – not Bairam Khan, Baz Bahadur or Pir Muhammad.
[129:2:6] - Aurangzeb was crowned twice (21 July 1658 Delhi; 5 June 1659); his first coronation was NOT at Kalanaur.
[129:2:7] # Conquests
[129:2:8] TABLE head: Region | Year | Ruler / queen opposed
  [129:2:8.0] Malwa | 1561 | Baz Bahadur (Afghan)
  [129:2:8.1] Gondwana | 1564 | Rani Durgavati – Akbar's contemporary (SSC 2003; not Ahilya Bai, Martanda Varma, Sawai Jai Singh)
  [129:2:8.2] Chittor (Mewar) | 1568 | Rana Udai Singh
  [129:2:8.3] Ranthambore | 1569 | Surjan Rai (Hada)
  [129:2:8.4] Gujarat | 1572-73 | Muzaffar Shah III; Buland Darwaza
  [129:2:8.5] Bengal and Bihar | 1576 | Daud Khan Karrani defeated, both merged (BPSC 2001; State PSC)
  [129:2:8.6] Kabul | 1581 | Half-brother Mirza Hakim, who backed the Bengal–Bihar rebels – not to reclaim Ferghana (UPSC 2003: A true, R false)
  [129:2:8.7] Kashmir | 1586 | Yusuf Shah Chak – exiled to Bihar; tomb at Biswak, Nalanda district (BPSC 2019)
  [129:2:8.8] Ahmednagar | 1600 | Chand Bibi
  [129:2:8.9] Khandesh (Asirgarh) | 1601 | Miran Bahadur – last campaign
[129:2:9] - Extent: **Bengal to Afghanistan, Kashmir to the Godavari**; **Khandesh, Kabul and Kashmir were inside – Bijapur was outside** (annexed by Aurangzeb, 1686) (NDA 2004).
[129:2:10] - **UPSC 1998 match:** **1556 – accession of Akbar**; 1600 – EIC charter; 1739 – Nadir Shah takes Delhi; the key pairs 1686 with Shivaji's death (strictly **1680**).
[129:2:11] - Mughal order: **Babur → Humayun → Akbar → Jahangir → Shah Jahan → Aurangzeb**; "Akbar, Shah Jahan, Jahangir" is the incorrect sequence (SSC 2020).
[129:2:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History Part 4 p.25-27; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian History Part 1 p.73; Wikipedia, Yusuf Shah Chak (tomb at Biswak, Nalanda; cites Kashmir histories); app notes 1:129 (sub 0, 1)
## SUB 3 | Rajput Policy, Mewar and Haldighati
[129:3:0] - Twin policy of **conquest and conciliation**: surrender followed by restoration of **autonomy and honour**; high posts, marriages, toleration.
[129:3:1] - **First marriage alliance – 1562**, with the daughter of **Raja Bharmal (Bihari Mal) of Amber – the Kachhwahas** (State PSC; UPRO 2016; UPPCS 2004) – not Rathores, Sisodias, Chauhans or Bundelas; on Akbar's pilgrimage to **Ajmer**.
[129:3:2] - Top Rajput mansabdars: **Man Singh, Bhagwan Das**; also Raja Todar Mal and Raja Birbal.
[129:3:3] - **Contemporaries of Akbar:** Man Singh, Amar Singh, Udai Singh – **Jaswant Singh** of Marwar belongs to Shah Jahan–Aurangzeb (WBCS 2018).
[129:3:4] # Mewar – the holdout
[129:3:5] - **Mewar did not accept Akbar's supremacy willingly** (UP Lower 2004) – Amber, Marwar, Bikaner did.
[129:3:6] - **Haldighati – 18 June 1576** (UKPSC 2010; CGPSC 2016) – **Maharana Pratap** vs Akbar's army under **Man Singh of Amber**; aim: **to subdue Rana Pratap** (RAS 1992).
[129:3:7] - **Hakim Khan Sur** commanded Pratap's army (vanguard of Afghans) – not Amar Singh, Man Singh or Shakti Singh.
[129:3:8] - Rana Pratap employed **Baksariya Muslims** in his army (APPSC G1 2019 key).
[129:3:9] - Mewar submitted only under **Jahangir** – **Amar Singh**'s treaty, **1615**.
[129:3:10] - **Rao Chandrasena of Marwar** never surrendered (Bhadrajun 1571, Siwana; died 1581) – Rai Singh of Bikaner and Bharmal submitted; Amar Singh submitted to Jahangir (RAS 2012).
[129:3:11] - Pairs: Chausa = 1539 (not 1538), Kannauj = 1540 (not 1539), **Haldighati = 1576**, Khajwa = 1659 (not 1657).
[129:3:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History Part 4 p.26-27; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian History Part 1 p.73-74; app notes 1:129 (sub 2)
## SUB 4 | Social and Educational Reforms
[129:4:0] - **Sati** was prohibited / curbed under **Akbar** (WBCS 2018) – widows not to be burnt against their will.
[129:4:1] - **Monogamy order:** a man to marry **only one wife**, a second only if the first was **barren** – **Akbar** (UPPCS 2002).
[129:4:2] - **Marriage age fixed** (16 for boys, 14 for girls) and **consent of bride and groom** required – **both statements true** (UPPSC 2020).
[129:4:3] - Discouraged child marriage, dowries, marriages between close relatives; allowed widow remarriage.
[129:4:4] - **Educational reforms:** **Akbar** (MPPSC 2014) – curriculum of arithmetic, logic, geometry, astronomy, accountancy, agriculture, ethics, medicine, history.
[129:4:5] - **Memoirs:** Babur – Tuzuk-i-Baburi in **Turki**; Jahangir – Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri in **Persian**; Akbar wrote none (Abul Fazl's Akbarnama); Humayun was learned in Persian, Arabic and Turkish.
[129:4:6] - **Akbar was unlettered (illiterate)** but a great patron of learning (APPSC G2 2011) – Babur, Jahangir and Aurangzeb were literate.
[129:4:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History Part 4 p.12 (education), p.27 (social reforms); app notes 1:129 (sub 3, 8)

=== NOTES 1:130 | Akbar's Institutions – Mansabdari System, Todar Mal's Bandobast, Dahsala, Zabti and Other Revenue Systems
## SUB 0 | Revenue Systems – Todar Mal's Bandobast, Dahsala, Zabti
[130:0:0] # Road to the Dahsala
[130:0:1] - Sher Shah's survey system → **Karori experiment (1574)** → **Dahsala (1580)** under **Raja Todar Mal**.
[130:0:2] - **Karori experiment (1574):** core provinces split into circles each yielding **one crore dams**, under officers called **karoris**, who collected revenue and cultivation data.
[130:0:3] - Mansabdari + zabti-dahsala = a **salaried, transferable nobility** + **predictable cash revenue**.
[130:0:4] # Raja Todar Mal
[130:0:5] - Earlier served **Sher Shah**; built on his survey-based system; **Diwan** (finance minister); one of the Navratnas.
[130:0:6] - **Todar Mal = land revenue reforms** (UP Mains 2012) – not law, literature or music.
[130:0:7] - **Muzaffar Khan Turbati** was the **first to be given the proper status of Diwan** by Akbar, with Todar Mal as assistant (UP Lower 2003) – not Asaf Khan, Munim Khan or Todar Mal; Todar Mal and **Khwaja Shah Mansur** came later.
[130:0:8] TABLE head: Unit | Fact
  [130:0:8.0] Gaz-i-Ilahi | Unit of length, about 82 cm
  [130:0:8.1] Jarib | Bamboo pieces joined with iron rings – replaced hemp rope
  [130:0:8.2] State share | One-third of average produce, paid in cash (dam); kind allowed in some areas
[130:0:9] # The systems
[130:0:10] TABLE head: System | Meaning | Region / year
  [130:0:10.0] Zabti | Land measured; dasturs = cash rates per crop per bigha | Introduced by Akbar; core North Indian provinces (Lahore to Allahabad, Malwa, Gujarat)
  [130:0:10.1] Dahsala (Ain-i-Dahsala) | Revenue on the average produce and prices of the last ten years (1571-80), converted into cash | 1580
  [130:0:10.2] Batai / Ghalla-bakhshi | Crop-sharing | Thatta, Kabul, Kashmir
  [130:0:10.3] Nasaq | Rough assessment from past revenue records | Mainly Bengal
  [130:0:10.4] Kankut | Yield estimated on the standing crop | Where measuring was impractical
  [130:0:10.5] Plough assessment | By number of ploughs | Parts of the Deccan under Akbar (UPPCS 2017; J.N. Sarkar)
[130:0:11] - **Dahsala = collection of revenue on the average of produce and prices of the last 10 years** (APPSC G2 2017) – NOT a fixed 10-year rate, a 10-yearly measurement, or a 10-year crop-sharing deal.
[130:0:12] - **"Bandobast system" = Dahsala** (Jharkhand 2013; JPSC 2013); also called Zabti-Bandobast.
[130:0:13] - **Zabti was introduced by Akbar** – not Ghiyasuddin Tughluq, Sikandar Lodi or Sher Shah.
[130:0:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian History Part 1 (src/indian-history/rocket-indian-history-01.txt) p.97; NextGen Indian History Part 4 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-04.txt) p.24; app notes 1:130 (sub 0, 1, 2)
## SUB 1 | Revenue Officials and Revenue Terms
[130:1:0] # Revenue officials
[130:1:1] TABLE head: Official | Duty
  [130:1:1.0] Amalguzar (amil) | Sarkar (district) revenue collector – assessment and collection of land revenue; extend cultivation
  [130:1:1.1] Qanungo | Kept the records of revenue payable by villages / pargana land records
  [130:1:1.2] Karkun | Prepared the seasonal crop statistics / recorded cultivation
  [130:1:1.3] Bitikchi | Accountant – records on land and produce
  [130:1:1.4] Karori | Circle yielding one crore dams
  [130:1:1.5] Potdar | Treasurer
  [130:1:1.6] Patwari | Village accountant
[130:1:2] - **Amalguzar = assessment and collection of land revenue** (NDA 2002) – law and order was the faujdar's, the household the Mir Saman's, the treasury the potdar's / khazanadar's.
[130:1:3] - **APPSC G1 match:** Amalguzar–district revenue collector (II), Karkuns–crop statistics (IV), Qanungo–village revenue records (I), Bitikchi–accountant (III) = **a-II, b-IV, c-I, d-III**.
[130:1:4] - **Deshmukh** (medieval Deccan): **collected land revenue** from the peasants and deposited it in the state treasury (APPSC G1) – a hereditary watandar over a pargana.
[130:1:5] # Revenue and grant terms
[130:1:6] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [130:1:6.0] Maal (mal) | Land revenue – the principal state income (UP Lower 2009)
  [130:1:6.1] Khalisa | Crown land; revenue straight to the imperial treasury
  [130:1:6.2] Jagir | Right to collect revenue in lieu of salary – not ownership
  [130:1:6.3] Madad-i-maash | Revenue-free land granted to learned persons, holy men, the needy (BPSC 2005; State PSC) – not toll tax, army pension or cultivation tax
  [130:1:6.4] Suyurghal | Another name for such charitable revenue-free grants
[130:1:7] - AP angle: **Qutb Shahi Golconda** took **one-third** (not one-half).
[130:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History Part 5 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.16 (Madad-i-Maash, Qanungo, Amils, Watandar); app notes 1:130 (sub 4, 8)
## SUB 2 | Mansabdari System
[130:2:0] - **Introduced by Akbar** (APPSC Technical Education) – not Sher Shah, Jahangir or Aurangzeb; of **Central Asian / Mongol** military origin; basis of Mughal civil and military administration.
[130:2:1] - Mansabdars held **combined civil-military, non-hereditary** ranks, paid by **jagir** (or cash).
[130:2:2] - Ranks: **10 to 5,000** for nobles (later **7,000**); higher ranks only for **royal princes**.
[130:2:3] - **Zat** = personal rank and pay; **Sawar** = horsemen to maintain – dual ranks from **1595-96**; sawar equal to zat = **1st class**.
[130:2:4] - **Dagh** (horse branding) – **1573-74**.
[130:2:5] - **Horses:** for **every ten cavalrymen, twenty horses** – because horses had to be **rested on the march and replaced in war** (IAS 1999: A and R true, R explains A).
[130:2:6] - **Du-aspa sih-aspa** – troopers with two/three horses without raising zat – **Jahangir** (first for Mahabat Khan).
[130:2:7] - Land grants: **Iqta – Delhi Sultans; Jagir – Mughals; Amaram – Vijayanagara; Mokasa – Marathas** (UPSC 2000).
[130:2:8] - Mansabdar = civil-military, non-hereditary, paid by jagir; ICS = purely civil, fixed salary.
[130:2:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History Part 4 p.32-33; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian History Part 2 (src/indian-history/rocket-indian-history-02.txt) p.34; app notes 1:130 (sub 5), 1:129 (sub 7)
## SUB 3 | Land Classification
[130:3:0] TABLE head: Class | Status
  [130:3:0.0] Polaj | Cultivated every year
  [130:3:0.1] Parauti | Fallow 1-2 years
  [130:3:0.2] Chachar | Fallow 3-4 years
  [130:3:0.3] Banjar | Uncultivated 5+ years
[130:3:1] - Akbar: **four** classes; Sher Shah: **three** (good, middling, bad).
[130:3:2] ~~ Sources: app notes 1:130 (sub 3)
## SUB 4 | Jagirs, Central Ministers and Provincial Units
[130:4:0] # Jagirs
[130:4:1] TABLE head: Type | Feature
  [130:4:1.0] Tankha | In lieu of salary; transferable every 3-4 years
  [130:4:1.1] Watan | Zamindar's homeland; hereditary, not transferable
  [130:4:1.2] Mashrut | Conditional, tied to specified duties
  [130:4:1.3] In'am | Reward; no service obligation
[130:4:2] - **Jagirdari crisis** (Aurangzeb): too many mansabdars for too few jagirs; pressure on peasants.
[130:4:3] # Central ministers
[130:4:4] TABLE head: Office | Function
  [130:4:4.0] Wakil | Highest in rank; lost financial powers
  [130:4:4.1] Wazir / Diwan-i-kul | Finance – revenue, treasury, accounts
  [130:4:4.2] Mir Bakhshi | Military – dagh, chehra, promotions
  [130:4:4.3] Sadr-us-sudur | Religious affairs, charitable grants
  [130:4:4.4] Mir Saman | Royal household and karkhanas
[130:4:5] # Provincial and local units
[130:4:6] TABLE head: Unit | Officials
  [130:4:6.0] Suba (12 in 1580) | Subedar (head), diwan, bakhshi, sadr, qazi
  [130:4:6.1] Sarkar | Faujdar (law and order), amalguzar (revenue)
  [130:4:6.2] Pargana | Shiqdar, amil, qanungo
  [130:4:6.3] Town | Kotwal – law and order in the city
  [130:4:6.4] Village | Muqaddam (headman), patwari, chowkidar
[130:4:7] - The provincial **Diwan** ran revenue and was an independent check on the subedar.
[130:4:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History Part 5 p.16; app notes 1:130 (sub 6, 7, 8)

3. Mansabs were hereditary.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
  *1 and 2 only | 2 and 3 only | 1 and 3 only | 1, 2 and 3
  x: Zat was personal rank and Sawar the horsemen to be kept; mansabs were non-hereditary.
[fec0059e64c4c] sub2
  In which class was a mansabdar whose sawar rank equalled his zat rank placed?
  Second class | *First class | Third class | Lowest class
  x: By the sawar-zat ratio, sawar equal to zat made a mansabdar first class.
[g02a3b46ccb6b] sub2
  What was the range of mansab ranks for nobles under Akbar?
  *10 to 5,000 | 100 to 10,000 | 1 to 1,000 | 500 to 12,000
  x: Nobles held mansabs from 10 to 5,000 (later 7,000); higher ranks went only to princes.
[na53ff701604] sub3
  Under Akbar's Zabti system, how was land that had been left fallow for three to four years classified?
  Polaj | Parauti | *Chachar | Banjar
  x: Chachar was land fallow for 3-4 years. Polaj was cultivated every year, Parauti was fallow for 1-2 years, and Banjar was uncultivated for 5 years or more.
[n183f8e4334a] sub3
  Under Akbar's land classification, what was land left fallow for one or two years called?
  Polaj | *Parauti | Banjar | Chachar
  x: Parauti lay fallow one or two years; Polaj was cultivated every year, Chachar fallow three or four years, Banjar five or more.
[ff309fbea2231] sub3
  Under Akbar's land classification, what was land left uncultivated for five years or more called?
  *Banjar | Polaj | Parauti | Chachar
  x: Banjar was fallow 5+ years; Parauti 1-2 and Chachar 3-4 years.
[f98c161a9ee8d] sub3
  In Akbar's classification, what kind of land was Polaj?
  Fallow for 1-2 years | Fallow for 3-4 years | *Cultivated every year | Fallow for 5 years or more
  x: Polaj land was cultivated every year.
[nc36c6e0d85d] sub4
  What condition is described as the jagirdari crisis under Aurangzeb?
  *Too many jagirdars competing for too few jagirs, placing pressure on the peasantry | The complete abolition of jagirs by Akbar | The transfer of all jagirs to Rajput rulers | Too few mansabdars controlling an excessive number of jagirs
  x: The jagirdari crisis arose because too many mansabdars chased too few jagirs, which increased pressure on the peasantry.
[f6e8328b06b07] sub4
  Which type of Mughal jagir was hereditary and not transferable?
  Tankha | *Watan | Mashrut | In'am
  x: Watan jagir, the zamindar's homeland, was hereditary and not transferable.
[fa09939e97f42] sub4
  After how many years were Tankha jagirs, given in lieu of salary, normally transferred?
  1 year | 10 years | 20 years | *3-4 years
  x: Tankha jagirs were transferable every 3-4 years, which prevented local power bases.
[f73cdaeb1ea94] sub4
  Which of the following pairs (Jagir type – feature) is correctly matched?
  *Mashrut – conditional, tied to specified duties | Watan – transferable every 3-4 years | In'am – tied to military service | Tankha – zamindar's homeland
  x: Mashrut was conditional; Watan was non-transferable, In'am carried no service obligation and Tankha was in lieu of salary.
[facfe3905e540] sub4
  Which Mughal central minister handled military matters such as dagh, chehra and promotions?
  Wakil | Sadr-us-sudur | *Mir Bakhshi | Mir Saman
  x: The Mir Bakhshi was the military head in charge of dagh, chehra and promotions.
[f71f3af27a5e1] sub4
  What was the Mughal Sadr-us-sudur in charge of?
  Royal household and karkhanas | Revenue and treasury | *Religious affairs and charitable grants | Military promotions
  x: The Sadr-us-sudur dealt with religious affairs, charitable grants and the Shariat.
[f06ba7787adb4] sub4
  Which of the following about Mughal central ministers is NOT correct?
  *The Mir Saman was in charge of religious affairs. | The Wakil was the highest in rank. | The Wazir handled revenue, treasury and accounts. | The Mir Bakhshi oversaw promotions.
  x: The Mir Saman looked after the royal household and karkhanas; religious affairs were with the Sadr-us-sudur.
[g1d9cf651803f] sub4
  Which Mughal central minister looked after the royal household and the karkhanas?
  *Mir Saman | Mir Bakhshi | Sadr-us-sudur | Wakil
  x: The Mir Saman was in charge of the royal household and karkhanas.
[ne0663c69686] sub4
  Who was the head of a Mughal suba, served by a Diwan, Bakhshi, Sadr and Qazi?
  Amil | Faujdar | Kotwal | *Subedar
  x: The Subedar headed the suba; the Diwan, Bakhshi, Sadr and Qazi were the other suba officials.
[n589f7b9803d] sub4
  Which of the following pairs (Unit – Officials) is correctly matched?
  Sarkar – Kotwal | Town – Muqaddam, patwari, chowkidar | Village – Faujdar, amalguzar | *Pargana – Shiqdar, amil, qanungo
  x: The pargana had the shiqdar, amil and qanungo. The sarkar had the faujdar and amalguzar, the town the kotwal, and the village the muqaddam, patwari and chowkidar.
[n5539347e28b] sub4
  Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
  Faujdar — military and law-and-order duties at the sarkar level | Subahdar — governor responsible for law and order | Provincial Diwan — revenue administration and an independent check on the governor | *Kotwal — maintenance of pargana land and revenue records
  x: The Kotwal was responsible for law and order in the city. Maintenance of land and revenue records at the pargana level was the duty of the Qanungo.
[f6caa35c7a4d1] sub4
  In 1580, Akbar's empire was divided into how many subas?
  10 | *12 | 15 | 21
  x: There were 12 subas in 1580.
[ff7111c7162c9] sub4
  Whose duty was law and order in a Mughal town?
  Amalguzar | Qanungo | Patwari | *Kotwal
  x: The kotwal kept law and order in the city; the faujdar did so at sarkar level.

=== NOTES 1:131 | Jahangir and Nur Jahan; Shah Jahan – Deccan and Central Asian Policy, the War of Succession
## SUB 0 | Jahangir (1605-27) – Events of the Reign and Nur Jahan's Junta
[131:0:0] # Jahangir – key events
[131:0:1] - **Accession:** Prince **Salim** (named after **Sheikh Salim Chishti** of Sikri; mother Jodha Bai/Harkha Bai), revolted against Akbar c. 1599-1604; crowned **1605** as **Nur-ud-din Muhammad Jahangir**.
[131:0:2] TABLE head: Event | Fact
  [131:0:2.0] Khusrau's revolt | Eldest son (mother Man Bai = Shah Begum) rebelled 1606; defeated near Lahore, imprisoned, blinded
  [131:0:2.1] Guru Arjan Dev (5th Guru) | Executed 1606 for backing Khusrau
  [131:0:2.2] Mewar – Treaty of Chittor | 1615: Rana Amar Singh submitted; Mewar and Chittor returned; son Karan Singh made a mansabdar
  [131:0:2.3] Deccan | 1616: Khan-i-Khanan beat Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Golconda with Maratha sardars; Malik Ambar rose
  [131:0:2.4] Kangra | Annexed 1620
  [131:0:2.5] Kandahar | Lost to Persia (Shah Abbas I) in 1622 – NOT annexed by Jahangir
  [131:0:2.6] Khurram's revolt | 1622-26; ordered to Kandahar, refused; Nur Jahan backed Shahryar
  [131:0:2.7] Mahabat Khan's coup | 1626: seized Jahangir on the Jhelum
  [131:0:2.8] English | Hawkins 1608-09, factory at Surat 1613, Roe 1615-19
[131:0:3] - **Rebels against Jahangir:** **Khusrau, Khurram, Mahabat Khan** – NOT **Asaf Khan** (UPPSC 2013).
[131:0:4] - **Events of Jahangir's reign (APPSC G1):** Arjan Dev's execution, Mewar's submission, the English arrival – **"annexation of Kabul and Kandahar" is the trap**.
[131:0:5] - **Shah Begum (Man Bai, Manbhawati Bai)** – Jahangir's Rajput wife, mother of Khusrau – **committed suicide (opium), 1605** over the father-son quarrel (UPPSC 2008).
[131:0:6] - **Orchha:** Bundela **Bir Singh Deo** of Orchha was Salim's ally (killed Abul Fazl, 1602, for him); the **Jahangir Mahal** at Orchha was built for him – the printed key for "fort where Jahangir took shelter".
[131:0:7] - Chain of justice; **Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri**; lived mostly at Lahore; painting at its zenith; pietra dura began.
[131:0:8] # Kandahar not recaptured under Jahangir (CDS 2000)
[131:0:9] - Khurram **refused to go**, an expedition was **hard to organise**, the **cold** of Afghanistan – (printed key II, III, IV).
[131:0:10] # Nur Jahan and the junta
[131:0:11] - **Mehr-un-Nisa** (Mehrunnisa), born **1577** at Kandahar; daughter of **Mirza Ghiyas Beg**; widow of **Sher Afghan**; married Jahangir **1611**; titles **Nur Mahal → Nur Jahan** ("Light of the World"), **Padshah Begum**; pen name **"Makhfi"**.
[131:0:12] - **Childhood name = Mehr-un-Nisa** ("Maharul Nisa" in APPSC's option) – the APPSC key's **"Bahu Begam" is wrong**.
[131:0:13] - **Name on coins and farmans** – the only Mughal consort with this privilege; built the **Tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah, Agra** for her father.
[131:0:14] TABLE head: Junta member (five) | Relation
  [131:0:14.0] Nur Jahan | Empress
  [131:0:14.1] Asmat Begum | Mother
  [131:0:14.2] Ghiyas Beg – Itimad-ud-Daulah | Father; Jahangir's diwan
  [131:0:14.3] Asaf Khan | Brother; Shah Jahan's father-in-law
  [131:0:14.4] Prince Khurram | Married her niece Arjumand Banu Begum (1612)
[131:0:15] - **NOT junta members: Jahangir himself and Mahabat Khan.**
[131:0:16] TABLE head: Emperor | Diwan
  [131:0:16.0] Akbar | Muzaffar Khan (Turbati)
  [131:0:16.1] Jahangir | Itimad-ud-Daulah (Ghiyas Beg)
  [131:0:16.2] Shah Jahan | Sa'adullah Khan
  [131:0:16.3] Aurangzeb | Asad Khan
[131:0:17] > Ask types: junta "NOT a member" (×4), events of the reign (statements), rebels, Nur Jahan's name.
[131:0:18] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 04 p.28-29; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.107; old app notes 1:131 (sub 0-1); Mehr-un-Nisa – Britannica "Nur Jahan"
[131:0:19] - **Emperor–amir pairs (IAS 2004):** Babur – Tardi Beg; Humayun – Bairam Khan; Aurangzeb – Jaswant Singh; **Sawai Jai Singh** rose under Aurangzeb and the later Mughals – **NOT Jahangir**.
## SUB 1 | Shah Jahan's Family, Titles and Court
[131:1:0] TABLE head: Person | Relation / title / fate
  [131:1:0.0] Jagat Gosain | Jahangir's Rathor wife; mother of Shah Jahan
  [131:1:0.1] Mumtaz Mahal | Arjumand Banu Begum, Asaf Khan's daughter; died 1631; buried in the Taj Mahal
  [131:1:0.2] Jahanara | Eldest daughter; backed Dara; nursed captive Shah Jahan; "Sahibat-uz-Zamani" (from Aurangzeb)
  [131:1:0.3] Roshanara | Backed Aurangzeb; Padshah Begum
  [131:1:0.4] Dara Shikoh | Eldest son, heir; titles "Shah-i-Iqbal" / "Shah Buland Iqbal" (Shahzada-e-Buland Iqbal); Persian translations (Upanishads – Sirr-i-Akbar; Yogvashishta, Gita)
  [131:1:0.5] Sulaiman Shikoh | Dara's son; refuge with Prithvi Shah of Srinagar Garhwal; handed over by Medini Shah; jailed at Gwalior
  [131:1:0.6] Aurangzeb's daughters | Zeb-un-Nisa, Zinat-un-Nisa, Mehr-un-Nisa, Badr-un-Nisa, Zubdat-un-Nisa – Jahan Ara, Roshan Ara, Gauhar Ara were Shah Jahan's daughters
[131:1:1] - Father-son pairs: Babur – Kamran; Akbar – Salim; **Jahangir – Khusrau**; **Shah Jahan – Murad**.
[131:1:2] # Shah Jahan (1628-58)
[131:1:3] - Crowned at **Agra, 1628**; early revolts: Bundela **Jujhar Singh**, **Khan Jahan Lodi**; Portuguese beaten at **Hughli (1632)** for trading abuses.
[131:1:4] - **Capital shifted from Agra to Shahjahanabad (Delhi), 1638-48**; Red Fort, Jama Masjid, **Taj Mahal** (for Mumtaz – not Jodha Bai or Nur Jahan); **Peacock Throne** (taken by **Nadir Shah, 1739**); reign = "golden age" of architecture.
[131:1:5] - **Poet laureate: Abu Talib Kalim (Kaleem)**; official historian **Abdul Hamid Lahori – Padshahnama**; **Inayat Khan – Shahjahannama**.
[131:1:6] - **Captivity:** deposed 1658 and kept in **Agra Fort** (nursed by Jahanara) till death in **1666** – Aurangzeb imprisoned his father for life.
[131:1:7] TABLE head: Work | Author / reign
  [131:1:7.0] Padshahnama | Abdul Hamid Lahori (Shah Jahan)
  [131:1:7.1] Adab-i-Alamgiri | Aurangzeb's letters – incl. the father-son money dispute
  [131:1:7.2] Fatawa-i-Alamgiri | Compiled under Aurangzeb, not Shah Jahan
[131:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 04 p.29-30; NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.14; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.110-112; old app notes 1:131 (sub 3-4)
## SUB 2 | War of Succession (1657-59)
[131:2:0] TABLE head: Prince | Post in 1657 | Fate
  [131:2:0.0] Dara Shikoh | Heir, at court (backed by Jahanara) | Lost Samugarh, Deorai; betrayed by Malik Jiwan of Dadar; executed 1659; buried in Humayun's Tomb, Delhi
  [131:2:0.1] Shah Shuja | Bengal | Fled to Arakan
  [131:2:0.2] Aurangzeb | Deccan (backed by Roshanara) | Won; crowned 1658 and 1659
  [131:2:0.3] Murad Bakhsh | Gujarat-Malwa | Jailed in Gwalior, executed 1661
[131:2:1] TABLE head: Battle | Place | Result
  [131:2:1.0] Bahadurgarh (Feb 1658) | Near Banaras | Sulaiman Shikoh beat Shuja
  [131:2:1.1] Dharmat (15 Apr 1658) | Near Ujjain (MP) | Aurangzeb + Murad beat Jaswant Singh (Dara's general)
  [131:2:1.2] Samugarh (29 May 1658) | Near Agra | Dara beaten – decisive
  [131:2:1.3] Khajwa (Jan 1659) | Near Fatehpur (UP) | Shuja beaten
  [131:2:1.4] Deorai (Mar 1659) | Near Ajmer | Dara's final defeat
[131:2:2] - **Order:** Banaras (Shuja) → Dharmat → Samugarh → Deorai (UPPSC 2022: 2, 4, 3, 1).
[131:2:3] - **Dharmat** = Aurangzeb vs Dara's forces (not Ghori–Jai Chand, Babur–Afghans, Abdali–Marathas).
[131:2:4] - Aurangzeb took the throne by force – **no rule of primogeniture** (Timurid coparcenary custom).
[131:2:5] - **Francois Bernier** witnessed Dara's humiliation in Delhi (1659); Manucci was Dara's artilleryman.
[131:2:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 04 p.29-30; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.110; old app notes 1:131 (sub 7)
## SUB 3 | Europeans at the Mughal Court
[131:3:0] TABLE head: Visitor | Facts
  [131:3:0.0] William Hawkins | English (EIC); reached Surat 1608 on the Hector; Agra 1609; mansab and title "English Khan"; no farman
  [131:3:0.1] Captain Best | Beat the Portuguese off Surat (Swally) 1612 → English factory at Surat 1613
  [131:3:0.2] Sir Thomas Roe | Ambassador of James I to Jahangir (not Akbar); came 1615 (Surat, Sept 1615), stayed till 1619; received at Ajmer (Jan 1616); followed Jahangir from Ajmer to Mandu; won factory rights
  [131:3:0.3] Pelsaert (Dutch) | Came 1620 under Jahangir
  [131:3:0.4] Peter Mundy (English) | Shah Jahan's reign
  [131:3:0.5] Tavernier (French) | Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb; described the Peacock Throne
  [131:3:0.6] Bernier (French physician) | 1656-68; physician to Dara, then Danishmand Khan
  [131:3:0.7] Manucci (Venetian) | Came 1656; artilleryman of Dara; later practised as a physician in Mughal service (Shah Alam); Storia do Mogor
  [131:3:0.8] Thevenot (French) | Reached Surat 1666 – Aurangzeb's reign

[131:3:2] - **Came under Aurangzeb:** **Thevenot (1666)**, Fryer, Careri – not Hawkins/Roe (Jahangir), Monserrate (Akbar), Mundy (Shah Jahan).
[131:3:3] - **Match (UPPSC 1997):** Firuz Tughlaq – canals; Balban – Nauroz; Alauddin – Diwan-i-Riyasat; **Jahangir – Thomas Roe**.
[131:3:4] - First Mughal–English clash: **1686** (Aurangzeb) – **Shaista Khan** drove **Job Charnock** out of **Hooghly** (Child's War).
[131:3:5] TABLE head: Visitor | Ruler

## SUB 4 | Central Asian Policy – Kandahar and Balkh
[131:4:0] TABLE head: Campaign | Commander | Result
  [131:4:0.0] Kandahar recovered, 1638 | Persian governor Ali Mardan Khan surrendered it | Mughal gain (lost 1622 → regained 1638)
  [131:4:0.1] Balkh-Badakhshan, 1646-47 | Murad Bakhsh, then Aurangzeb (not Dara) | Failed, heavy losses
  [131:4:0.2] Kandahar lost, 1649 | – | To Persia (Shah Abbas II)
  [131:4:0.3] Sieges 1649, 1652 | Aurangzeb | Failed
  [131:4:0.4] Siege 1653 | Dara Shikoh | Failed – Kandahar lost for good
[131:4:1] - **Aim of the Balkh campaign:** to set up a **friendly ruler in Balkh and Badakhshan, which bordered Kabul** – not to conquer Samarqand/Farghana or fix the Amu Darya "scientific line" (UPSC 2002).
[131:4:2] - **Kandahar:** frontier fortress on the routes India–Persia–Central Asia – its loss was a blow as a **strategic stronghold** (UPSC 1998).
[131:4:3] - **UPSC 1998 A-R:** Dara led only the **Qandahar** siege (1653); Balkh-Badakhshan were Murad and Aurangzeb; the expeditions **failed** – so R is false.
[131:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 04 p.29; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.110; Satish Chandra, Medieval India II (Balkh aim); old app notes 1:131 (sub 5)
## SUB 5 | Deccan Policy of Shah Jahan
[131:5:0] - **1633:** **Daulatabad** fell to Mahabat Khan when **Fath Khan** (son of **Malik Ambar**) surrendered it – Malik Ambar had **died in 1626**; **1636:** Nizam Shahi **Ahmadnagar** extinguished.
[131:5:1] - **1636 ahdnamas** with **Bijapur and Golconda**: Mughal suzerainty, tribute, Mughal arbitration; Golconda's **Inqiyad Nama** (Abdullah Qutb Shah) put Shah Jahan's name in **khutba and coins**.
[131:5:2] - Four Deccan subas: **Khandesh, Berar, Telangana, Daulatabad**.
[131:5:3] - **Aurangzeb – viceroy of the Deccan** for most of the reign: **1636-44** and **1652/53-58**; attacked Golconda in **1656**, urged by **Mir Jumla**.
[131:5:4] TABLE head: Kingdom | Annexed | Last ruler
  [131:5:4.0] Bijapur | 1686 | Sikandar Adil Shah
  [131:5:4.1] Golconda | 1687 | Abul Hasan Tana Shah – exiled to Daulatabad
[131:5:5] - AP angle: Jahangir's envoy to Golconda **Mir Makki**; Tana Shah employed **Madanna and Akkanna** and helped Shivaji.
[131:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 04 p.29; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.110; old app notes 1:131 (sub 6)

=== NOTES 1:132 | Aurangzeb – Religious Policy, Deccan Policy and Resistance
## SUB 0 | Resistance – Jats, Satnamis, Rajputs and Sikhs
[132:0:0] TABLE head: Revolt | Leader | Region / fact
  [132:0:0.0] Jat (1669) | Gokula | Mathura (Tilpat); peasant revolt against heavy revenue
  [132:0:0.1] Jat (1680s) | Rajaram | Plundered Akbar's tomb at Sikandra
  [132:0:0.2] Jat (after 1700) | Churaman | Built the power that became Bharatpur
  [132:0:0.3] Satnami (1672) | Satnami sect | Narnaul (Haryana); peasants and artisans – Aurangzeb's reign
[132:0:1] - **Agrarian roots:** the **Satnami and Jat** revolts grew out of peasants' problems – the Rajput, Sikh and Maratha conflicts did not (MPPSC 2010).
[132:0:2] - **Bharatpur state:** built by **Churaman and Badan Singh** (Badan Singh founded it, 1722); **Suraj Mal** (r. 1755-63) – **"the Plato of the Jat tribe"**.
[132:0:3] - Satnamis of 1672 ≠ **Guru Ghasidas** (19th-century Satnampanth, Chhattisgarh); Jat Rajaram ≠ Maratha Rajaram.
[132:0:4] # Rajputs – Marwar and Mewar (1679-81)
[132:0:5] - **Aurangzeb changed the Rajput policy** of Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan (SSC 2019).
[132:0:6] - **Trigger:** **Jaswant Singh** of Marwar died **1678**; Aurangzeb took Marwar under direct control; posthumous son **Ajit Singh** championed by **Durgadas Rathore**; **Rana Raj Singh** of Mewar joined.
[132:0:7] - **Prince Akbar** (Aurangzeb's son; "Akbar II" in UPPSC options) **revolted, joined the Rajputs (1681)** → fled to Sambhaji → Persia – weakened Aurangzeb against the Rajputs.
[132:0:8] - Result: the Rajput alliance – pillar of Akbar's empire – broke.
[132:0:9] # Sikhs and others
[132:0:10] - **Guru Tegh Bahadur** (9th Guru) executed at Delhi, **1675**; **Guru Gobind Singh** wrote the **Zafarnama** after **Chamkaur (1704)**.
[132:0:11] - Afghans: **Yusufzai and Afridi** risings.
[132:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 04 p.30-31; old app notes 1:132 (sub 2-4); Satish Chandra, Medieval India II (Jat state, Suraj Mal)
## SUB 1 | Deccan Policy – Bijapur, Golconda and the Marathas
[132:1:0] - **Phases (NextGen):** 1658-68 recover Bijapur's 1636 gains; 1668-84 alliance against the Marathas; **1686-87 outright annexation**; **1687-1707** war with the Marathas.
[132:1:1] - Aurangzeb **spent the last ~25-27 years of his reign in the Deccan** – more than any other Mughal ("Deccan ulcer").
[132:1:2] # Bijapur (1686)
[132:1:3] - Siege 1685-86, Aurangzeb in person; fell **September 1686**; last ruler **Sikandar Adil Shah**.
[132:1:4] # Golconda (1687)
[132:1:5] - Ministers **Madanna-Akkanna** murdered (1686); siege 1687; **Abdur Razzaq Lari** defended; traitor **Abdullah Pani** opened the gate – fort taken with "**keys of gold**" (as Akbar took Asirgarh).
[132:1:6] - Ruler: **Abul Hasan Qutb Shah (Tana Shah)** – exiled to **Daulatabad**, died 1699, buried at **Khuldabad**.
[132:1:7] - AP angle: ended **Qutb Shahi rule over Andhra**; **Bhakta Ramadasu** was the nephew of Madanna-Akkanna.
[132:1:8] - **Greatest extent:** with Bijapur, Golconda and the chase of the Marathas to **Jinji**, the empire reached **Tamil territory** under Aurangzeb; the UPSC 2000 map (Bijapur and Golconda inside) = **Aurangzeb's empire at his death, 1707**.
[132:1:9] # Marathas
[132:1:10] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [132:1:10.0] 1666 | Shivaji at Agra – insulted, house arrest, escaped in fruit baskets
  [132:1:10.1] 1689 | Sambhaji captured at Sangameshwar, executed
  [132:1:10.2] 1689-1700 | Rajaram resisted from Jinji; died at Sinhagad (1700)
  [132:1:10.3] From 1700 | Tarabai led the war as regent for Shivaji II
[132:1:11] # Last years
[132:1:12] - **Died 1707 at Ahmednagar**; simple grave at **Khuldabad** (near Aurangabad).
[132:1:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 04 p.30; NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.20; old app notes 1:132 (sub 5-7)
## SUB 2 | Religious Policy, Titles and Coronations
[132:2:0] - Regnal title **Alamgir**; epithet **"Zinda Pir"** (living saint) / Darvesh for his simple, pious life.
[132:2:1] - **Double coronation:** 1658 (after Samugarh) and **1659** (after Deorai). **Child's War (1686-90)** – first Mughal war with the English.
[132:2:2] TABLE head: Measure | Detail
  [132:2:2.0] Jizya | Re-imposed 1679 (Akbar had abolished it, 1564)
  [132:2:2.1] Temples | 1669 order – Kashi Vishwanath and Keshava Rai (Mathura) demolished
  [132:2:2.2] Muhtasibs | Officers who saw that people lived by the Sharia
  [132:2:2.3] Court customs | Jharokha darshan, tuladan, Navroz stopped; music banned at court – yet he played the veena
  [132:2:2.4] Zawabit | State-made secular regulations
[132:2:3] - **Jihad** = **holy war** – war to turn **dar-ul-harb** (land of non-believers) into **dar-ul-Islam**; the BPSC 1999 printed key "Dar-ul-Islam" is the aim, not the meaning.
[132:2:4] - Hindu nobles rose to about **31.6% (1679-1707)** (Athar Ali), many of them Marathas.
[132:2:5] - Titles of royal women: **Roshanara = Padshah Begum**; **Jahanara = Sahibat-uz-Zamani**.
[132:2:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 04 p.30-31; old app notes 1:132 (sub 0-1); Oxford Dictionary of Islam "jihad" (holy war)

=== NOTES 1:138 | Mughal Painting, Music, Language and Literature; Persian-sanskrit Translation Movement
## SUB 0 | Mughal Painting – Emperor-wise Evolution, Zenith and European Influence
[138:0:0] # Emperor → emphasis
[138:0:1] TABLE head: Emperor | Emphasis
  [138:0:1.0] Babur, Humayun | Humayun laid the foundation: brought the Persian masters Mir Sayyid Ali (of Tabriz) and Khwaja Abdus Samad from Persia (met at Tabriz/Kabul) – they formed the nucleus of the Mughal school, fusing Persian (Islamic) and Indian (non-Islamic) elements
  [138:0:1.1] Akbar | Separate painting department / atelier Tasvir Khana of 100+ painters under Abdus Samad; painting karkhanas at Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Lahore; frescoes at Fatehpur Sikri; mostly illustrated manuscripts (Hamzanama, Tutinama, Akbarnama, Razmnama) and portraits; 3-D figures, foreshortening; Persian style became Indianised
  [138:0:1.2] Jahangir | Zenith / golden age of Mughal painting; shift from illustrated manuscripts to albums and individual portraits; events of his own life, birds, flowers, animals (naturalism); his own private atelier, a keen judge who could name the artist of a painting; decorated margins; halo (nimbus) behind the emperor's head; patronised European and Persian art
  [138:0:1.3] Shah Jahan | More interested in architecture; formal court scenes, albums (muraqqas), floral borders, more gold and silver, artificial stillness; painters Mir Hashim, Anup, Chitra
  [138:0:1.4] Aurangzeb | Opposed pictorial art, withdrew patronage → painters moved to provincial courts (Awadh, Hyderabad, Mysore, Bengal), Rajasthan, the Punjab Hills and Bihar → fed the Rajput and Pahari schools
[138:0:2] - **Zenith under Jahangir** (UPSC 1996; State PSC; UKPSC Lower 2010) – not Akbar (built the atelier) or Shah Jahan (architecture). **Jahangir mainly patronised painting** (UPPCS 2016).
[138:0:3] - **Shift from illustrated manuscripts to albums and individual portraits = Jahangir** (UPSC 2019).
[138:0:4] - Subjects of Mughal painting: **battle scenes, animals-birds-nature, court scenes – all of the above** (UPPSC 1991).
[138:0:5] - NDA 2012: **Akbar's paintings were mostly book illustrations and portraits** (I) and **Mir Sayyid Ali + Abdus Samad formed the nucleus of the school fusing non-Islamic and Islamic elements** (II) – **both correct**.
[138:0:6] - **Foundation laid by Humayun** (UPPSC 2012), not Akbar.
[138:0:7] # European influence
[138:0:8] - European pictures reached **Akbar's court through the Portuguese (Jesuit priests)** → **portraiture** and **smaller distant objects for spatial depth**; Mughal style = muted naturalistic colour, perspective and shading. So **European painting was introduced in Akbar's court** (BPSC 2019) – not Jahangir's, and **not by Danish merchants**.
[138:0:9] - **First Jesuit mission from Goa** reached Akbar in **1580**: Father **Rudolf Acquaviva** with Father **Antonio Monserrate** and Brother Francis Henriques; they brought the **Polyglot Bible**, whose pictures Akbar showed to his painters.
[138:0:10] - **APPSC G2 Prelims 2024:** a (Humayun brought Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad) and b (Jahangir = golden period) are **correct**; c (European painting brought by **Danish merchants** under Jahangir) is **incorrect** → **c only**.
[138:0:11] > Exam angle: "zenith / golden age" and "albums and portraits" = Jahangir; "foundation" = Humayun; "European painting arrived" = Akbar via the Portuguese.
[138:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 4 p.13-14 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-04.txt); NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian History Part 2 p.16-17 (#71); Nitin Singhania, Indian Art and Culture, Ch.2 (src/indian-history/singhania-art-culture-02.txt p.48-51)
## SUB 1 | Mughal Painters, Titles and Illustrated Manuscripts
[138:1:0] # Painter → reign → title / known for
[138:1:1] TABLE head: Painter | Reign | Title / known for
  [138:1:1.0] Mir Sayyid Ali | Humayun–Akbar | Persian master of Tabriz; first led the Hamzanama
  [138:1:1.1] Abdus Samad | Humayun–Akbar | Shirin Qalam; headed Akbar's atelier; completed the Hamzanama
  [138:1:1.2] Daswant(h) | Akbar | Leading painter of Akbar; son of a potter; Razmnama
  [138:1:1.3] Basawan | Akbar | Leading Akbar-era master (not Jahangir's)
  [138:1:1.4] Kesu, Lal, Mukund, Miskin, Jagan, Mahesh, Khemkaran, Tara | Akbar | Listed by Abul Fazl in the Ain-i-Akbari
  [138:1:1.5] Muhammad Husain Kashmiri | Akbar | Calligrapher, title Zari Qalam / Zarin Qalam
  [138:1:1.6] Ustad Mansur | Jahangir | Greatest painter of birds, animals, flowers (flora and fauna); title Nadir-ul-Asr (Nadir-ul-Asra)
  [138:1:1.7] Abul Hasan | Jahangir | Portraits; title Nadir-uz-Zaman (Nadir-ul-Zaman); painted Jahangir embracing Shah Abbas of Persia
  [138:1:1.8] Bishan Das | Jahangir | Master of portraiture; sent by Jahangir to Persia with the embassy to Shah Abbas to paint the Shah and his court
  [138:1:1.9] Manohar | Akbar–Jahangir | Son of Basawan; court portraits
  [138:1:1.10] Aqa Reza, Farrukh Beg, Govardhan, Muhammad Nadir, Muhammad Murad, Madhav, Daulat | Jahangir | Other Jahangiri painters
[138:1:2] - **Jahangir's painters = Manohar, Bishan Das, Mansur; Basawan = Akbar** → "2, 3, 4 only" (UKPSC 2025). **Abul Hasan + Aqa Reza = Jahangiri** (II and III), while Abdus Samad and Mir Sayyid Ali served **Humayun and Akbar** (UPPSC 2012; MPPSC 2010).
[138:1:3] - **Kalyan Das** was not one of Akbar's court painters (CDS 2019); Daswanth, Abdus Samad and Basawan were.
[138:1:4] - **Famous painter of Akbar = Daswant** (RAS 1992); Abul Hasan and Mansur belong to Jahangir.
[138:1:5] # Illustrated manuscripts
[138:1:6] TABLE head: Manuscript | Reign / persons | Nature
  [138:1:6.0] Dastan-i-Amir Hamza (Hamzanama) | Begun under Humayun, finished under Akbar; supervised first by Mir Sayyid Ali, then Abdus Samad | First great Mughal illustrated manuscript; tales of Amir Hamza; ~100 artists, ~1,400 paintings; 15 years
  [138:1:6.1] Baburnama | Copies illustrated under Akbar | Babur's memoir
  [138:1:6.2] Akbarnama | Akbar – Abul Fazl | Extensively illustrated official history
  [138:1:6.3] Razmnama | Akbar (Maktab Khana) | Persian Mahabharata, illustrated
  [138:1:6.4] Tutinama, Anvar-i-Suhaili, Gulistan of Sadi | Akbar | Illustrated
  [138:1:6.5] Tarikh-i-Alfi | Akbar (1582-88) | History of the first thousand years of Islam; mainly a text chronicle
  [138:1:6.6] Ayar-i-Danish | Jahangir's atelier | Animal fable, illustrated
  [138:1:6.7] Padshahnama | Shah Jahan – Abdul Hamid Lahori | Major illustrated history
[138:1:7] - **Hamzanama illustrated by:** keys give **Abdus Samad** (BPSC 2004; State PSC), who completed it; Mir Sayyid Ali began it, so both are right.

## SUB 3 | Music at the Mughal Court
[138:3:0] # Musicians
[138:3:1] TABLE head: Musician | Facts
  [138:3:1.0] Tansen | Original name Ramtanu Pande (Tanna Mishra); trained at Man Singh Tomar's Gwalior school; disciple of Swami Haridas; first at the court of Raja Ramchandra of Rewa (Bandhavgarh) – Akbar sent a firman for him; one of Akbar's Navaratnas; composed dhrupads on Hindu gods and on his patrons; invented ragas (Mian ki Todi, Mian ki Malhar, Darbari Kanada); tomb at Gwalior
  [138:3:1.1] Tansen's titles | 'Tansen' from Raja Vikramjit of Gwalior – NOT from Akbar; 'Mian' from Akbar
  [138:3:1.2] Baiju Bawra | Dhrupad singer at the court of Raja Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior, later of Bahadur Shah of Gujarat
  [138:3:1.3] Swami Haridas | Dhrupad singer of Akbar's period (Vrindavan), Tansen's guru
  [138:3:1.4] Vilas Khan | Tansen's son; main singer under Jahangir
  [138:3:1.5] Baz Bahadur | Last Sultan of Malwa (1555-62), musician-poet; Rupmati; later served Akbar
[138:3:2] - **Dhrupad singers of Akbar's reign: Tansen and Haridas** (1 and 2); Vilas Khan belongs to Jahangir.
[138:3:3] - Abul Fazl lists **36 singers** at Akbar's court. **Aurangzeb** ended court music yet **played the veena**; many Persian works on music date from his reign.
[138:3:4] # Form → origin / patron
[138:3:5] TABLE head: Form | Origin / patron
  [138:3:5.0] Dhrupad | Oldest Hindustani vocal form; roots in Vedic chanting; devotional/spiritual; alap uses Sanskrit syllables from mantras; developed by Raja Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior (1486-1516) – before the Mughals; non-Islamic (indigenous) in character
  [138:3:5.1] Khayal | Persian-influenced; Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela' – composers Sadarang and Adarang
  [138:3:5.2] Tappa | Folk songs of camel riders of the north-west; made a court form under Muhammad Shah; refined by Shori Miyan (Lucknow, late 18th c.)
  [138:3:5.3] Qawwali | Sufi (Islamic) devotional form
[138:3:6] - UPSC 2012 Dhrupad: 1 (originated in Rajput kingdoms during the Mughal period) is **wrong**; 2 and 3 are right → **2 and 3**.
[138:3:7] - **Mal Gurjari** = a **raga** of Man Singh Tomar, not a person; greats = Man Singh Tomar, Tansen, Sadarang-Adarang.
[138:3:8] - **Sitar** = Persian long-necked lute (**setar**) + Indian **veena**.
[138:3:9] # Hindustani music – instruments and ragas
[138:3:10] - **Ustad Amjad Ali Khan = sarod**; Ravi Shankar = sitar; Zakir Hussain = tabla.
[138:3:11] - **Todi** = early-morning raga; Bhimpalasi = afternoon; Bhopali = evening; Darbari Kanada = late night.
[138:3:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 4 p.1-2, p.15; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian History Part 1 p.115 (#47); Singhania Ch.5 p.144, p.152-153
[138:3:13] - **CGPSC 2020 Akbar statements:** **Man Bai, Man Singh's sister, married Jahangir (Salim)** – Akbar married Harkha Bai, Bharmal's daughter; **Todar Mal headed revenue**, not the army; only 'Abul Fazl wrote the Ain-i-Akbari' is true.
## SUB 4 | Translation Movement and Dara Shikoh
[138:4:0] # Akbar's translation department
[138:4:1] - **Maktab Khana** at **Fatehpur Sikri**, under **Faizi**; rendered **Sanskrit, Arabic, Turki and Greek** works into **Persian**.
[138:4:2] TABLE head: Persian work | Original | Translator | Reign
  [138:4:2.0] Razmnama ("Book of Wars") | Mahabharata | Badauni, Naqib Khan, Mulla Sheri, with Faizi | Akbar
  [138:4:2.1] Ramayana (Persian) | Valmiki Ramayana | Abdul Qadir Badauni | Akbar
  [138:4:2.2] Atharvaveda | Atharvaveda | Haji Ibrahim Sirhindi | Akbar
  [138:4:2.3] Lilavati | Bhaskaracharya's mathematics | Faizi | Akbar
  [138:4:2.4] Jog Bashisht | Yoga Vasistha | Nizamuddin Panipati, for Prince Salim | Akbar
  [138:4:2.5] Rajatarangini | Kalhana | Maulana Shah Muhammad Shahabadi | Akbar
  [138:4:2.6] Kaliyadaman, Ayar-i-Danish | Panchatantra (Ayar-i-Danish) | Abul Fazl | Akbar
  [138:4:2.7] Anwar-i-Suhaili | Panchatantra | Mulla Husain Waiz Kashifi | –
  [138:4:2.8] Kalila-wa-Dimnah | Panchatantra | Nasrullah Munshi Shirazi | –
  [138:4:2.9] Mufarrih-ul-Qulub | Hitopadesha | Taj-ul-Mali (Tajuddin Maliki) | –
  [138:4:2.10] Sirr-i-Akbar ("The Great Secret", 1657) | 52 Upanishads | Dara Shikoh | Shah Jahan
[138:4:3] - **Molla Ramayanam** – Telugu (not a Persian translation).
[138:4:4] # Dara Shikoh
[138:4:5] - **Shah Jahan's eldest son**; **Qadiri** Sufi, disciple of **Miyan Mir** of Lahore (and Mulla Shah Badakhshi).
[138:4:6] - Translated the **Upanishads (Sirr-i-Akbar)**, the **Bhagavad Gita** and the Yoga Vasistha into Persian – the answer to "**first Muslim to study Hindu scriptures**" in keys.
[138:4:7] - Original work **Majma-ul-Bahrain** ("Mingling of the Two Oceans") – common ground of **Sufism and Vedanta**.
[138:4:8] - Sirr-i-Akbar's Latin version by **Anquetil-Duperron** took the Upanishads to Europe.
[138:4:9] > Exam angle: Razmnama = Mahabharata; Sirr-i-Akbar = Upanishads, by Dara under Shah Jahan (not Akbar); Yoga Vasistha = Akbar's reign.
[138:4:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 4 p.9-10; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian History Part 2 p.36 (#85); Singhania (src/indian-history/singhania-art-culture-04.txt p.91)
## SUB 5 | Hindi Literature and Languages – Persian, Urdu, Deccani
[138:5:0] # Hindi poets
[138:5:1] - **16th-17th centuries = golden age of Hindi literature**; Akbar extended patronage to Hindi.
[138:5:2] TABLE head: Poet | Works | Period
  [138:5:2.0] Malik Muhammad Jayasi | Padmavat (Awadhi), Akhiri Kalam (1529-30) | Babur's time – keyed as the first Hindi scholar of the Mughal period
  [138:5:2.1] Tulsidas | Ramcharitmanas (Awadhi, begun 1574 – Akbar's reign), Vinay Patrika | Contemporary of Akbar and Jahangir; not a court poet
  [138:5:2.2] Surdas | Sur Sagar | Akbar's age
  [138:5:2.3] Keshavdas | Ramachandrika, Kavipriya, Rasikpriya, Ratan Bavani | Bundela court of Orchha
  [138:5:2.4] Padmakar | Ram Rasayan, Ganga Lahari, Prabodh Pachasa | Later poet – Ram Rasayan is not by Keshavdas
  [138:5:2.5] Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khana | Hindi dohas; Persian Baburnama | Akbar's Navaratna – the Muslim scholar with the biggest contribution to Hindi
  [138:5:2.6] Kavindracharya Saraswati | Kavindra-kalpataru | Shah Jahan; got the pilgrim tax at Banaras and Prayag remitted
[138:5:3] # Languages
[138:5:4] - **Persian = court language** of the Mughals (state language till **1835**) – not Turkish, Arabic or Urdu.
[138:5:5] - **Urdu** (Zaban-i-Hindavi → Rekhta) grew in **military camps and bazaars**; first encouraged by the Deccan sultans; **Muhammad Shah** was the first Mughal to encourage Urdu (invited the Deccani poet Wali); later courts of **Delhi and Lucknow**.
[138:5:6] - **Mirza Ghalib**: born at **Agra** (1797), settled in Delhi.
[138:5:7] - **Deccani (Dakhni) Urdu** under the Qutb Shahis: **Mulla Khiali** – first Deccani poetry in Telangana; **Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah** – first Urdu poet with a diwan, built the Charminar; **Abdullah Qutb Shah's era = Golden Age of Urdu**; **Ghavvasi** – Tuti Nama (1639) from the Sanskrit Shuka Saptati.
[138:5:8] - Qutb Shahi official language **Persian**, people's language **Telugu**; translation + painting + Hindavi/Urdu = **composite Indo-Persian culture**.
[138:5:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 4 p.9-11; NextGen Part 5 p.14-15; app notes 1:138 sub 6-7 (old-notes.txt)
## SUB 6 | Regional and Later Painting Schools
[138:6:0] TABLE head: School | Region / features
  [138:6:0.0] Rajput | Rajasthan; Hindu epics, love legends; bold colours, flat; Jaipur and Nathdwara centres
  [138:6:0.1] Pahari | North-western Himalayan hill states (Himachal, J&K, Tehri/Paudi Garhwal); 17th-19th c.
  [138:6:0.2] Kangra | Pahari sub-school; peak under Raja Sansar Chand
  [138:6:0.3] Kishangarh | Rajasthan; patron Raja Sawant Singh (pen-name Nagari Das, throne 1748, Krishna verses, Nimbarka sect); Bani Thani by Nihal Chand, inspired by Sawant Singh's poem Bihari Jas Chandrika; Radha-Krishna theme
  [138:6:0.4] Deccani | Began at the Bahmani court; at Golconda Mir Hashim
  [138:6:0.5] Kalighat | Bengal, 19th c.; indigenous bazaar style (Kali, Sita-Rama, Radha-Krishna) – not affected by Mughal painting
  [138:6:0.6] Company paintings | 18th-19th c. hybrid of Indian and European styles for the East India Company
[138:6:1] - **Mughal painting influenced the Pahari, Rajasthani and Kangra schools; Kalighat was not affected** (UPSC 1995).
[138:6:2] - Pahari, Rajput, Mughal and Kangra **schools = styles of painting** (UPPCS 1994).
[138:6:3] - **CDS 2015 (18th-early 19th c. visual culture):** Patna and Murshidabad painters moved to Calcutta and made **English-style watercolours** (I); **landscape and portraiture** became important (II); **Zayn-al-Din, Bhawani Das and Ram Das** made albums of Indian birds and animals for the English (Impey) (III) – all true; IV is false, **European artists did visit regional courts** (Tilly Kettle, Zoffany at Lucknow) → **I, II and III**.
[138:6:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian History Part 2 p.17 (#71); NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 4 p.14; Singhania Ch.2 p.64-65

=== NOTES 1:139 | Decline of the Mughal Empire – Causes, Historiography, Later Mughals and Successor States
## SUB 0 | Later Mughals – Order, Reigns and Epithets
[139:0:0] TABLE head: Ruler | Reign | Key facts
  [139:0:0.0] Bahadur Shah I (Muazzam; Shah Alam I) | 1707-12 | Succeeded Aurangzeb (1707); released Shahu (1707); called "Shah-i-Bekhabar"
  [139:0:0.1] Jahandar Shah | 1712-13 | Wazir Zulfiqar Khan; mistress Lal Kunwar; "Lampat" (the profligate); defeated by his nephew Farrukhsiyar (with the Sayyids)
  [139:0:0.2] Farrukhsiyar | 1713-19 | Puppet of the Sayyid brothers; Banda Bahadur executed (1716); 1717 farman to the English; blinded and killed by the Sayyids
  [139:0:0.3] Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela' (Roshan Akhtar) | 1719-48 | Longest later-Mughal reign (~29 yrs); Sayyids removed (1720); Nadir Shah at Karnal, 1739; Abdali's first raid 1748
  [139:0:0.4] Ahmad Shah | 1748-54 | Rule left to Udham Bai (queen mother) and the eunuch Javed Khan – "eunuchs and ladies"; blinded and deposed by Imad-ul-Mulk (1754)
  [139:0:0.5] Alamgir II | 1754-59 | Plassey (1757); Abdali in Delhi (1757); Punjab and Multan ceded; murdered by Imad-ul-Mulk
  [139:0:0.6] Shah Alam II (Ali Gauhar) | 1759-1806 | Panipat III (1761), Buxar (1764); first Mughal pensioner of the Company; blinded by Ghulam Qadir Rohilla (1788); English took Delhi 1803
  [139:0:0.7] Akbar II | 1806-37 | Gave Ram Mohan Roy the title "Raja"
  [139:0:0.8] Bahadur Shah II (Zafar) | 1837-57 | Son of Akbar II; last Mughal emperor; exiled to Rangoon after 1857 (died 1862)
[139:0:1] - **Order (APPSC G1, UPPSC 2018, UPRO 2023):** **Bahadur Shah I → Jahandar Shah → Farrukhsiyar → Muhammad Shah → Ahmad Shah → Alamgir II → Shah Alam II**.
[139:0:2] - **Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela':** wine, beauty, animal fights, apathy to administration; **last emperor to sit on the Peacock Throne** (Takht-i-Taus / Mayur Singhasan) – Nadir Shah carried it off in 1739.
[139:0:3] - **Eunuchs and ladies dominated the court under Ahmad Shah (1748-54)** – Udham Bai with the eunuch Javed Khan (PMF, Spectrum); some guides wrongly print Muhammad Shah.
[139:0:4] - **Shah Alam II's exile:** **not allowed into Delhi by Wazir Ghaziuddin (Imad-ul-Mulk)**; stayed away for years out of fear of his wazir and court intrigue (UPSC 2003 A-R: A and R true, R not the explanation); lived at **Allahabad** under Company protection after Buxar; returned to Delhi **1771-72** with **Mahadji Scindia**.
[139:0:5] - **Shrunken empire:** by Zafar's time Mughal authority ran only round Delhi to **Palam** – "**Chandni Chowk (Lal Qila) to Palam**"; the saying "Sultanat-e-Shah Alam, az Dilli ta Palam" was first made of Shah Alam II.
[139:0:6] - Not matched: Ahmad Shah = 1748-**54** (not 1757); exiled to Rangoon = **Bahadur Shah II**, not Muhammad Shah; Sayyids dominated **Farrukhsiyar**, not Jahandar Shah.
[139:0:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.20-21 (list of Mughal emperors); PMF Modern History 01 p.38-41; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.117 (Udham Bai, Javed Khan); Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India ch.4; old app notes 1:139 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Asaf Jahi Hyderabad – Founding and the Nizams
[139:1:0] - **Founder:** **Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan Siddiqi = Chin Qilich Khan = Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I** – first Nizam; founded the **Asaf Jahi dynasty (Asafzahi clan)** and **Hyderabad State in 1724** (APPSC G1 2003, G2 1993, 2002, 2011, DL 2020).
[139:1:1] - **1724:** defeated the Mughal governor **Mubariz Khan** at **Shakar Kheda** → virtually independent. **Died 1748** (APPSC G2 1993, MPDO 1997).
[139:1:2] - Background: Hyderabad first envisaged by Deccan viceroy **Zulfiqar Khan** (through **Daud Khan**, from 1708); Farrukhsiyar made him **Subedar of the Deccan**; he helped **overthrow the Sayyids**; **Wazir** (1722-24) before leaving for the Deccan.
[139:1:3] - Tolerant: **Puran Chand** as Diwan; Mughal-type jagirdari administration; **kept the Marathas out** in his lifetime (but lost at Palkhed 1728).
[139:1:4] TABLE head: Title | Conferred by
  [139:1:4.0] Chin Qilich Khan | Aurangzeb
  [139:1:4.1] Nizam-ul-Mulk | Farrukhsiyar (1713)
  [139:1:4.2] Asaf Jah | Muhammad Shah (1725)
[139:1:5] - **CGPSC 2022 trap:** Kilich Khan was **not** Mubariz Khan (Mubariz was the man he defeated); the title Asaf Jah was **not** given by Zulfiqar Khan.
[139:1:6] TABLE head: Nizam | Rule / fact
  [139:1:6.0] Asaf Jah I (Nizam-ul-Mulk) | 1724-48
  [139:1:6.1] Nasir Jung, Muzaffar Jung, Salabat Jung | 1748-62 – not counted among the seven Nizams (never received the title Asaf Jah)
  [139:1:6.2] Nizam Ali Khan (Asaf Jah II) | 1762-1803; first Indian ruler to accept Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance (1798)
  [139:1:6.3] Mir Mahbub Ali Khan | 1869-1911
  [139:1:6.4] Mir Osman Ali Khan | 1911-48; seventh and last Nizam; founded Osmania University
[139:1:7] - **Hyderabad city ≠ Hyderabad State:** the city was founded in **1591 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah**; the **State** (Asaf Jahi dominion) by Asaf Jah I in 1724 (APPSC 2022: only statement I correct).
[139:1:8] - **Operation Polo (September 1948)** integrated Hyderabad State into the Indian Union.
[139:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.17, p.35 (Hyderabad); PMF Modern History 01 p.58; Rocket Sheets Indian History 02 p.9 (Chin Qilich Khan = Nizam-ul-Mulk / Asaf Jah); old app notes 1:139 sub 6
## SUB 2 | Other Successor States – Awadh, Bengal, Carnatic, Rohilkhand, Rajputs, Jats
[139:2:0] TABLE head: State | Founder | Mughal post / fact
  [139:2:0.0] Awadh | Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk | Subedar of Awadh 1722; first Nawab of Oudh; independent under Muhammad Shah
  [139:2:0.1] Bengal | Murshid Quli Khan | Diwan (1700), then Nazim; started revenue farming (ijaradari)
  [139:2:0.2] Carnatic (Arcot) | Saadatullah Khan | Nawab under the Nizam; made nephew Dost Ali heir without the Nizam's approval
  [139:2:0.3] Rohilkhand | Ali Muhammad Khan | Afghan; carved it out during Nadir Shah's invasion
  [139:2:0.4] Farrukhabad | Muhammad Khan Bangash | Afghan adventurer
  [139:2:0.5] Jaipur (Amber) | Sawai Jai Singh II (1699-1743) | Founded Jaipur; astronomer
[139:2:1] - **Awadh:** Saadat Khan **joined the plot against the Sayyids** (siding with Muhammad Shah) – both statements true (UPRO 2023). **Safdar Jung** (nephew and son-in-law) = **Nawab of Awadh and Mughal Wazir** (from 1748) – hence the "**Nawab Wazir**" style; **Shuja-ud-Daula** was later wazir too, sided with Abdali at Panipat and lost at Buxar.
[139:2:2] - **First Nawab (Wazir) of Awadh = Saadat Khan** (CDS 2018 key); the wazirship itself began with Safdar Jung.
[139:2:3] - **Turanis** established Hyderabad; **Iranis** established Oudh. **Saadat Khan = Awadh; Saadatullah Khan = Carnatic**.
[139:2:4] - **Match (APPSC G1):** Husain Ali Khan – a Sayyid brother; Murshid Quli Khan – Bengal; Chin Qilich Khan – Nizam of Hyderabad; Safdar Jung – Awadh.
[139:2:5] - **Pairs (AEE):** Hyderabad – Nizam-ul-Mulk ✓; Bengal – **not** Saadat Ali Khan; Awadh – **not** Murshid Quli Khan.
[139:2:6] - **Sawai Jai Singh II:** **observatories (Jantar Mantar) at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura**; drew up the astronomical tables **Zij-i-Muhammad Shahi** (named for Muhammad Shah); law against lavish wedding expenses.
[139:2:7] - **Jats (Bharatpur):** Churaman, Badan Singh; **Suraj Mal** (1755-63) = "**Plato of the Jat tribe**", built **Lohagarh** fort.
[139:2:8] - Titles in options: Saadat Khan = **Burhan-ul-Mulk**; **Sarvalokeshvara = Vima Kadphises** (Kushana), not Saadat Khan.
[139:2:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.17, p.36-37 (Carnatic, Awadh, Rajputana, Rohilkhand); PMF Modern History 01 p.61 (Awadh), p.63-64 (Bengal), p.83 (Jai Singh); Rocket Sheets Indian History 02 p.9; CDS 2018 key (examrobot.com, testbook.com); old app notes 1:139 sub 5
## SUB 3 | Invasions – Nadir Shah, Ahmad Shah Abdali and Earlier Invaders
[139:3:0] TABLE head: Invader | Year | Consequence
  [139:3:0.0] Nadir Shah (Persia) | 1739 | Beat Muhammad Shah at Karnal; sacked Delhi; took the Koh-i-Noor and Peacock Throne
  [139:3:0.1] Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani, Afghan) | Raids 1748-67 | Had been Nadir Shah's general; Punjab and Multan ceded; Delhi looted 1757; Third Panipat 1761
[139:3:1] - Nadir Shah's contemporary historian: **Anand Ram Mukhlis**. Koh-i-Noor plunderer = **Nadir Shah** (APPSC 2018), not Abdali or Timur.
[139:3:2] - **1757:** Abdali placed **Alamgir II** on the throne, **Imad-ul-Mulk** as wazir and the Rohilla **Najib Khan (Najib-ud-Daulah)**, his confidant, as chief agent / Mir Bakhshi.
[139:3:3] - **Chronology (UKPSC 2002):** **Genghis Khan (Indus, under Iltutmish, 1221) → Timur (sacked Delhi 1398) → Nadir Shah (1739) → Abdali (1748-67)**.
[139:3:4] TABLE head: Earlier invader | Period | Fact
  [139:3:4.0] Darius I (Persia) | c. 518 BCE | First foreign ruler to invade NW India
  [139:3:4.1] Alexander | 326 BCE | Defeated Porus on the Hydaspes (Jhelum)
  [139:3:4.2] Sakas / Kushanas | 1st c. BCE / 1st c. CE | Sakas in western India; Kushanas under Kanishka
  [139:3:4.3] Hunas | 5th-6th c. | Yashodharman defeated Mihirakula
  [139:3:4.4] Muhammad bin Qasim | 712 | First successful Muslim invader – Sindh (not North India)
  [139:3:4.5] Mahmud of Ghazni | 1000-1027 | 17 raids
  [139:3:4.6] Muhammad Ghori | from 1175 | Tarain I (1191), Tarain II (1192), Chandawar (1194)
  [139:3:4.7] Timur | 1398 | Sacked Delhi under Nasiruddin Mahmud Tughlaq
  [139:3:4.8] Babur | 1526 | Panipat I vs Ibrahim Lodi (not Timur)
[139:3:5] - Order: Greeks → Kushanas → Hunas → Arabs.
[139:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.13 (Timur), p.21 (Nadir Shah 1739); PMF Modern History 01 p.41-43; old app notes 1:139 sub 3
## SUB 4 | Sayyid Brothers, Farmans and Grants
[139:4:0] - **Abdullah Khan = Wazir**; **Husain Ali Khan = Mir Bakhshi** – the "**king-makers**" (1713-20): made and unmade Farrukhsiyar, then puppets (Rafi-ud-Darajat, Rafi-ud-Daulah).
[139:4:1] - Eliminated under **Muhammad Shah** with **Nizam-ul-Mulk's** help; Husain Ali killed 1720; Saadat Khan sided with Muhammad Shah against them.
[139:4:2] TABLE head: Year | Grant | Content
  [139:4:2.0] 1717 | Farrukhsiyar's farman (Surman embassy) | English Company freed from customs duties in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year – the Company's "Magna Carta"
  [139:4:2.1] 1719 | Grant through the Sayyids | Shahu recognised; swarajya + chauth and sardeshmukhi of the six Deccan subas to Balaji Vishwanath
[139:4:3] - **Murshid Quli Khan** accepted the 1717 customs exemption but refused the 38 villages near Calcutta.
[139:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.10, p.12 (1717 farman); PMF Modern History 01 p.67 (1719 grant); old app notes 1:139 sub 2, 4
## SUB 5 | Causes and Historiography of Decline
[139:5:0] - **Greatest extent under Aurangzeb:** Kashmir to **Jinji**, Hindukush to Chittagong; long **Deccan wars** (last ~27 years) drained the treasury → foundations weakened after him.
[139:5:1] - Causes: weak successors and noble factions (Iranis, Turanis, Hindustanis); **jagirdari and agrarian crises**; Maratha rise; **invasions of Nadir Shah and Abdali**; European companies. Power gap filled by **regional states → Marathas → East India Company**.
[139:5:2] TABLE head: Historian | Work | View
  [139:5:2.0] Jadunath Sarkar | History of Aurangzeb; Fall of the Mughal Empire | Aurangzeb's religious policy; weak successors
  [139:5:2.1] Irfan Habib | The Agrarian System of Mughal India (1963) | Agrarian crisis – the state "itself the principal instrument of exploitation" (CDS 2017)
  [139:5:2.2] Satish Chandra | Parties and Politics at the Mughal Court | Jagirdari crisis – too few jagirs for too many nobles
  [139:5:2.3] M. Athar Ali | The Mughal Nobility under Aurangzeb | Enlarged nobility (Deccanis, Marathas) worsened the jagir shortage
  [139:5:2.4] W.H. Moreland | From Akbar to Aurangzeb | Economic exploitation and stagnation
  [139:5:2.5] François Bernier | Travels in the Mogul Empire | No private property in land
[139:5:3] - **Revisionist view:** the 18th century = **regional growth**, not collapse; successor states had their own economy and law-and-order and controlled the peasant surplus (NextGen).
[139:5:4] - **Marathas = strongest native power** after the Mughals, but they had **no concept of a united Indian nation** (A true, R false).
[139:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.14 (books: Sarkar, Habib), p.35 (18th-century states); PMF Modern History 01 p.48 (Habib, Satish Chandra); PMF Modern History 01 p.66 (Maratha limits); old app notes 1:139 sub 7-8
