=== NOTES 1:140 | Rise of the Marathas – Shivaji's Career, Ashtapradhan, Revenue System, Chauth and Sardeshmukhi
## SUB 0 | Ashtapradhan and Shivaji's Officials
[140:0:0] TABLE head: Minister | Persian / other title | Portfolio
  [140:0:0.0] Peshwa | Mukhya Pradhan | Prime Minister, general administration
  [140:0:0.1] Amatya | Majumdar (Mazumdar) | Finance – treasury, accounts, revenue
  [140:0:0.2] Sachiv | Shurunavis (Surnis) | Royal correspondence and records (PMF: land revenue)
  [140:0:0.3] Mantri | Waqia-navis (Waknis) | Intelligence, king's diary of daily doings and court happenings, household
  [140:0:0.4] Senapati | Sar-i-Naubat (Sarnobat) | Military commander
  [140:0:0.5] Sumant | Dabir | Foreign affairs; master of ceremonies, received envoys
  [140:0:0.6] Nyayadhish | – | Chief justice
  [140:0:0.7] Panditrao | Danadhyaksha | Religious affairs and charitable grants
[140:0:1] - **Shivaji's council of eight (by 1674)** – Maratha, not Gupta, Chola, Vijayanagara, Harsha or Mughal (UPSC 1995, IAS 1998, BPSC 2019 …).
[140:0:2] - **Advisory only**: each minister was **directly responsible to the Chhatrapati**; Shivaji could accept or reject advice; not a cabinet – so "each held **independent** charge" is false (UPPCS 1997: A true, R false). Ashtapradhan advisory vs the hierarchical Mughal wazir system.
[140:0:3] - Posts **not hereditary**; ministers transferable. All except **Panditrao and Nyayadhish** led campaigns. The Peshwa became hereditary and supreme only later (1720 onwards).
[140:0:4] - **All four Persian titles – Mazumdar, Dabir, Waqia-navis, Surnis – were Ashtapradhan officers** (CGPSC 2017).
[140:0:5] - **Chitnis** = secretary who **assisted the king with correspondence** (CDS 2002).
[140:0:6] - **Sarnobat** also = military officer of a fort; **Deshmukh** (pargana) collected **land revenue** for the state (APPSC G1 2019).
[140:0:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.129-130 (Ashta Pradhan); NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.16 (Peshwa, Amatya, Sumant); old app notes 1:140 sub 4
## SUB 1 | Shivaji's Career – Birth, Guru, Forts, Bijapur and the Mughals
[140:1:0] - **Born at Shivneri fort** near Pune, **19 February 1630** (Maharashtra government date; PMF); Jadunath Sarkar's **1627** gives the key "**1627, 1674**" (UPPCS 2015). Parents **Shahaji Bhonsle and Jijabai**; **Dadaji Kondadev** = keeper of the **Pune jagir** and tutor.
[140:1:1] - **Pune jagir:** first granted to grandfather Maloji by the **Nizam Shahis** (1595); **Shahaji held it as a mansabdar of Bijapur (Adil Shahi)** after 1636 – the key "Adil Shahi" (MPPSC 2010).
[140:1:2] - **Guru:** **Samarth Ramdas** (Dasbodh, Shivastuti); saint contemporary **Tukaram**. Ramdas, not Eknath (died 1599), is the APPSC G1 2012 answer.
[140:1:3] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [140:1:3.0] 1646 | Torna – first fort, from Bijapur, at age 16
  [140:1:3.1] 1656 | Raigad (and Javli) from the Mores of Javli – later capital
  [140:1:3.2] 1659 | Afzal Khan (Bijapur) killed with a wagh nakh at the foot of Pratapgad
  [140:1:3.3] 1660 | Siddi Jauhar besieges Panhala; escape to Vishalgad
  [140:1:3.4] 1663 | Night raid on Shaista Khan (Aurangzeb's maternal uncle, sent 1660) at Pune (Lal Mahal)
  [140:1:3.5] 1664, 1670 | Surat sacked twice
  [140:1:3.6] 1665 | Treaty of Purandar with Raja Jai Singh of Amber (with Diler Khan): 23 of 35 forts ceded; Sambhaji to Mughal service
  [140:1:3.7] 1666 | Agra – house arrest at Jaipur Bhawan; escaped with Sambhaji in fruit/sweet baskets
  [140:1:3.8] 1672 | Salher – Mughals beaten in open battle
  [140:1:3.9] 1674 | Coronation at Raigad (6 June)
  [140:1:3.10] 1677 | Hyderabad visit; Karnataka campaign – Gingee, Vellore (from Venkoji/Ekoji), Ballari
  [140:1:3.11] 1680 | Died (3 April)
[140:1:4] - After Agra he **recaptured** most Purandar forts (Purandar, Lohagarh, Mahuli …) – but **Shivneri**, held by the Mughals, was **never retaken** (UPPSC 2009).
[140:1:5] - **Coronation:** priest **Gaga Bhatt** (Vishweshwar) of Banaras; titles "**Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati**" and **Haindava Dharmoddharak** (not "Hindavi Sultan"); era **Rajyabhisheka Shaka**.
[140:1:6] - **Golconda alliance (1677, AP angle):** with **Abul Hasan Tana Shah** via **Madanna (Mir Jumla)** and **Akkanna (Sar Lashkar)** – Golconda to fund the southern conquests and share the spoils (Shivaji did not share).
[140:1:7] - **Causes of the Maratha rise:** Sahyadri geography (**geographical security**), **Bhakti saints** (religious consciousness), service in **Bijapur and Ahmadnagar** (political awakening) – all of the above (UPPSC 1992); Aurangzeb's 27-year Deccan war **drained** Mughal finances.
[140:1:8] - **Big Deshmukhs opposed Shivaji** – they wanted to stay feudal lords of Bijapur (UPPCS 2024: A and R true, R explains A).
[140:1:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.127-129 (Shivneri 1630, Pune jagir, Afzal Khan, Shaista Khan, Purandar 23/35, Agra, 1674 coronation); NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.13 (Purandar); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shahaji (jagirdar of Pune in Bijapur); old app notes 1:140 sub 1-3
## SUB 2 | Revenue System – Chauth, Sardeshmukhi and Land Terms
[140:2:0] TABLE head: Levy | Rate | Nature
  [140:2:0.0] Chauth | 25% (one-fourth) of land revenue | Protection money levied on neighbouring territories outside direct Maratha rule (Mughalai) to be spared Maratha raids
  [140:2:0.1] Sardeshmukhi | Additional 10% | Claimed by the king's hereditary right as Sardeshmukh
[140:2:1] - The pair **Chauth and Sardeshmukhi** = Maratha taxation (not iqta–jagir, zat–sawar, polaj–parauti) (SSC CGL 2019).
[140:2:2] - Funded expansion and political hegemony **without the cost of direct governance**. Recognised by the **Mughals (1719)** and the **Nizam at Palkhed (1728)**; the 1795 chauth burden pushed the Nizam into the Subsidiary Alliance (1798).
[140:2:3] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [140:2:3.0] Ryotwari-type settlement | State dealt directly with the cultivator; demand 30%, later 40%
  [140:2:3.1] Kathi | Measuring rod – Annaji Datto's survey
  [140:2:3.2] Jirayat / Bagayat | Dry land / irrigated land
  [140:2:3.3] Saranjam | Service land grants – abolished by Shivaji, restored under Shahu and the Peshwas
  [140:2:3.4] Upari | Tenancy tenure of tenants-at-will (no hereditary rights); Thalkari / Mirasdar held hereditary rights
[140:2:4] - **Jagirs abolished** – officials paid in **cash**; hereditary rights of **deshmukhs and deshpandes** (watandars) curbed.
[140:2:5] TABLE head: Unit | Official
  [140:2:5.0] Prant (province) | Subedar / Sarsubedar
  [140:2:5.1] Pargana, Tarf | Deshmukh, Deshpande
  [140:2:5.2] Mauza (village) | Patil (head), Kulkarni (accountant)
[140:2:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.130 (chauth 25%, sardeshmukhi 10%, revenue 30-40%); NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.13, p.16 (Palkhed; watandar); old app notes 1:140 sub 5-6
## SUB 3 | Military, Navy, Coins and Records
[140:3:0] - **Guerrilla warfare (Ganimi Kava)** with swift cavalry in the Sahyadri; chain of **hill forts on the table mountains** of the Western Deccan – both statements true (CDS 2012).
[140:3:1] - **Over 300 forts**; each under three officers of equal rank – **Havaldar** (garrison commander), **Sabnis** (records), **Sarnaubat** (military).
[140:3:2] TABLE head: Fort type | Examples
  [140:3:2.0] Giri Durg (hill) | Raigad, Pratapgad, Torna, Rajgad, Sinhagad, Panhala
  [140:3:2.1] Bhu Durg (land) | Vishalgad
  [140:3:2.2] Jal Durg (sea) | Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg, Khanderi, Suvarnadurg, Kolaba
[140:3:3] - Cavalry: **Bargirs** – horses and arms from the **state**; **Shiledars** – **own horses**. Infantry: **Mavalis**.
[140:3:4] - **Navy:** sea forts guarded the **Konkan**; Shivaji = "**Father of the Indian Navy**".
[140:3:5] - **Cannons and ammunition** were obtained from the **Portuguese** (treaty supplies from Goa) (SSC 2011).
[140:3:6] - **UNESCO 2025:** "**Maratha Military Landscapes of India**" (12 forts) inscribed as World Heritage.
[140:3:7] TABLE head: Term | Meaning

## SUB 4 | Successors of Shivaji – Sambhaji, Rajaram, Tarabai, Shahu
[140:4:0] TABLE head: Ruler | Period | Key steps
  [140:4:0.0] Sambhaji | 1680-89 | Won the succession fight with Rajaram (backed by Shivaji's widow Soyarabai); sheltered Prince Akbar; captured at Sangameshwar and executed by Aurangzeb (1689)
  [140:4:0.1] Rajaram | 1689-1700 | Resisted from Gingee (Jinji); created the post of Pratinidhi
  [140:4:0.2] Tarabai (regent for Shivaji II) | 1700-07 | Rajaram's widow; led the struggle against the Mughals from 1700; led the Marathas when Aurangzeb died (1707)
  [140:4:0.3] Shahu | 1707-49 | Sambhaji's son; released by Bahadur Shah I (1707); beat Tarabai at Khed (1707); ruled from Satara; made Balaji Vishwanath Peshwa (1713)
[140:4:1] - **Order (UPPSC 2005):** **Sambhaji → Rajaram → Shivaji II (Tarabai) → Shahu**.
[140:4:2] - **Treaty of Warna (1731):** between **Sambhaji II of Kolhapur and Shahu of Satara** – Tarabai's line settled at **Kolhapur**.
[140:4:3] - **Current linkage:** **Aurangabad was renamed Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar** (state decision 2022, notified 2023) after Sambhaji; Osmanabad became Dharashiv.
[140:4:4] - Peak of Maratha power: **Attock to Cuttack**; major northern expansion under **Baji Rao I**.
[140:4:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.131 (Sambhaji, Rajaram, Tarabai); NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.13 (Warna), p.20 (Shahu released by Bahadur Shah I); old app notes 1:140 sub 9-10

=== NOTES 1:141 | Peshwas and the Maratha Confederacy; Third Battle of Panipat (1761); Three Anglo-maratha Wars
## SUB 0 | Third Battle of Panipat – 14 January 1761
[141:0:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [141:0:0.0] Date | 14 January 1761 (Panipat I = 1526, II = 1556)
  [141:0:0.1] Opponents | Marathas vs Ahmad Shah Abdali (Afghans) – not Mughals, Rajputs, Sikhs, English or Rohillas alone (APPSC G1 2019)
  [141:0:0.2] Maratha commander | Sadashiv Rao Bhau (overall); Vishwas Rao (Peshwa's son, nominal) – both killed
  [141:0:0.3] Artillery | Ibrahim Khan Gardi – the Muslim commander who died fighting for the Marathas (loyal, not a traitor)
  [141:0:0.4] Peshwa | Balaji Baji Rao – died soon after (June 1761)
  [141:0:0.5] Abdali's allies | Najib-ud-Daula (Rohilla, invited him) and Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh
  [141:0:0.6] Eyewitness historian | Kashiraj Pandit, an official of Shuja-ud-Daula
[141:0:1] - **Immediate cause (UPSC 2010):** the Marathas (Raghunath Rao, 1758) **expelled Abdali's son and viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore**.
[141:0:2] - **Causes of defeat (CDS 2002):** **Bhau's tactical errors**, **Abdali's superior generalship**, **large numbers of non-combatants** and baggage; no northern allies (Jats, Rajputs alienated); supply collapse – treachery of Gardi is **not** a cause.
[141:0:3] - **Coded message to the Peshwa:** "**Two pearls have been dissolved, 27 gold coins lost …**" – the defeated power was the **Peshwa's** (Vishwas Rao and Bhau = the pearls).
[141:0:4] - **Result:** Maratha northern ambition halted; vacuum helped the Company; "it decided not who was to rule India, but who was not"; recovery under **Madhav Rao I** within a decade.
[141:0:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History 01 p.69-70; NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.17-18; old app notes 1:141 sub 5
## SUB 1 | Peshwas and the Maratha Confederacy
[141:1:0] TABLE head: Peshwa | Tenure | Contribution
  [141:1:0.0] Balaji Vishwanath | 1713-20 | Made Peshwa by Shahu (1713); streamlined administration after Sambhaji; 1719 grant (swarajya, chauth, sardeshmukhi of the Deccan) via the Sayyids; assigned collection areas to sardars
  [141:1:0.1] Baji Rao I | 1720-40 | Most charismatic after Shivaji; Hindu Pad Padshahi; "strike the trunk, the branches will fall"; Palkhed 1728; Malwa, Bundelkhand; raided Delhi 1737; Bhopal / Doraha Sarai 1738 (Malwa)
  [141:1:0.2] Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) | 1740-61 | Zenith; Orissa 1751; Gujarat (Ahmedabad, 1753); Udgir 1760; Sangola 1750; lost Panipat
  [141:1:0.3] Madhav Rao I | 1761-72 | Revived power after Panipat – beat the Nizam, Haidar Ali, Rohillas, Rajputs, Jats; died 1772
  [141:1:0.4] Narayan Rao | 1772-73 | Murdered (uncle Raghunath Rao / Raghoba)
  [141:1:0.5] Madhav Rao II | 1774-95 | Infant; ruled through Nana Phadnavis (Barabhai); Kharda 1795
  [141:1:0.6] Baji Rao II | 1796-1818 | Treaty of Bassein (1802); last Peshwa
[141:1:1] - **Order (UPPCS 2004, 2025):** **Balaji Vishwanath → Baji Rao I → Balaji Baji Rao → Madhav Rao I**.
[141:1:2] - **Peshwa as virtual ruler:** office hereditary from 1720; after **Shahu's death (1749)** the **Sangola agreement (1750)** made the Chhatrapati nominal – the king became a non-entity from **Balaji Baji Rao's** time; by 1750 a **confederacy presided over by the Peshwa** (A and R true, R explains A). Seat: **Poona** (Chhatrapati at Satara).
[141:1:3] - **Confederacy:** areas were divided among military chiefs **in Shahu's reign** (Balaji Vishwanath's assignments; organised by **Baji Rao I** to satisfy the old chiefs under **Senapati Dabhade**). Main weakness: rivalries of semi-independent chiefs.
[141:1:4] TABLE head: House | Seat | Founder
  [141:1:4.0] Peshwa | Poona | Balaji Vishwanath
  [141:1:4.1] Bhonsle | Nagpur | Raghuji Bhonsle
  [141:1:4.2] Gaekwad | Baroda | Pilaji Gaekwad
  [141:1:4.3] Holkar | Indore | Malhar Rao Holkar
  [141:1:4.4] Scindia (Shinde) | Gwalior | Ranoji Scindia
[141:1:5] - **Nana Phadnavis** = "**Maratha Machiavelli / Chanakya of Maratha politics**"; led the **Barabhai**; died **1800**. **Mahadji Scindia** restored **Shah Alam II** to Delhi (1771-72).
[141:1:6] - **Shahu**, Shivaji's grandson, was the first Maratha chief to offer **nazr at the Ajmer dargah** of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti (RAS 2013).
[141:1:7] - **Pindaris** = irregular plundering horsemen with the **Maratha armies**; leaders **Chitu**, Karim Khan, Wasil Muhammad; crushed by **Lord Hastings (1817-18)**.
[141:1:8] - **Saranjam** = land assigned to chiefs for military service; **Peshwa Daftar** (Pune) in **Modi script**, preserved by **Elphinstone**.
[141:1:9] - By the **1720s** the Marathas had seized **Malwa and Gujarat** from the Mughals (NCERT VII).
[141:1:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.17 (Peshwas); PMF Modern History 01 p.66-69; Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India ch.5 (confederacy under Bajirao I in Shahu's name); NCERT Class VII ch.10; old app notes 1:141 sub 0-3
## SUB 2 | Battles with the Nizam and the Three Anglo-Maratha Wars
[141:2:0] TABLE head: Battle / treaty | Year | Result
  [141:2:0.0] Palkhed → Treaty of Mungi-Shevgaon | 1728 | Baji Rao I beat Nizam-ul-Mulk; chauth and sardeshmukhi of the Deccan conceded
  [141:2:0.1] Bhopal → Doraha Sarai | 1737-38 | Nizam ceded Malwa
  [141:2:0.2] Udgir / Rakshasbhuvan | 1760 / 1763 | Nizam defeated
  [141:2:0.3] Kharda | 1795 | Nizam defeated; blamed Sir John Shore's neutrality → Subsidiary Alliance (1798)
[141:2:1] - **First war (1775-82):** after **Narayan Rao's murder**; **Treaty of Surat (1775)** – Bombay to back **Raghunath Rao** with 2,500 troops; **Treaty of Purandar (1776)** – **Marathas and the English** (Calcutta council) annulled Surat; **Convention of Wadgaon (1779)** rejected by **Warren Hastings**; **Treaty of Salbai (1782)** with **Mahadji Scindia** – status quo.
[141:2:2] - **Raghunath Rao (Raghoba)** = uncle of Madhav Rao I and Narayan Rao; father of Baji Rao II.
[141:2:3] - **Road to the second war:** **Nana Phadnavis died (1800)** → **Holkar and Scindia fought over the weak Peshwa** (Holkar won at Poona, 1802) → Baji Rao II fled to the British.
[141:2:4] - **Second war (1803-05):** **Treaty of Bassein (1802)** – Baji Rao II accepted Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance; **Assaye** (Arthur Wellesley vs Scindia-Bhonsle), **Laswari** (Lord Lake vs Scindia); **Deogaon** (Bhonsle: Cuttack, Balasore), **Surji-Anjangaon** (Scindia).
[141:2:5] - **Third war (1817-18):** Governor-General **Lord Hastings**; Khadki, Koregaon, Sitabuldi, Mahidpur; **Peshwaship abolished in 1818** under **Baji Rao II**, pensioned to **Bithur near Kanpur**; small Satara state kept.
[141:2:6] - **Chronology (UPPCS 2024):** Nana Phadnavis's death (**1800**) → recall of Wellesley (**1805**) → **Vellore Mutiny (10 July 1806)** → Anglo-Nepalese war (**1814-16**).
[141:2:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India ch.5 (Surat, Purandar 1776, Wadgaon, Salbai); PMF Modern History 01 p.68, p.72 (Palkhed, Kharda); PMF Modern History 02 p.39-49 (wars, Bithur); NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 p.18-19; old app notes 1:141 sub 4, 6

=== NOTES 1:142 | Bhakti Movement – Origins, Alvars and Nayanars, Nirguna and Saguna Streams, Social Base
## SUB 0 | Alvars and Nayanars – the Tamil Beginning
[142:0:0] TABLE head: Feature | Alvars | Nayanars
  [142:0:0.0] Devotees of | Vishnu (Vaishnava) | Shiva (Shaiva)
  [142:0:0.1] Number | 12 | 63 (3 women)
  [142:0:0.2] Hymns / canon | Nalayira Divya Prabandham (4,000 hymns, "Tamil Veda"; called pasurams), compiled by Nathamuni (10th c.) | Tirumurai (12 books, "Fifth Veda"), compiled by Nambi Andar Nambi; Tevaram = hymns of Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar
  [142:0:0.3] Women | Andal – only woman Alvar | Karaikkal Ammaiyar
  [142:0:0.4] Notable | Poigai, Bhoothath, Pey = first three Alvars; Nammalvar = foremost (Tiruvaymoli); Periyalvar | Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar, Manikkavachakar = the Nalvar / Samayacharyas; Tiruvasagam = Manikkavachakar
[142:0:1] - **Bhakti movement was started by the Alvar (and Nayanar) saints** of the Tamil South, **6th-9th c.** – not by the Sufis, Surdas or Tulsidas.
[142:0:2] - **First Vaishnava devotees of South India = Alvars** (APPSC G2 2000, AP History PYQ; HPSC 2012) – not Nayanars, Bhagavatas or Virashaivas.
[142:0:3] - **Pasurams (pasuras)** = Tamil hymns of the Alvars **in praise of Vishnu** (AP Police 2016); Nayanar hymns on Shiva are the Tevaram.
[142:0:4] - **Composers of the Nalayira Divya Prabandham = the Alvars** (CDS 2018); Appar and Sambandar were Nayanars.
[142:0:5] - **Nayanars = Shaivites** (UP UDA 2006, UPRO 2014).
[142:0:6] - Both came from **all castes**, even "untouchables" (Panars, Pulaiyars), and were critical of Buddhism and Jainism.
[142:0:7] - **Periya Puranam** (lives of the 63 Nayanars) = **Sekkizhar** under **Kulottunga II** (12th Tirumurai).
[142:0:8] > Alvars = Vishnu, 12, Divya Prabandham (pasurams); Nayanars = Shiva, 63, Tevaram/Tirumurai.
[142:0:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.116, p.120-121; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 4 p.36; old app notes row 142
## SUB 1 | Regional Bhakti Poets – Shankaradeva, Jayadeva, Raskhan and Others
[142:1:0] TABLE head: Poet | Region / language | Fact asked
  [142:1:0.0] Shankaradeva (Sankardev) | Assam (Kamarupa), Cooch Behar | Introduced / popularised Vaishnavism there; Ekasarana Dharma – one deity Krishna; Namghars; Vaishnava cult
  [142:1:0.1] Jayadeva | Bengal / Odisha, 12th c. (Lakshmana Sena's court) | Gita Govinda (Sanskrit)
  [142:1:0.2] Raskhan (Sayyid Ibrahim) | Braj; Muslim devotee of Krishna | Prem Vatika, Sujan Raskhan
  [142:1:0.3] Keshavdas (Keshav) | Orchha, Riti poet | Ramchandrika, Rasikpriya
  [142:1:0.4] Nabhadas / Dhruvdas / Usman | Hindi | Bhaktmal / Bhakt Namavali / Chitravali
  [142:1:0.5] Tayumanavar (1706-44) | Tamil | Sittar poetry against temple abuses and caste
  [142:1:0.6] Waris Shah | Punjabi | Heer Ranjha
  [142:1:0.7] Kunchan Nambiar | Malayalam | Ottan Thullal
  [142:1:0.8] Dayaram | Gujarati (not Marathi) | Krishna lyrics, late 18th c.
[142:1:1] - **Vaishnavism in Kamarupa / Assam and Cooch Behar = Shankaradeva** (UPPSC 2002, 2011) – not Chaitanya, Nimbarka, Madhva or Ramananda.
[142:1:2] - **Raskhan – Rasikpriya is a wrong pair** (UPPSC 2018): Rasikpriya is **Keshavdas's**; Raskhan wrote **Prem Vatika**.
[142:1:3] - **18th-century wrong pair = Dayaram – Marathi** (APPSC G1 2024): Dayaram wrote in Gujarati.
[142:1:4] > Assam = Shankaradeva; Gita Govinda = Jayadeva; Prem Vatika = Raskhan; Rasikpriya = Keshavdas.
[142:1:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.124-126; PMF Modern History Part 1 p.60 (Dayaram); Spectrum Modern India ch.1 (18th-century literature); old app notes row 142-143
## SUB 2 | Origins, Roots and Common Features
[142:2:0] - **Bhakti** from the root **"bhaj"** – to share / participate; devotion to a personal God.
[142:2:1] - **Roots:** **Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita, Bhagavata Purana** – not the Arthashastra.
[142:2:2] - **Bhagavad Gita gives equal importance to Jnana, Karma and Bhakti** as means of liberation (UPPSC 2005); **Chapter 12 = Bhakti Yoga**. Advaita privileges jnana.
[142:2:3] - **Bhagavata Purana** (Tamil land, 9th-10th c.) put bhakti at the centre; **Navadha (ninefold, 9) bhakti** – shravana, kirtana, smarana, padasevana, archana, vandana, dasya, sakhya, atmanivedana (UP UDA 2010).
[142:2:4] - **Spread:** Tamil South 6th-9th c. → north from the 12th-13th c.; **reborn / zenith in the 15th-16th c.** with Kabir, Nanak, Sur, Tulsi, Mira (UPPCS 1993).
[142:2:5] - **Why it arose:** reaction against ritual, priestly dominance and caste; **jnana and karma margas too hard** for ordinary people.
[142:2:6] - **Common feature of all Bhakti saints:** they **composed in the language of the people** (vernacular) (State PSC) – not all rejected priests or idols (Saguna saints kept idols).
[142:2:7] - **Ramanuja's movement in Andhra** (Vishnu devotion + social equality) = the **Bhakti movement** (APPSC 2022) – not Arya Samaj or Lingayatism.
[142:2:8] - Core beliefs: **monotheism**, **guru** essential, **prapatti** (self-surrender); devotion above birth and status.
[142:2:9] - Modern scholars trace its roots to the **Alvars and Nayanars**, not to Islam; Islam shaped later egalitarian ideas.
[142:2:10] > Gita = jnana + karma + bhakti; Bhagavata = 9 forms; vernacular = the common feature.
[142:2:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 4 p.34-38; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.115, p.118; old app notes row 142
## SUB 3 | Women Saints, Guru Lines and the Social Base
[142:3:0] TABLE head: Woman saint | Region | Link
  [142:3:0.0] Andal | Tamil | Only woman Alvar
  [142:3:0.1] Karaikkal Ammaiyar | Tamil | Nayanar
  [142:3:0.2] Akkamahadevi | Karnataka | Virashaiva, 12th c.
  [142:3:0.3] Mirabai | Rajasthan | Krishna; guru Ravidas (tradition)
  [142:3:0.4] Daya Bai | Rajasthan / Delhi | Disciple of Saint Charandas (Charandasi Sampradaya); Dayabodh, Vinay Malika
  [142:3:0.5] Sahajobai | Rajasthan / Delhi | Disciple of Charandas; Sahaj Prakash
  [142:3:0.6] Gangabai | Vallabha sect | Ganesh Dev Leela is wrongly matched with her (UPPCS 2023)
[142:3:1] - **Daya Bai = disciple of Saint Charandas** (RAS 2018) – not Nimbarka, Raidas or Ramcharan.
[142:3:2] - **Buddha and Mirabai – common view:** both held that **the world is full of sorrow** and turned away from worldly life (RAS 1992 key).
[142:3:3] TABLE head: Guru | Disciple(s)
  [142:3:3.0] Ramananda | Kabir (weaver), Raidas (cobbler), Dhanna (Jat), Sena (barber), Pipa (Rajput), Padmavati
  [142:3:3.1] Ravidas | Mirabai
  [142:3:3.2] Vallabhacharya | Surdas
  [142:3:3.3] Charandas | Daya Bai, Sahajobai
[142:3:4] - **Ramananda** – **first medieval reformer to denounce caste outright**; the movement weakened caste and brought **Hindus and Muslims** closer, but did not end caste.
[142:3:5] - **Palnati Brahmanayudu** (Andhra) – **Chapakudu**, common dining for all castes.
[142:3:6] > Charandas → Daya Bai; Ravidas → Mirabai; Vallabha → Surdas; Ramananda → Kabir.
[142:3:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.121-124; testbook.com UPPCS Pre 2023 solution (Gangabai); old app notes row 142
## SUB 4 | Nirguna and Saguna Streams
[142:4:0] TABLE head: Stream | Idea of God | Saints
  [142:4:0.0] Nirguna | Formless, without attributes; rejects idols | Kabir, Guru Nanak, Dadu Dayal, Ravidas
  [142:4:0.1] Saguna – Ramamargi | Rama | Tulsidas
  [142:4:0.2] Saguna – Krishnamargi | Krishna | Surdas, Mirabai, Chaitanya, Vallabha
[142:4:1] - Both streams drew on Upanishadic **Advaita**; both monotheistic.
[142:4:2] - **Dadu Panth** – founded by **Dadu Dayal** in Rajasthan, in Kabir's tradition.
[142:4:3] - **Raskhan** was a devotee of **Krishna**, not Rama.
[142:4:4] > Nirguna = Kabir, Nanak, Dadu, Ravidas; Saguna = Tulsi (Rama), Sur, Mira, Chaitanya (Krishna).
[142:4:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.117; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 4 p.37; old app notes row 142
## SUB 5 | Virashaiva Movement and the Vachanas
[142:5:0] - **Basavanna (Basaveshwara)** (12th c., born **Bagewadi**) led the **Virashaiva / Lingayat** movement in **Karnataka**; treasurer at **Kalyana** under Kalachuri **Bijjala**.
[142:5:1] - **Anubhava Mantapa** – assembly of sharanas, presided by **Allama Prabhu**; **Akkamahadevi** a leading woman sharana.
[142:5:2] - **Vachanas** – short **Kannada** sayings, signed **Kudalasangamadeva**.
[142:5:3] - Rejected caste, temple ritual and idol worship.
[142:5:4] - **Andhra:** Veerashaivism came through **Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya** and **Palkuriki Somanatha** (**Basava Puranam**, Telugu).
[142:5:5] > Basavanna – Kalyana – Bijjala – Kannada vachanas – Kudalasangama.
[142:5:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.125; old app notes row 142
## SUB 6 | Nathpanthis, Siddhas and Yogis
[142:6:0] - Popularised devotional religion in **Northern India**; led by **Matsyendranath** and **Gorakhnath**.
[142:6:1] - Practised **hatha yoga**, meditation and **renunciation**; rejected ritual and caste; open to "low" castes.
[142:6:2] - **Charyapada** – songs of the Buddhist **Siddhacharyas** (earliest Bangla poems); manuscript found by **Haraprasad Shastri** in the Nepal royal library (1907).
[142:6:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.115-116; old app notes row 142

=== NOTES 1:143 | Bhakti Saints and Their Teachings – Ramanuja, Madhva, Nimbarka, Vallabha, Ramananda
## SUB 0 | Acharyas → Philosophy (Vedanta Schools)
[143:0:0] TABLE head: Acharya | School | Teaching | Deity / sect
  [143:0:0.0] Shankaracharya (788-820) | Advaita (Kevaladvaita, non-dualism) | Brahman alone real; knowledge (jnana) | Smarta; four mathas
  [143:0:0.1] Ramanuja (1017-1137) | Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism) | Salvation through devotion / prapatti | Vishnu-Lakshmi; Sri Vaishnava (followers = Vaishnavas)
  [143:0:0.2] Nimbarka (12th c.) | Dvaitadvaita (Bhedabheda) | Dualistic non-dualism | Radha-Krishna; Nimbarka Sampradaya
  [143:0:0.3] Madhvacharya (13th c.) | Dvaita (dualism) | God, souls, world eternally distinct; Saguna bhakti | Vishnu; Brahma Sampradaya, Udupi
  [143:0:0.4] Vallabhacharya (1479-1531) | Shuddhadvaita (pure non-dualism) | Pushtimarga – "path of grace"; householder life | Child Krishna (Shrinathji)
  [143:0:0.5] Chaitanya | Achintya Bhedabheda | Sankirtan | Gaudiya Vaishnavism
  [143:0:0.6] Ramananda | – | Rama bhakti | Ramanandi
[143:0:1] - **Correct pair: Ramanuja – Vishishtadvaita** (AP Police 2016; NDA 2018). Wrong: Vallabha – Jainism, Shankara – Vaishnavism, Madhva – Advaita, Ramananda – Kevaladvaita, Chaitanya – Advaita.
[143:0:2] - **Pushtimarga = Vallabhacharya** (APPSC G1 2019, G1 PYQ); **Shuddhadvaita = Vallabhacharya** (UP UDA 2002) – he developed the views of **Vishnuswami**.
[143:0:3] - **Madhva did NOT preach Nirguna bhakti** (RAS 2024) – he taught Dvaita, a Saguna Vaishnava path.
[143:0:4] - **Bijak is Kabir's** (not Dadu Dayal's) and **Pushtimarg is Vallabha's** (not Madhva's) → both statements wrong (UPSC 2014).
[143:0:5] - **Abhinavagupta** (Kashmir Shaiva) is **not** a Vedantin; Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva are.
[143:0:6] - **Sanskrit commentaries on the Vedanta (Brahma) Sutra:** Shankara (Brahmasutra-bhashya), Ramanuja (**Sri Bhashya**), Vallabhacharya (**Anubhashya**), Nimbarka (Vedanta Parijata Saurabha) – not Tulsidas or Lalleshwari (UPSC 2007).
[143:0:7] > Advaita–Shankara; Vishishtadvaita–Ramanuja; Dvaita–Madhva; Dvaitadvaita–Nimbarka; Shuddhadvaita–Vallabha.
[143:0:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.121, p.123, p.125; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 4 p.39; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 4 (Abhinavagupta); old app notes row 143
[143:0:9] - **Vallabhacharya** set up **84** Pushtimarg centres (baithaks).
## SUB 1 | Ramananda – Hindi, Caste and Disciples
[143:1:0] - **Born at Prayag** (tradition, 1299/1300) in a **Kanyakubja Brahmin** family; educated and settled at **Varanasi** (NextGen gives Varanasi as his home).
[143:1:1] - Follower of **Ramanuja's** school; replaced Vishnu worship with **Rama (and Sita)**.
[143:1:2] - **First Bhakti saint to use Hindi** (vernacular) to preach (UPSC 2002) – not Kabir, Dadu or Tulsidas.
[143:1:3] - "**Let no man ask a man's sect or caste**" (jati-panti puchhe nahin koi) – **Ramananda** (UPPCS 2009); first medieval reformer to denounce caste.
[143:1:4] - **Kabir was his disciple** (one of 12) (UP Lower 2002); others: Raidas, Dhanna, Sena, Pipa, Padmavati, Sadhana.
[143:1:5] - Liberal ideas that echo Islamic monotheism and equality → among the options **Ramananda is the leader "influenced by Islam"** (APPSC G2 2011) – not Ramanuja, the Nayanars or Chaitanya.
[143:1:6] - **Born at Prayag** – Ramananda; Raidas – Varanasi; Tulsidas – Rajapur; Kumbhandas – Mathura (UPPCS 2010).
[143:1:7] > Ramananda: Prayag, Hindi, Rama, "no caste", guru of Kabir.
[143:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 5 p.1; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.121; old app notes row 143
## SUB 2 | Ramanuja – Teaching, Andhra and Recent Links
[143:2:0] - Born at **Sriperumbudur** (Tamil Nadu); centre **Srirangam**; called **Ilaya Azhwar**; incarnation of **Adisesha / Lakshmana**.
[143:2:1] - **First true exponent of Bhakti**; reaction against Shankara's Advaita; wrote the **Sri Bhashya**.
[143:2:2] - **Teaching:** **the best means of salvation is devotion** (UPSC 2022) – not Vedic authority, logic or meditation.
[143:2:3] - Made the **Pancharatra Agama** the basis of Sri Vaishnava temple worship (APPSC Endowment 2022).
[143:2:4] - Sri Vaishnava ascetics (**yatis**) carry the **tridanda** (triple staff) (APPSC Endowment 2022).
[143:2:5] - **1000th birth anniversary:** PM released a **stamp on Sri Ramanujacharya** (1 May 2017); **Statue of Equality**, Hyderabad – sitting statue, inaugurated **Feb 2022**.
[143:2:6] - **Andhra:** patrons **Velanati Cholas**, **Palnati Haihayas**; inspired **Palnati Brahmanaidu's Veera Vaishnava** movement; gave **Panchamas** temple entry; installed **Govindaraja** at Tirupati.
[143:2:7] - **Sri Vaishnava split:** **Vadakalai** (**Vedanta Desika**) and **Tengalai** – both Vishishtadvaita.
[143:2:8] > Ramanuja: Sriperumbudur → Srirangam; devotion; Pancharatra; 1017 → stamp 2017.
[143:2:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.121; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 4 p.39; PIB, 1 May 2017 (stamp); old app notes row 143
## SUB 3 | Shankaracharya – Advaita, the Forerunner
[143:3:0] - Born at **Kaladi, Kerala** (788); died 820; **founder of Advaita** philosophy (APPSC Endowment 2022) – not Bhaskaracharya, Prabhakara or Madhusudana Saraswati.
[143:3:1] - **Guru = Govinda Bhagavatpada** (disciple of Gaudapada); **Padmapada** was Shankara's own disciple.
[143:3:2] - Wrote **Saundarya Lahari** in praise of the **Goddess**; Sivananda Lahari praises Shiva.
[143:3:3] - **Forerunner / pioneer of the Bhakti cult** (NextGen); four mathas – Sringeri, Puri, Dwarka, Jyotirmath.
[143:3:4] > Shankara: Kaladi – Govinda Bhagavatpada – Advaita – Saundarya Lahari.
[143:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 4 p.39; Britannica 'Shankara'; old app notes row 143
## SUB 4 | Chronology, Birthplaces and Contemporaries
[143:4:0] - **Order:** **Shankaracharya (8th c.) → Ramanuja (11th-12th c.) → Chaitanya (15th-16th c.)** (UPSC 2004, JPSC 2011).
[143:4:1] - Full order: Shankara → Ramanuja → Nimbarka → Madhva → Ramananda → Vallabha → Chaitanya.

  [143:4:2.0] Shankaracharya | Kaladi (Kerala) | Mathas
  [143:4:2.1] Ramanuja | Sriperumbudur | Srirangam
  [143:4:2.2] Madhva | Udupi region | Udupi
  [143:4:2.3] Nimbarka | Telugu Brahmin family | Brindavan / Mathura
  [143:4:2.4] Vallabhacharya | Champaranya (Chhattisgarh), son of Telugu Brahmin Lakshmana Bhatta | Gujarat, Braj
  [143:4:2.5] Ramananda | Prayag | Varanasi
[143:4:3] - **Contemporaries:** Vallabha and Chaitanya; Vallabha and **Krishnadevaraya**.
[143:4:4] - **Nimbarka was not a contemporary of Akbar.**
[143:4:5] > Shankara 8th → Ramanuja 11th → Chaitanya 15th-16th.

## SUB 5 | Vijayanagara Court and Dvaita in the Deccan
[143:5:0] - **Purandara Dasa** (1484-1564), Haridasa and "Pitamaha of Carnatic music", was a contemporary of **Sri Krishnadevaraya** (1509-29).
[143:5:1] - **Vallabha** at Krishnadevaraya's court defeated Dvaita scholar **Vyasaraya (Vyasa Tirtha)**; Vyasa Tirtha was **Rajaguru** of Saluva Narasimha and Krishnadevaraya; works Nyayamrita, Tarka Tandava.
[143:5:2] - **Narahari Tirtha** spread **Dvaita** in Andhra-Kalinga from **Srikurmam**.
[143:5:3] - **Amuktamalyada** (Krishnadevaraya; Mala Dasari Katha) – inclusion of lower groups.
[143:5:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 2 p.20 (Purandara Dasa); old app notes row 143

=== NOTES 1:144 | Kabir, Guru Nanak, Chaitanya, Mirabai, Tukaram, Namdeva, Surdas, Tulsidas
## SUB 0 | Chronology and Contemporaries
[144:0:0] TABLE head: Saint | Period | Contemporary ruler
  [144:0:0.0] Namdev | 1270-1350 (earliest) | Tughlaq age
  [144:0:0.1] Kabir | 15th c. (trad. 1398-1518) | Sikandar Lodi
  [144:0:0.2] Guru Nanak | 1469-1539 | Sikandar Lodi, Ibrahim Lodi, Babur
  [144:0:0.3] Chaitanya | 1486-1533/34 | Prataparudra Gajapati, Husain Shah
  [144:0:0.4] Mirabai | 1498-1546 | Rana Sanga's Mewar
  [144:0:0.5] Tulsidas | 1532-1623 | Akbar and Jahangir
  [144:0:0.6] Tukaram | 1608-1649/50 | Jahangir, Shah Jahan; Shivaji
  [144:0:0.7] Ramdas | 1608-1681 | Guru of Shivaji
[144:0:1] - **Order:** **Namdev → Kabir → Nanak → Chaitanya → Mirabai** (UPPCS 2005, 2014, 2025).
[144:0:2] - **Mirabai** overlapped with **Guru Nanak, Chaitanya and the young Tulsidas**; "Mirabai was a contemporary of Guru Nanak" is true (CDS 2005).
[144:0:3] - **Ramdas was a contemporary (and guru) of Shivaji** (CDS 2005).
[144:0:4] - **Sikh religion founded in the time of Sikandar Lodi** (1489-1517) (UPPCS 2008).
[144:0:5] - **Tukaram – Jahangir** (UPSC 2006) – not Babur, Akbar or Aurangzeb.
[144:0:6] - **Nimbarka (12th c.) was not Akbar's contemporary**; **Kabir could not be influenced by Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi** (1564-1624) (UPSC 2019).
[144:0:7] > Namdev 1270 → Kabir → Nanak 1469 → Chaitanya 1486 → Mira 1498 → Tulsi 1532 → Tukaram 1608.
[144:0:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.121-124; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 5 p.3 (Nanak), p.15 (Akbar–Tulsidas list); old app notes row 144
## SUB 1 | Literary Works and Language
[144:1:0] TABLE head: Saint | Work(s) | Language
  [144:1:0.0] Tulsidas | Ramcharitmanas, Vinay Patrika, Kavitavali, Gitavali, Dohavali, Hanuman Chalisa | Awadhi (Braj too)
  [144:1:0.1] Surdas | Sur Sagar, Sur Saravali, Sahitya Lahari | Braj Bhasha
  [144:1:0.2] Mirabai | Rag Govind, Padavali | Rajasthani, Braj

  [144:1:0.4] Kabir | Bijak | Sadhukkadi
  [144:1:0.5] Tukaram / Namdev | Abhangas | Marathi (Namdev also Hindi)
[144:1:1] - **Not by Tulsidas:** **Sahitya Lahari** (Surdas) (State PSC) and **Sahitya Ratna** (MPPSC 2014).
[144:1:2] - **Vinay Patrika = Tulsidas** (CGPSC 2018, State PSC); **Ramcharitmanas = Tulsidas**, not Valmiki or Vyasa.
[144:1:3] - **Sur Sagar = poetic work of Surdas** (CDS 2015) – not Tansen's music treatise.
[144:1:4] - **Rag Govind = Mirabai** (CGPSC 2014).
[144:1:5] - **Dasbodh = Ramdas** (MPPSC 2013); Bijak = Kabir; Vinay Patrika = Tulsidas; Sahitya Lahari = Surdas.
[144:1:6] > Ramcharitmanas = Awadhi; Sur Sagar = Braj; Dasbodh = Ramdas; Rag Govind = Mira.
[144:1:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.120, p.123-124; old app notes row 144
## SUB 2 | Kabir
[144:2:0] - Born (tradition) to a **Brahmin widow**, raised by Muslim weavers **Niru and Nima**; disciple of **Ramananda**; **Nirguna Bhakti** (APPSC FRO).
[144:2:1] - One God of many names – Ram, Rahim, Allah, Hari; **condemned pilgrimage, idol worship** and ritual of Hindus and Muslims; stood for Hindu-Muslim unity, universal love, and **householder life** → "he was not against idol worship" is the **wrong** statement (CDS 2011).
[144:2:2] - **Bijak** = his dohas and sakhis, holy book of the **Kabirpanthis** (MPPSC 2000, 2002); also **Sakhi, Sabad, Ramaini**.
[144:2:3] - **Amarmul (Anurag Sagar)** = dialogues of **Kabir and Dharamdas** (UPPCS 2003).
[144:2:4] - "**Pothi padh padh jag mua … dhai akhar prem ka, padhe so pandit hoy**" = **Kabir** (MPPSC 2022).
[144:2:5] - Language **Sadhukkadi** (panchmel khichri); hymns in the Adi Granth.
[144:2:6] > Kabir: Ramananda's disciple, Nirguna, Bijak, Amarmul (with Dharamdas).
[144:2:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 5 p.2; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.122; old app notes row 144
## SUB 3 | Maharashtra Saints and the Varkari Sect
[144:3:0] - **Varkari sect** worships **Vithoba (Vitthala)** at **Pandharpur** (Chandrabhaga / Bhima, Solapur) – its **seat** (RAS 2008, 2018) – not Sringeri, Nadia or Varanasi.
[144:3:1] - **Jnaneshwar (1275-96)** – **Jnaneshwari = Bhavartha Dipika**, Marathi commentary on the Gita (APPSC G1 1990-91) – not Ramanuja; Amritanubhava.
[144:3:2] - **Namdev** – **Varkari saint** (UPPCS 2004) – not Nimbarka, Chakradhara (Mahanubhava) or Ramdas (Samarth); tailor family; teacher **Visoba Khechar**; hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib; his nirguna bhakti **showed Islamic (Sufi) influence** (UP UDA 2010).
[144:3:3] - **Eknath** (1533-99) – Eknathi Bhagavata; **Tukaram** – abhangas; **Ramdas** – Dasbodh, guru of Shivaji.
[144:3:4] - Namdev was **not** Shivaji's contemporary; Tukaram and Ramdas were.
[144:3:5] > Varkari = Pandharpur Vithoba; Jnaneshwari = Bhavartha Dipika; Namdev = Islam-influenced Varkari saint.
[144:3:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.115, p.121-124; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 4 p.39; old app notes row 144
## SUB 4 | Chaitanya, Mirabai and Puri
[144:4:0] - **Chaitanya** (1486, **Nabadwip**, Nadia; childhood name **Nimai**) – **Vaishnava**, Krishna devotee; founded **Gaudiya Vaishnavism**; **Sankirtan**; lived at **Puri** under Prataparudra Gajapati.
[144:4:1] - Preached Krishna love to all, even chandalas; had **disciples from both Hindus and Muslims** (e.g. Haridas Thakur, born Muslim) (WBPSC 2007).
[144:4:2] - **Ratha Yatra** = festival of **Jagannatha at Puri** (APPSC Endowment 2022).
[144:4:3] - **Mirabai** – Rathore princess of Merta (born Kudki); married **Bhojraj**, son of **Rana Sanga** of Mewar (RAS 1997); widowed young; Krishna devotee.
[144:4:4] > Chaitanya = Nabadwip → Puri, Gaudiya; Mira's husband = Bhojraj (Sanga was her father-in-law).
[144:4:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.122, p.124; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 5 p.2; Britannica 'Mira Bai', 'Caitanya'; old app notes row 144
## SUB 5 | Guru Nanak
[144:5:0] - **Founder of Sikhism**; born **1469, Talwandi (Nankana Sahib)**, Khatri family; companion **Bhai Mardana**; **Guru ka Langar** (began at Kartarpur).
[144:5:1] - "**God knows man's virtues and inquires not his caste; in the next world there is no caste**" = **Guru Nanak** (RAS 2010).
[144:5:2] - Against idol worship; one formless God; householder life; **Babur Vani**.
[144:5:3] - **Baba Guru Nanak International University** – foundation stone laid at **Nankana Sahib, Pakistan** (Oct 2019, 550th birth anniversary).
[144:5:4] > Nanak: Talwandi 1469, Langar, "no caste in the next world".
[144:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 5 p.3; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.122-123; news reports Oct 2019 (Dawn, The Hindu); old app notes row 144
## SUB 6 | Saint → Region and Guru Links
[144:6:0] TABLE head: Saint | Region
  [144:6:0.0] Vallabhacharya | Gujarat (Telugu Brahmin family; Krishnadevaraya's court)
  [144:6:0.1] Tulsidas | Uttar Pradesh
  [144:6:0.2] Chaitanya | Bengal (and Puri)
  [144:6:0.3] Tukaram | Maharashtra
  [144:6:0.4] Mirabai | Rajasthan
  [144:6:0.5] Kabir / Ravidas | Varanasi
[144:6:1] - Match: **A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV** (APPSC G1).
[144:6:2] - **Not a Bhakti proponent: Nagarjuna** (Buddhist Madhyamika) (UPSC 2010); Tukaram, **Tyagaraja** and Vallabhacharya were.
[144:6:3] - **Malukdas** – saint poet of **Kada (Kara, near Prayagraj)** (UPPSC 2008).
[144:6:4] TABLE head: Guru | Disciple
  [144:6:4.0] Ramananda | Kabir, Raidas, Sena (barber), Dhanna (Jat), Pipa
  [144:6:4.1] Raidas | Mirabai
  [144:6:4.2] Vallabhacharya | Surdas
  [144:6:4.3] Guru Nanak | Mardana
  [144:6:4.4] Namdev | Janabai
[144:6:5] - Birthplaces: Tulsidas – **Rajapur**; Surdas – **Sihi**; Mirabai – **Kudki**; Basavanna – Bagewadi. Ravidas – leather-tanner, **41 shabdas** in the Guru Granth Sahib; **Begampura**.
[144:6:6] - Andhra parallels to Kabir: **Vemana, Potuluri Veerabrahmam**. Bhakti saints enriched **Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati** and stirred **Maratha and Sikh** awakening.

=== NOTES 1:145 | Bhakti in Andhra - Annamacharya, Bammera Potana, Vemana, the Tallapaka Poets
## SUB 0 | Telugu Bhakti Composers – Bhakta Ramadasu, Tyagaraja, Kshetrayya and Others
[145:0:0] # Bhakta Ramadasu (Kancherla Gopanna)
[145:0:1] - **Kancherla Gopanna = Bhakta Ramadasu**: Golconda revenue official (tahsildar of **Bhadrachalam**); used state revenue to rebuild the **Bhadrachalam Rama temple**.
[145:0:2] - Jailed **12 years in Golconda fort** by **Abul Hasan Tana Shah**; in prison he composed the **Dasarathi Satakam** (104 poems to Rama) and the Ramadasu kirtanas.
[145:0:3] - **Dasarathi Satakam = Gopanna** (APPSC G1 2002, asked three times) – NOT **Sumati Satakam** (Baddena), Bhaskara Satakam (Maravi Venkayya) or Vemana Satakam.
[145:0:4] - English translation of Dasarathi Satakam credited (APPSC G2 2001 key) to **Dr. Bhanumathi Ramakrishna**.
[145:0:5] # Other composers
[145:0:6] TABLE head: Figure | Deity / place | Work / fact
  [145:0:6.0] Tyagaraja (1767–1847) | Rama; born Tiruvarur, lived and attained samadhi at Tiruvaiyaru (Thanjavur district) | Thousands of kritis, mostly in Telugu, mostly in praise of Rama; Pancharatna kritis (five gems, in Ghana ragas); created new ragas; musical dramas Prahlada Bhakti Vijayam and Nauka Charitram; Carnatic Trinity with Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri
  [145:0:6.1] Kshetrayya (Varadayya of Movva, Krishna dt.) | Muvva Gopala (Krishna) | 1,000+ Shringara padams; sang at Abdullah Qutb Shah's court
  [145:0:6.2] Tarigonda Vengamamba | Venkateswara, Tirumala | Venkatachala Mahatyamu (18th c.)
  [145:0:6.3] Dhurjati | Srikalahasti | Srikalahasteeswara Satakam
[145:0:7] - **Thyagaraja Aradhana** (yearly festival) = **Tiruvaiyaru, Thanjavur** district (UPPCS 2000) – not Adyar, Mamallapuram or Udipi.
[145:0:8] - **Nauka Charitram = Tyagaraja** (APPSC G1 1994), not Annamacharya, Kshetrayya or Ramadasu.
[145:0:9] - **Foremost composer of Carnatic music = Tyagaraja** (APPSC G2 2019); **pioneer of the kriti / sankirtana form = Annamacharya** (APPSC G2) – the same four options, two different stems.
[145:0:10] - **UPSC 2018:** Tyagaraja created new ragas (2 ✔); Annamacharya's kirtanas praise **Venkateswara** (4 ✔); most Tyagaraja kritis praise **Rama, not Krishna** (1 ✘); Annamacharya (1408–1503) and Tyagaraja (1767–1847) were **not contemporaries** (3 ✘) → **2 and 4 only**.
[145:0:11] - Carnatic Trinity = Tyagaraja, Dikshitar, Syama Sastri – **Annamacharya is not one of them**.
[145:0:12] - Telugu Bhakti poets fed Carnatic music through **padams, keertanas, satakas and dvipadas**.
[145:0:13] > Exam angle: book → author (Dasarathi Satakam, Nauka Charitram, Pancharatna) and statement sets mixing Annamacharya with Tyagaraja.
[145:0:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History – previous papers (src/ap-history/nextgen-previous-papers.txt): Gopanna = Bhadrachala Ramadasu; NextGen Qutb Shahis (src/ap-history/nextgen-11-qutbshahis.txt); PMF Art & Culture Part 2 p.20-22 (src/indian-history/pmf-art-culture-02.txt): Annamacharya, Trinity, Tyagaraja; old app notes 1:145 sub 8
## SUB 1 | Tallapaka Annamacharya and the Tallapaka Family
[145:1:0] # Annamacharya (1408–1503)
[145:1:1] - Born at **Tallapaka** village (Rajampet mandal) – historically **Cuddapah (Kadapa) district** (APPSC 2012 key). The area went to the new **Annamayya district** (named after him) in April 2022 and, with the **Rajampet division, back to YSR Kadapa district** from 1 Jan 2026 (as of 2026).
[145:1:2] - Contemporary of **Saluva Narasimha Raya** (APPSC G2 2011) – not Harihara, Deva Raya I or III; also a contemporary of **Purandara Dasa**.
[145:1:3] - About **32,000 sankirtanas** to **Lord Venkateswara of Tirumala**; about **12,000** survive on **copper plates** found at Tirumala (1922); recovered and edited by **Veturi Prabhakara Sastry**. Compositions are Adhyatma (spiritual) and Sringara.
[145:1:4] - Titles: **Pada Kavita Pitamaha**, Sankirtanacharya; earliest composer of sankirtanas → **pioneer of the kriti form**; the kirtana structure shaped later Carnatic music. Opposed untouchability (**Brahmam Okkate**).
[145:1:5] - Other works: **Sri Venkateswara Satakam** (first Telugu Shringara Satakam), Sringara Manjari, Sankirtana Lakshanam (Sanskrit).
[145:1:6] - **Arudra** called him "Incarnated Telugu".
[145:1:7] # The Tallapaka poets
[145:1:8] TABLE head: Member | Relation | Works / title
  [145:1:8.0] Tallapaka Timmakka (Tirumalamma) | Annamacharya's wife | Subhadra Kalyanam (= Subhadra Parinayam), also Rukmini Kalyanam; first woman poet of Telugu
  [145:1:8.1] Peda Tirumalacharya | Son | Vairagya Vachanamalika, sankirtanas
  [145:1:8.2] China Tirumalacharya | Grandson | Title Ashtabhasha Kavi Chakravarti
  [145:1:8.3] Chinnanna (Tiruvengalanatha) | Grandson | Paramayogi Vilasam, Annamacharya Charitra (dvipada biography), Usha Kalyanam, Ashtamahishi Kalyanam
[145:1:9] - **Subhadra Kalyanam / Parinayam = Tallapaka Timmakka** (APPSC G2; G2 2012) – not Molla, Rangajamma, Madhuravani or Gangadevi.
[145:1:10] - **Paramayogi Vilasamu = Tallapaka Tiruvengalanatha** (APPSC Degree Lecturers 2011) – not Annamayya himself, Dhurjati or Ramaraja Bhushana.
[145:1:11] > Exam angle: contemporary ruler, birthplace district, and "who wrote" within the family.
[145:1:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Vijayanagara (src/ap-history/nextgen-10-vijayanagara.txt p.4): Annamacharya = Saluva Narasimha's contemporary, 32,000 kirtans, Timmakka = Subhadra Kalyanam; NextGen AP previous papers (Tallapaka = Cuddapah); PMF Art & Culture Part 2 p.20-22; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tallapaka,_Andhra_Pradesh; Deccan Chronicle / NewsMeter on the AP district rejig (Rajampet to YSR Kadapa, 2025-26)
## SUB 2 | Bhakti Shrines of Andhra – Kotappakonda, Srisailam, Pancharamas, Tirumala
[145:2:0] TABLE head: Shrine | Deity / fact
  [145:2:0.0] Kotappakonda (near Narasaraopet, Palnadu dt.) | Lord Shiva as Trikoteswara Swamy; famous Maha Shivaratri prabhala festival
  [145:2:0.1] Srisailam (Nandyal dt.) | Mallikarjuna Swamy = Lord Shiva (jyotirlinga) with Bhramaramba
  [145:2:0.2] Pancharama Kshetras | Five ancient Shiva temples: Amararama (Amaravati), Draksharama, Somarama (Bhimavaram), Ksheerarama (Palakollu), Kumararama (Samalkot)
  [145:2:0.3] Tirumala | Lord Venkateswara; TTD set up under the TTD Act, 1932; Annamacharya, Tallapaka family, Vengamamba
  [145:2:0.4] Bhadrachalam (now Telangana) | Bhakta Ramadasu
  [145:2:0.5] Mantralayam (Kurnool dt., AP) | Samadhi of Raghavendra Swami (Dvaita)
  [145:2:0.6] Srikurmam | Narahari Tirtha spread Dvaita here
[145:2:1] - **Kotappakonda = Shiva temple** (AEE 2011; APPSC) – not Venkateswara, Vishnu or Krishna.
[145:2:2] - **Not in AP after reorganisation:** the **Akka Mahadevi caves** – on the Krishna's north bank across from Srisailam, in **Nagarkurnool district, Telangana**; Vedadri (NTR dt.), Nagarjunakonda (Palnadu dt.) and Mantralayam (Kurnool dt.) are in AP.
[145:2:3] > Exam angle: deity of a shrine, "Pancharama = five Shiva temples", TTD Act year.
[145:2:4] ~~ Sources: old app notes 1:145 sub 8 (Kotappakonda); NextGen AP History (src/ap-history/nextgen-06-eastern-chalukyas.txt, Draksharama/Samalkot); tirumala.org (TTD history, 1932 Act); Deccan Chronicle report on Akka Mahadevi caves, Nagarkurnool district (deccanchronicle.com)
## SUB 3 | Virashaivism and Saiva Bhakti in Andhra
[145:3:0] # Basava and the Virashaivas (Lingayats)
[145:3:1] - Founder: **Basavanna (Basaveshwara)**, 12th c., a **Brahmana** and **minister of the Kalachuri ruler Bijjala II** at **Kalyana**; Anubhava Mantapa ("religious parliament"); **Akka Mahadevi** and Allama Prabhu were Vachana saints (12th-c. Karnataka).
[145:3:2] - Lingayats worship **Shiva** in the form of the **Ishtalinga** worn on the body; theology **Shakti Vishishtadvaita**; **Kayaka** = honest labour, **Dasoha** = sharing.
[145:3:3] - Social message: rejected caste, **untouchability** and Brahmanical ritual, **condemned child marriage**, **questioned the theory of rebirth**, and encouraged practices the **Dharmashastras disapproved** – **post-puberty marriage and widow remarriage**.
[145:3:4] - **NDA 2019:** I (Basavanna, a Brahmana, minister of a Kalachuri ruler) ✔; II says the practices were "approved by the Dharmashastras" ✘ → **only I**.
[145:3:5] - **UPSC 2016:** Siddhas (Sittars) of Tamil Nadu were **monotheistic and condemned idolatry** ✔; Lingayats **questioned rebirth and rejected caste hierarchy** ✔ → **both**.
[145:3:6] # Spread into Andhra
[145:3:7] TABLE head: Person | Contribution
  [145:3:7.0] Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya | Spread Virashaivism in Andhra (Kakatiya age); founder of Aradhya Saivism (moderate, kept Vedic learning and varna); Sivatattvasaram; originator of the Sataka form in Telugu; one of the Panchacharyas
  [145:3:7.1] Palkuriki Somanatha | Basava Puranam (Telugu dwipada) and Panditaradhya Charitra; Vrushadhipa Satakam (first full-featured satakam)
[145:3:8] - **Virashaivism spread in Andhra by Panditaradhya** (APPSC G1 1983-84) – Basava founded it in Karnataka; Somanatha was its later Telugu poet.
[145:3:9] - **Basava Purana = Palkuriki Somanatha** – not Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya (Sivatattvasaram).
[145:3:10] - Panchacharyas: Revanaradhya, Marularadhya, Ekoramaradhya, **Panditaradhya**, Vishwaradhya.
[145:3:11] > Exam angle: founder and Andhra propagators; statement questions on Lingayat social ideas (NCERT wording).
[145:3:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 5 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-05.txt: "spread of Veera Saivism by Panditaradhya"); NextGen AP previous papers (src/ap-history/nextgen-previous-papers.txt: Basavanna founded Veera Shaivam at Kalyani; Somanatha = Basava Puranam & Panditaradhya Charitra); PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 3 p.130 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-03.txt); NCERT Themes in Indian History II ch.6 (Virashaiva tradition)
## SUB 4 | Bammera Potana
[145:4:0] - Native of **Bammera** (Jangaon dt., Telangana); one tradition places him at **Vontimitta (Ontimitta), Kadapa** (APPSC MPDO 1997).
[145:4:1] - Titles: **Sahaja Panditudu**, Nigarva Chudamani; contemporary of **Srinatha** and Pedakomati Vema Reddy's age.
[145:4:2] TABLE head: Work | Fact
  [145:4:2.0] Veerabhadra Vijayam | His first work, at the request of his guru Ivaturi Somanaradhya
  [145:4:2.1] Andhra Maha Bhagavatamu | Telugu Bhagavata Purana, dedicated to Lord Rama; Potana wrote 8 of 12 skandhas (5th Bopparaju Gangana, 6th Erchuri Singana, 11-12th Veligandala Narayana); printed by C.P. Brown, 1840
  [145:4:2.2] Bhogini Dandakam | First Telugu Dandakam
  [145:4:2.3] Narayana Satakam | Satakam
[145:4:3] - **Veerabhadra Vijayam = Potana** (APPSC G2 2011, asked three times) – not Srinatha, Tikkana or Errapragada.
[145:4:4] - **Refused to dedicate** his work to a king (**Sarvajna Singabhupala of Rachakonda**).
[145:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP previous papers (src/ap-history/nextgen-previous-papers.txt): "Potana was the author of Virabhadra Vijayam", "Narayana Satakam, Andhra Bhagavatham"; Rocket AP History (src/rocket-ap-history.txt); old app notes 1:145 sub 5
## SUB 5 | Telugu Women Poets
[145:5:0] TABLE head: Poet | Work | Note
  [145:5:0.0] Tallapaka Timmakka | Subhadra Kalyanam | First woman poet of Telugu
  [145:5:0.1] Atukuri Molla | Molla Ramayanam | Potter family of Gopavaram; first Telugu poetess to write the Ramayana
  [145:5:0.2] Gangadevi | Madhura Vijayam (Veera Kamparaya Charitam), Sanskrit | Wife of Kumara Kampana (Sangama); his conquest of Madurai; student of Agastya
  [145:5:0.3] Mohanangi | Marichi Parinayam | Krishnadevaraya's daughter
  [145:5:0.4] Oduva Tirumalamba | Varadambika Parinayam | Marriage of Achyuta Deva Raya and Varadambika
  [145:5:0.5] Ramabhadramba | Raghunathabhyudayam | Sanskrit
[145:5:1] - **Wrong match (APPSC G2): Gangadevi – Marichi Parinayam** (Marichi Parinayam is Mohanangi's); Molla – Ramayanam, Timmakka – Subhadra Kalyanam, Tirumalamba – Varadambika Parinayam are correct.
[145:5:2] - **Madhura Vijayam = Gangadevi** – not Molla, Ramabhadramba or Madhuravani.
[145:5:3] - **First Telugu poetess to write the Ramayana = Molla** (APPSC Geologist 2007).
[145:5:4] - **Amuktamalyada = Krishnadevaraya** (not Tirumalamba); Allasani Peddana was his court poet.
[145:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Vijayanagara (src/ap-history/nextgen-10-vijayanagara.txt): Gangadevi Madhura Vijayam, Timmakka; NextGen AP previous papers ("Madhura Vijayam was composed by Ganga Devi"; "Gangadevi was the student of Agastya"); old app notes 1:145 sub 9
## SUB 6 | Vemana, Veerabrahmam and the Social Message of Andhra Bhakti
[145:6:0] TABLE head: Feature | Vemana | Potuluri Veerabrahmendra Swamy
  [145:6:0.0] Work | Vemana padyalu (Vemana Satakam), colloquial Telugu | Kalagnanam – prophecies of the evils of Kali Yuga
  [145:6:0.1] Form / theme | Ataveladi metre; refrain "Vishwadabhirama Vinura Vema"; satire on caste, ritual, idol worship, superstition | Condemned caste; disciples of all castes and faiths – Siddaiah (a Muslim, Dudekula), Kakkaiah (Madiga)
[145:6:1] - **Kalagnanam = Veerabrahmam** (Dy. EO 2008) – not Vemana Satakam.
[145:6:2] - **C.P. Brown** collected and translated **Verses of Vemana (1829)**.
[145:6:3] - **Social impact:** Bhakti did not uniformly uphold Brahmanical dominance – Basava, Vemana, Veerabrahmam attacked caste; **satakam and dwipada** carried Bhakti to common people; Telugu replaced Sanskrit as its vehicle.
[145:6:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP previous papers ("C.P. Brown collected the poems of Vemana"); NextGen Qutb Shahis (src/ap-history/nextgen-11-qutbshahis.txt); old app notes 1:145 subs 7, 10

  x: The Virashaivas promoted widow remarriage and condemned child marriage; they rejected caste and untouchability, so statement 2 is wrong.

  Assertion (A): The Bhakti traditions did not uniformly uphold Brahmanical dominance.

  *Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A | Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A | A is true but R is false | A is false but R is true

## SUB 2 | The Chishti Line – Masters, Disciples and Rulers
[147:2:0] - Chain: **Usman Harooni → Moinuddin Chishti → Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki → Baba Farid → Nizamuddin Auliya → Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Delhi**; Amir Khusrau = disciple of Nizamuddin; Baba Farid's other main disciple = Alauddin Sabir Kaliyari.
[147:2:1] TABLE head: Saint | Dates | Ruler link
  [147:2:1.0] Moinuddin Chishti | 1143–1236 | Came with Muhammad Ghori's army (1192), in the age of Prithviraj Chauhan; first Chishti in India, earliest Sufi settled at Ajmer
  [147:2:1.1] Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki | 1173–1235 | Iltutmish (also contemporary of Suhrawardi Bahauddin Zakariya)
  [147:2:1.2] Baba Farid | 1178–1271 | Born Kothewal (Multan dt.)
  [147:2:1.3] Nizamuddin Auliya | 1238–1325 | Saw seven Sultans but never visited their court; "Hunuz Dilli dur ast" of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq
  [147:2:1.4] Nasiruddin Chiragh | 1274–1356 | Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Firuz Tughlaq
[147:2:2] - **Moinuddin was the disciple of Khwaja Usman Harooni** (UPPSC 2014). **Nizamuddin was the disciple of Baba Farid** (UPPCS 2006).
[147:2:3] - **Most reputed disciple of Shaikh Farid who saw seven Sultans = Nizamuddin Auliya** (UPPCS 2014 ×2).
[147:2:4] - **UPSC 2002:** Sirhindi was a contemporary of **Akbar–Jahangir**, not Ibrahim Lodi (I ✘); Nasiruddin was Nizamuddin's disciple (II ✔); Salim Chishti was **Akbar's** contemporary, not Aurangzeb's (III ✘); **Qadiri order introduced in India by Shah Niamatullah and Makhdum Muhammad Jilani** (IV ✔) → **II and IV**.
[147:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 5 p.10; Singhania App.2 p.178-180; Rocket IH Part 2 p.1; old app notes 1:147 subs 0, 3
## SUB 3 | Baba Farid, Malfuzat and Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi
[147:3:0] - **Baba Farid (Fariduddin Ganj-i-Shakar):** his Punjabi verses are in the **Adi Granth / Guru Granth Sahib** (UPPSC 1994 ×2) – not Moinuddin, Kaki or Nizamuddin.
[147:3:1] TABLE head: Text | Author / compiler
  [147:3:1.0] Fawaid-ul-Fuad | Conversations (malfuzat) of Nizamuddin Auliya, compiled by Amir Hasan Sijzi – not Amir Khusrau, Barani or Hasan Nizami
  [147:3:1.1] Siyar-ul-Auliya | Mir Khwurd Kirmani (tazkira)
  [147:3:1.2] Maktubat-i-Imam Rabbani | Letters of Ahmad Sirhindi
  [147:3:1.3] Radd-i-Rawafiz | Sirhindi – anti-Shia tract
[147:3:2] # Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi
[147:3:3] - **Naqshbandi**, disciple of **Khwaja Baqi Billah**; **Mujaddid Alf-i-Sani**; doctrine **Wahdat-ush-Shuhud** against Wahdat-ul-Wujud.
[147:3:4] - Opposed Akbar's **Sulh-i-kul**, Din-i-Ilahi, Shia influence and sama; **imprisoned by Jahangir in Gwalior Fort** (UPSC 1998).
[147:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 5 p.10 (Farid's verses in Adi Granth; Naqshbandi arrested by Jahangir); Singhania App.2 p.179-180; old app notes 1:147 subs 5-7

=== NOTES 1:149 | Sikhism - the Ten Gurus, Guru Granth Sahib, the Khalsa; Banda Bahadur and Ranjit Singh
## SUB 0 | Guru Gobind Singh and the Khalsa
[149:0:0] - **Guru Gobind Singh** (1666-1708) = **tenth and last human Guru** of the Sikhs – not Tegh Bahadur, Har Krishan or Banda Bahadur.
[149:0:1] - **Born 1666 at Patna** (Bihar) – Takht Sri Patna Sahib marks the birthplace.
[149:0:2] - **Founded the Khalsa** ("army of the pure") on **Baisakhi, 13 April 1699**, at **Anandpur** (Takht Sri **Keshgarh Sahib**, Rupnagar) – not Amritsar; the **Panj Pyare** (five volunteers) were baptised first with sacred nectar.
[149:0:3] - **His greatness:** he **turned the Sikhs into a military order** (Khalsa; surnames **Singh / Kaur**) – he did **not** found the Sikh state (that was Banda Bahadur, 1710) and did not defeat Aurangzeb.
[149:0:4] - **Five Ks:** **Kesh** (hair), **Kangha** (comb), **Kara** (steel bangle), **Kachera** (undergarment), **Kirpan** (sword) – **Kirtan is not** one of them.
[149:0:5] - Wrote the **Zafarnama** (Persian letter to Aurangzeb accusing the Mughals of betrayal); Dasam Granth at **Paonta Sahib**; the **Chali Mukte** (40 liberated ones) died defending him at **Muktsar** (Maghi).
[149:0:6] - Fought Aurangzeb from 1699; made peace with **Bahadur Shah**; killed at **Nanded** (1708); declared the **Guru Granth Sahib the eternal Guru** – personal Guruship ended.
[149:0:7] - **"How many years ago" (MPPSC 2000):** 1699 → about **300 years**.
[149:0:8] - **350th birth anniversary (Prakash Parv):** PM attended the celebrations at **Patna** (Gandhi Maidan) on **5 January 2017** and released a stamp – not Nanded, Amritsar or Anandpur.
[149:0:9] > Gobind Singh: Patna 1666 → Khalsa, Anandpur, Baisakhi 1699 → Nanded 1708; 10th and last Guru.
[149:0:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.70-72; Rocket Indian History 02 (Rocket Sheet #59-60); PMF Modern History Part 1 p.74; pmindia.gov.in release, 5 Jan 2017; old app notes row 149
## SUB 1 | Maharaja Ranjit Singh
[149:1:0] - Born **1780** (13 Nov; Spectrum gives 2 Nov) at **Gujranwala**; son of **Maha (Mahan) Singh**, chief of the **Sukerchakia misl** – not Bhangi, Ahluwalia, Ramgarhia, Singhpuria or Sandhawalia.
[149:1:1] - Father died when he was a boy (12 per Spectrum; PMF gives 1790, aged 10); called **"Sher-e-Punjab" (Lion of Punjab)**.
[149:1:2] - **Zaman Shah** of Afghanistan invaded Punjab (1798); Ranjit Singh returned his cannons lost in the Jhelum, and in **1799 Zaman Shah made him governor of Lahore with the title "Raja"**.
[149:1:3] - **1799: captured Lahore** → **political capital Lahore**, **religious capital Amritsar** (Amritsar taken 1802/1805) – not Patiala, Kapurthala or Multan.
[149:1:4] - **1801:** proclaimed **Maharaja**; army on European lines (**Allard**, Ventura; **Fauj-i-Khas**); commander **Hari Singh Nalwa**.
[149:1:5] - **Treaty of Amritsar, 25 April 1809** (Lord **Minto**; negotiated by **Charles Metcalfe**): **Sutlej** = boundary; Ranjit Singh gave up the cis-Sutlej states and turned west.
[149:1:6] - **Conquests:** **Multan 1818, Kashmir (Srinagar) 1819**, Peshawar 1834 – his empire included **Srinagar**, not Delhi, Kabul or Makrana (Rajasthan).
[149:1:7] - **1813:** got the **Kohinoor** from **Shah Shuja** (Nadir Shah had taken it from Delhi in 1739); **Tripartite Treaty 1838** (British, Shah Shuja, Ranjit Singh).
[149:1:8] - **Secular ruler:** Hindu and Muslim ministers; blind in one eye – "**God intended me to look upon all religions with one eye, that is why He took away the light from the other**" = **Ranjit Singh**.
[149:1:9] - High court at Lahore = **Adalat-i-Ala**; covered the Harmandir Sahib in gold → "Golden Temple".
[149:1:10] > Sukerchakia → Lahore 1799 (Zaman Shah's "Raja") → Amritsar treaty 1809 (Sutlej) → Kohinoor 1813 → Kashmir 1819 → died 1839.
[149:1:11] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 1 p.74-76; Spectrum Modern India p.146-147 (book p.114-115); NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 5 p.17; PMF Modern History Part 2 p.52; old app notes row 149
## SUB 2 | Gurus and the Mughal Emperors – Martyrdoms
[149:2:0] TABLE head: Guru | Emperor | Relation
  [149:2:0.0] Ram Das (4th) | Akbar | Friendly – grant of about 500 bighas of land where Ramdaspur (Amritsar) grew
  [149:2:0.1] Arjan Dev (5th) | Jahangir | Executed 1606 for helping rebel Prince Khusrau – first martyr Guru
  [149:2:0.2] Hargobind (6th) | Jahangir | Held in Gwalior Fort, freed 1619 (with 52 prisoners – Bandi Chhor Divas) – not executed
  [149:2:0.3] Har Rai, Har Krishan | Aurangzeb | Conflict, summoned / detained
  [149:2:0.4] Tegh Bahadur (9th) | Aurangzeb | Publicly executed at Delhi (Chandni Chowk), 1675, for refusing Islam – "Hind-di-Chadar"
  [149:2:0.5] Gobind Singh (10th) | Aurangzeb, then Bahadur Shah | Wars from 1699; Zafarnama; later peace with Bahadur Shah
[149:2:1] - **Sikh Guru executed by Aurangzeb = Tegh Bahadur** (not Arjan Dev, Gobind Singh, Ram Das or Angad).
[149:2:2] - **Gurus put to death by the rulers = Arjan Dev (1606) and Tegh Bahadur (1675)** – Angad was not, and Hargobind was only imprisoned.
[149:2:3] - **Sis Ganj** = place of Tegh Bahadur's execution; **Rakab Ganj** = his cremation; 350th martyrdom year observed in 2025-26.
[149:2:4] > Akbar–Ram Das (land); Jahangir–Arjan (1606) and Hargobind (Gwalior); Aurangzeb–Tegh Bahadur (1675).
[149:2:5] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian History 02 (Rocket Sheet #63: Jahangir – Arjan Dev's execution; Aurangzeb – Tegh Bahadur's); Rocket Indian History 02 Sheet #60; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 4 (Jahangir, Aurangzeb); Singhania Art & Culture Part 4 p.46-47; old app notes row 149 (Amritsar gazetteer, 500 bighas)
## SUB 3 | After Ranjit Singh – Kharak Singh to Duleep Singh
[149:3:0] - Ranjit Singh died **June 1839** → disputed successions: **Kharak (Khadag) Singh (1839, immediate successor)** → Nau Nihal Singh → Sher Singh → **Duleep (Dalip) Singh (1843)** – **Hari Singh Nalwa** was a general, not a successor.
[149:3:1] - **Duleep Singh** = youngest son, crowned at five (1843) with mother **Rani Jindan (Jind Kaur)** as regent = **last king of the Sikh empire (1843-1849)**.
[149:3:2] - First Anglo-Sikh War 1845-46 (Treaty of **Lahore**, 9 March 1846; Treaty of **Bhairowal**, Dec 1846); Second 1848-49 → **Dalhousie annexed Punjab (1849)**.
[149:3:3] - Raised in England, **converted to Christianity (1853)**, **returned to Sikhism (1886)**; **went to Russia** (1887) seeking Tsar Alexander III's help.
[149:3:4] - **Died in Paris, October 1893** (22 Oct in most references; some books and the UPPCS key give 23 Oct); **buried with Christian rites at Elveden, England** – not cremated at Nasik.
[149:3:5] > Kharak Singh first, Duleep Singh last; Duleep: Christian 1853 → Sikh 1886 → Russia 1887 → died Paris 1893, buried Elveden.
[149:3:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 2 p.52-55; Spectrum Modern India p.147-148; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duleep_Singh (death 22/23 Oct 1893, Elveden burial, Russia 1887); old app notes row 149
## SUB 4 | Guru Nanak, the Word "Sikh" and the Ten Gurus
[149:4:0] - **"Sikh"** = **disciple** (from Sanskrit **shishya**, learner) – not soldier, monk or devotee; **Khalsa** = "pure".
[149:4:1] - **Guru Nanak** (**1469-1539**) = **founder of Sikhism**; born at **Talwandi = Nankana (Sahib)** near the Ravi (now Pakistan) – not Amritsar, Nabha, Nanded, Gurdaspur or Lahore.
[149:4:2] - Teachings: one formless God (**Ik Onkar**), **Naam Simran**, **Sangat**, **Langar**, honest householder life; against idol worship and rituals of both faiths.
[149:4:3] - **Successor = Bhai Lehna → Guru Angad** (appointed by Nanak before his death, 1539) – not Amar Das or Ram Das.
[149:4:4] TABLE head: No. | Guru | Contribution
  [149:4:4.0] 1 | Nanak Dev | Founder; Ik Onkar; appointed Angad
  [149:4:4.1] 2 | Angad Dev | Started / standardised Gurmukhi script
  [149:4:4.2] 3 | Amar Das | 22 Manjis; strengthened langar
  [149:4:4.3] 4 | Ram Das | Founded Ramdaspur (Amritsar); land from Akbar; holy tank
  [149:4:4.4] 5 | Arjan Dev (1581-1606) | Compiled Adi Granth (1604); built Harmandir Sahib; first martyr
  [149:4:4.5] 6 | Hargobind | Militarised the Panth; Miri-Piri; Akal Takht (1609); Gwalior Fort; battle of Kartarpur
  [149:4:4.6] 7 | Har Rai | Herbal medicine, service
  [149:4:4.7] 8 | Har Krishan | Child (youngest) Guru
  [149:4:4.8] 9 | Tegh Bahadur | Born Tyag Mal; founded Anandpur Sahib (Chak Nanki); 116 hymns; executed 1675
  [149:4:4.9] 10 | Gobind Singh | Born Patna 1666; Khalsa 1699; Five Ks; Guruship to the Granth
[149:4:5] > Sikh = disciple; Nanak (Talwandi 1469) → Angad (Gurmukhi) → Amar Das (Manjis) → Ram Das (Amritsar) → Arjan (Adi Granth).
[149:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 5 p.3; PMF Modern History Part 1 p.74; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.70-71; Rocket Indian History 02 (Rocket Sheet #59-60); old app notes row 149
## SUB 5 | Amritsar, the Golden Temple and Sacred Places
[149:5:0] TABLE head: Place | Link
  [149:5:0.0] Amritsar (first Ramdaspur) | City and tank founded by Guru Ram Das on land granted by Akbar
  [149:5:0.1] Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) | Built / completed by Guru Arjan Dev (1604), who installed the Adi Granth; gold covering by Ranjit Singh
  [149:5:0.2] Akal Takht, Amritsar | Guru Hargobind, 1609 – temporal seat
  [149:5:0.3] Anandpur Sahib (Rupnagar) | Founded by Tegh Bahadur; Khalsa born here 1699 (Keshgarh Sahib); Hola Mohalla
  [149:5:0.4] Patna Sahib | Birthplace of Gobind Singh
  [149:5:0.5] Damdama Sahib (Talwandi Sabo, Bathinda) | Final version of the Guru Granth Sahib (1705); Baisakhi fair
  [149:5:0.6] Hazur Sahib, Nanded (Godavari, Maharashtra) | Death / cremation place of Guru Gobind Singh (1708) – Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Abchalnagar Sahib
  [149:5:0.7] Sri Muktsar Sahib | Maghi Mela (Chali Mukte)
[149:5:1] - **Amritsar was established by Guru Ram Das**; **Golden Temple completed by Guru Arjan Dev**.
[149:5:2] - **Nanded is sacred because of Guru Gobind Singh** (stabbed by an Afghan, died there 1708) – not Amar Das, Angad or Arjan.
[149:5:3] > Ram Das = city; Arjan = temple; Hargobind = Akal Takht; Nanded = Gobind Singh's samadhi.
[149:5:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.71-72; Singhania Art & Culture Part 6 p.8; Rocket Indian History 02 Sheet #60; old app notes row 149
## SUB 6 | Guru Granth Sahib
[149:6:0] - **Adi Granth compiled by Guru Arjan (5th) in 1604**; **final version by Guru Gobind Singh at Damdama Sahib (1705)**; declared the **eternal Guru** (1708).
[149:6:1] - Script **Gurmukhi**; language "Sant Bhasha" (mix of Punjabi, Hindi and dialects).
[149:6:2] - Contains hymns of six Gurus (incl. **116 hymns of Tegh Bahadur**) and of non-Sikh saints: **Kabir**, Sufi **Sheikh (Baba) Farid**, **Namdev**, **Ravidas** (**41 shabdas**), Jaidev.
[149:6:3] - Sikh marriage **Anand Karaj** = four circumambulations of the Granth while **Lavan** hymns are sung.
[149:6:4] > Arjan 1604 (Adi Granth) → Gobind Singh 1705 (final) → eternal Guru 1708.
[149:6:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.70, p.72; old app notes row 149
## SUB 7 | Banda Bahadur and the Sikh Misls
[149:7:0] - **Original name Lachhman Dev**; Guru Gobind Singh named him **Banda** and sent him north from **Nanded (1708)**.
[149:7:1] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [149:7:1.0] 1709 | Seized Samana
  [149:7:1.1] 1710 | Defeated Wazir Khan at Chappar Chiri; conquered Sirhind → first sovereign Sikh state, capital Lohgarh (Sirhind Fateh Diwas, 12-14 May)
  [149:7:1.2] 1715 | Eight-month siege of Gurdas Nangal; captured by Farrukhsiyar's forces
  [149:7:1.3] 1716 | Executed at Delhi by Farrukhsiyar for refusing to convert
[149:7:2] - Abolished zamindari, gave farmers ownership of land; **coins in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh**.
[149:7:3] - After him: Bandai and Tat Khalsa split (healed 1721, Bhai Mani Singh); **Dal Khalsa** (Kapur Singh) = combined force; Khalsa rule between the **Sutlej and Jamuna**.
[149:7:4] - **12 misls** (misl = "equal"; democratic military brotherhoods): **Bhangi, Ahluwalia, Ramgarhia, Kanhaiya, Sukerchakia, Phulkian** … – Kanphata were Nath yogis, not a misl.
[149:7:5] > Banda: Lachhman Dev → Sirhind 1710 (Lohgarh) → executed 1716 by Farrukhsiyar; 12 misls → Ranjit Singh (Sukerchakia).
[149:7:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Lens May 2026 p.3 (Banda Singh Bahadur, PIB); Spectrum Modern India p.145-146; PMF Modern History Part 1 p.74-75; old app notes row 149
