=== NOTES 1:150 | Age of Discovery and the Sea Route to India – Vasco Da Gama; Motives of European Expansion
## SUB 0 | Vasco da Gama and the Sea Route, 1498
[150:0:0] # The voyage
[150:0:1] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [150:0:1.0] Sponsor | King Manuel I of Portugal
  [150:0:1.1] Left Lisbon | 8 July 1497 (four ships incl. a store ship; São Gabriel carried Vasco himself)
  [150:0:1.2] Route | Lisbon → Cape of Good Hope → East African coast (Malindi) → Calicut
  [150:0:1.3] Guide | the Gujarati pilot Abdul Majid, taken on at Malindi
  [150:0:1.4] Landfall | Kappad, near Calicut (Kozhikode), Malabar (western) coast
  [150:0:1.5] Arrival | May 1498 – land sighted ~17-18 May, anchored 20 May 1498
  [150:0:1.6] Received by | the Zamorin (Samuthiri), Hindu ruler of Calicut
  [150:0:1.7] Stay / return | about three months; back in Portugal 1499 with a cargo sold at a huge profit
[150:0:2] - **Year asked (×10):** Vasco da Gama reached Calicut / found the sea route in **1498** (the voyage = **1497-98**); 1492 = Columbus, 1453 = fall of Constantinople, 1488 = Dias.
[150:0:3] - **"May 17, 1498"** (APPSC G2-B 1989 option) is the only 1498 option – accept it; the usual date is 20 May.
[150:0:4] - **First landing port:** **Calicut** (not Cochin, Quilon or Surat); he went to the court of the **Zamorin of Calicut**, not Travancore, Poona or Cambay.
[150:0:5] - **Sea route via the Cape of Good Hope** = Vasco da Gama (not Columbus, Cabot or Amundsen).
[150:0:6] - **Contemporaries in 1498:** Delhi – **Sikandar Lodi**; Vijayanagara – **Immadi Narasimha Raya** (Saluva); Portugal – Manuel I.
[150:0:7] # Later voyages
[150:0:8] TABLE head: Voyage | Outcome
  [150:0:8.0] 2nd, 1502 (Spectrum: 1501) | Zamorin refused to expel Arab traders; war; factory at Cannanore; Portuguese settle at Kochi
  [150:0:8.1] 3rd, 1524 | came as Viceroy; died at Kochi the same year
[150:0:9] - **Cabral (1500):** first Portuguese factory at **Calicut**, then trading centres at **Cannanore and Cochin**.
[150:0:10] - **Profit:** the first cargo sold at about **60 times** its cost (old app notes); buying pepper through Muslim middlemen cost ten times more (Spectrum).
[150:0:11] > Contemporaries angle: Krishnadeva Raya (1509-29) came after da Gama; Sikandar, not Ibrahim, Lodi ruled Delhi in 1498.
[150:0:12] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.55-57; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.24-25; PMF Modern History Part 1 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.100; old app notes row 150
## SUB 1 | Order of European Arrival – First and Last
[150:1:0] TABLE head: Power | Arrival / company | First factory | Headquarters
  [150:1:0.0] Portuguese | 1498 (no company; state enterprise) | Calicut 1500 (Cabral) | Cochin → Goa (1530)
  [150:1:0.1] Dutch | VOC 1602 | Masulipatnam 1605 | Pulicat → Nagapattinam (1690)
  [150:1:0.2] English | EIC 31 Dec 1600 | Surat 1613 (permanent) | Surat → Bombay / Madras / Calcutta
  [150:1:0.3] Danes | 1616 | Tranquebar 1620 | Tranquebar; Serampore (1755)
  [150:1:0.4] French | 1664 (Colbert) | Surat 1668 | Pondicherry
[150:1:1] - **Arrival order:** **Portuguese → Dutch → English → Danes → French** (code "4, 2, 1, 3" for English-Dutch-French-Portuguese).
[150:1:2] - **Formation order:** English 1600 → Dutch 1602 → Danes 1616 → French 1664.
[150:1:3] - **First Europeans** to come for trade / to land / to set up sea-trade centres = **Portuguese**; **last** to come as traders = **French** ("the last Europeans to come to India with the purpose of trade", Spectrum).
[150:1:4] - **First to come and last to leave** = Portuguese (Goa, Daman, Diu freed **1961**).
[150:1:5] - **Chronology (IAS 2000):** Qutub Minar (begun by Aibak, finished by Iltutmish) → death of **Firuz Tughlaq (1388)** → arrival of the **Portuguese (1498)** → reign of **Krishnadeva Raya (1509-29)** = **2, 4, 3, 1**.
[150:1:6] - **VOC (1602)** is widely called the **first joint-stock company to sell shares to the public**.
[150:1:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.61, p.67-69, p.74; PMF Modern History Part 2 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-02.txt) p.1, p.4, p.21; old app notes rows 150-151
## SUB 2 | Explorers and Motives of European Expansion
[150:2:0] # Why Europe sought a sea route
[150:2:1] - **1453:** Ottoman Sultan **Mehmed II** took **Constantinople**, closing the overland route; the Asian trade was controlled by **Arabs**, and **Venice and Genoa** distributed the goods in Europe.
[150:2:2] - **Motives:** spices (pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, ginger), silk and Indian textiles; profit; breaking the **Arab (Muslim) monopoly**; spreading **Christianity** (Prester John legend); rivalry of Portugal, Spain and later Holland, England, France. "Roman imperial administration" is NOT a motive.
[150:2:3] - **Aids:** **Prince Henry the Navigator** (naval school; papal bull of 1454); the **caravel** (ship) and **astrolabe**.
[150:2:4] - **"Bear in mind that the commerce of India is the commerce of the world"** – **Peter the Great** of Russia, about **18th-century** India (APPSC G2 2017); not da Gama, Clive or Dupleix.
[150:2:5] # Explorers
[150:2:6] TABLE head: Explorer | Sponsor | Year | Achievement
  [150:2:6.0] Bartholomew Dias | Portugal | 1487-88 | rounded the Cape of Good Hope ("Cape of Storms", renamed by King John II)
  [150:2:6.1] Christopher Columbus | Spain | 1492 | the Americas ("West Indies")
  [150:2:6.2] John Cabot | England | 1497 | North America
  [150:2:6.3] Vasco da Gama | Portugal | 1498 | sea route to India
  [150:2:6.4] Pedro Alvares Cabral | Portugal | 1500 | Brazil; factory at Calicut
  [150:2:6.5] Ferdinand Magellan | Spain | 1519-22 | first circumnavigation of the globe (completed by Elcano after Magellan's death)
[150:2:7] - **Dividing the world:** papal bull **Inter caetera (1493**, Alexander VI) and **Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)** – line 370 leagues west of Cape Verde; **east → Portugal, west → Spain**.
[150:2:8] - **New World civilisations, north → south:** **Aztec** (central Mexico) → **Maya** (Yucatan, Central America) → **Muisca** (Colombia) → **Inca** (Peru).
[150:2:9] - **AP and Brazil:** Brazil's **Nelore** cattle descend from **Nellore** (AP) cattle; in **July 2025** the PM's visit for the **17th BRICS Summit** (Rio de Janeiro) recalled ties going back to Cabral's landing (1500).
[150:2:10] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.55 (Prince Henry, Tordesillas, Dias 1487), p.107 (Peter the Great); NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.23; old app notes row 150 (sub 0-3); general knowledge for Magellan and the New World order (not checked)
## SUB 3 | World History I – American and French Revolutions, Napoleon
[150:3:0] # American Revolution
[150:3:1] - **Cause:** colonists refused taxes voted by a Parliament where they had no seats – **"No taxation without representation"**; merchants **boycotted British goods**. It was colonists vs Britain, not settlers vs Native Americans.
[150:3:2] - **Stamp Act 1765** (repealed 1766) → **Stamp Act Congress, New York City, October 1765** (9 of the 13 colonies).
[150:3:3] - **Coercive (Intolerable) Acts 1774** made reconciliation virtually impossible; the earlier Stamp Act repeal does not explain that.
[150:3:4] - **First Continental Congress, Philadelphia, Sept 1774:** rejected **Galloway's plan** of union under British authority, drew up a **statement of grievances**, agreed the **Continental Association** (stop trade with England).
[150:3:5] # French Revolution
[150:3:6] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [150:3:6.0] June 1789 | Tennis Court Oath – Third Estate (National Assembly)
  [150:3:6.1] 1791 | Olympe de Gouges' Declaration of the Rights of Woman and the Female Citizen
  [150:3:6.2] 1792 | National Convention meets; monarchy abolished, republic
  [150:3:6.3] June 1793 – July 1794 | Jacobins (with the sans-culottes) purge the Girondins; Reign of Terror; ends with Robespierre's execution, July 1794
  [150:3:6.4] 1804 | Napoleon Emperor of the French (first emperor of France); Napoleonic Code
[150:3:7] - **Reign of Terror:** the **Law of Suspects (Sept 1793)** let anyone be arrested, not only the political class; the Jacobins were **anti-clerical** (de-Christianisation), not allies of the clergy.
[150:3:8] - **Olympe de Gouges:** politically active writer; "the nation is the **union of woman and man**"; not on the committee that drafted the Rights of Man (1789); opposed the Jacobins and was guillotined **1793**.
[150:3:9] # Napoleon
[150:3:10] - **Third Coalition (1805):** Britain, **Austria, Russia, Sweden** (Prussia joined 1806) against **France**.
[150:3:11] - **Austerlitz 1805** → Treaty of Pressburg; **Tilsit 1807** = treaties, not a battle; **Wagram 1809 → Treaty of Schönbrunn**.
[150:3:12] ~~ Sources: general knowledge, not checked (no world-history text in the library); web searches on the Reign of Terror (worldhistory.org, Macmillan Hunt text) for the June 1793 purge
## SUB 4 | World History II – Industrial, Russian and Chinese Revolutions; Ancient Firsts
[150:4:0] # Industrial Revolution (Britain first)
[150:4:1] - **Why Britain first:** **coal and iron**, **steam power**, regular **raw materials** (colonies), **navigable rivers/canals**, favourable social-political order, **capitalist** practice and scientific inventions; railways (1825-30) sustained rather than started it.
[150:4:2] - **Cotton inventions:** **Kay's flying shuttle 1733 → Hargreaves' spinning jenny 1764 → Arkwright's water frame 1769 → Crompton's mule 1779**.
[150:4:3] - **Factory system:** production under one roof in towns ruined the **guilds**; **merchant capitalists** gained control (not "production moved to the countryside").
[150:4:4] - **Impact:** cottage industry → **factory system**; **working-class movements**; overcrowded **towns** (not villages).
[150:4:5] # Russian Revolution, 1917
[150:4:6] - **Provisional Government (Feb/March 1917):** first headed by **Prince Lvov**, then by **Alexander Kerensky** (July-Oct 1917); overthrown in the **October (Bolshevik) Revolution**.
[150:4:7] - **Lenin** = father of the Revolution; Russia = first **Marxist** revolution.
[150:4:8] - **Bolsheviks** (Lenin): small, disciplined party; **Mensheviks**: party open to all, as in Germany.
[150:4:9] # Asia and other events
[150:4:10] - **Crimean War 1853-56:** **Russia vs Ottoman Turkey** (Britain, France, Sardinia on the Turkish side).
[150:4:11] - **Boxer Rebellion:** China, 1899-1901, peak **1900**.
[150:4:12] - **1911 Revolution (Xinhai):** ended the Qing; **Republic of China** (1912).
[150:4:13] # Ancient and Renaissance firsts
[150:4:14] - **First proper writing system:** **Sumerian** cuneiform (Mesopotamia), before Egyptian hieroglyphs; Indus script undeciphered.
[150:4:15] - **Mona Lisa** = **Leonardo da Vinci** (Italian Renaissance).
[150:4:16] ~~ Sources: general knowledge, not checked; web search on the CDS 2017 Industrial Revolution question (examrobot.com, prepp.in answer keys: all four)

=== NOTES 1:152 | Portuguese in India – Almeida's Blue Water Policy, Albuquerque, Estado Da India, Cartaz System, Decline
## SUB 0 | Viceroys and Governors – Almeida's Blue Water Policy, Albuquerque, da Cunha
[152:0:0] TABLE head: Governor | Years | Title | Key acts
  [152:0:0.0] Francisco de Almeida | 1505-09 | first Governor and Viceroy (appointed by Manuel I) | Blue Water Policy; forts at Anjediva, Cannanore (Cochin); Battle of Diu 1509 – beat Gujarat + Egyptian Mamluks + Zamorin
  [152:0:0.1] Afonso de Albuquerque | 1509-15 | real founder of Portuguese power | took Goa (1510) from Bijapur; Malacca 1511, Hormuz 1515; mixed marriages; abolished sati; enforced the cartaz permit system
  [152:0:0.2] Nino (Nuno) da Cunha | 1529-38 | Governor | HQ Cochin → Goa (1530); Bassein 1534 and Diu from Bahadur Shah; settlers in Bengal (Hooghly)
[152:0:1] - **Blue Water Policy** = **Portuguese**, introduced by **Almeida**: mastery of the Indian Ocean ("As long as you may be powerful at sea you will hold India as yours"), trade not land – not Albuquerque, Cabral or da Cunha.
[152:0:2] - **⚠ Trap:** Albuquerque **reversed** it with territorial conquest; Spectrum calls the Blue Water Policy the "cartaze system", but the pass system is a separate tool (see Cartaz).
[152:0:3] - **Real founder** = **Albuquerque**, not Vasco da Gama, Dias, Almeida or Drake; **first Viceroy** = **Almeida**, not Albuquerque.
[152:0:4] - **Goa (1510)** = "the first bit of Indian territory under the Europeans since Alexander the Great".
[152:0:5] - **Pairs:** Blue Water Policy – Portuguese naval supremacy; Market Policy – **Alauddin Khalji**; Swadeshi – boycott; Home Rule – self-government.
[152:0:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.57-59; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.26-28; PMF Modern History Part 1 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.100-101
## SUB 1 | Portuguese Bases, Forts and Indian Rulers
[152:1:0] TABLE head: Place | Year | How
  [152:1:0.0] Calicut | 1500 | first factory (Cabral)
  [152:1:0.1] Cochin | 1503 | first Portuguese fort (Albuquerque, first visit); first capital
  [152:1:0.2] Cannanore, Anjediva | 1505 | forts of Almeida
  [152:1:0.3] Goa | 1510 | from Bijapur; capital from 1530
  [152:1:0.4] Bassein / Diu | 1534 / 1535 | from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat, pressed by Humayun
  [152:1:0.5] Daman | 1559 | captured
  [152:1:0.6] Hooghly | c. 1579 | Akbar's farman
  [152:1:0.7] San Thome, Nagapattinam, Masulipatnam, Pulicat | 16th c. | east-coast posts
[152:1:1] - **Bahadur Shah of Gujarat** was **killed by the Portuguese (1537)** – invited aboard a Portuguese ship during talks.
[152:1:2] - **Krishnadeva Raya** of Vijayanagara was **friendly with the Portuguese** (horse trade; fort at **Bhatkal**; Friar Luis' mission; help at Goa).
[152:1:3] - **Bengal:** first factory at **Chittagong (1528)**; **Satgaon and Chatgaon** factories from **1534**.
[152:1:4] - **Goa 1510:** **Friar Luis** negotiated with Krishnadeva Raya (1509-10); the Vijayanagara naval chief **Timmaju** helped Albuquerque.
[152:1:5] - **Marathas** took **Salsette and Bassein (1739)**.
[152:1:6] - **Diu:** naval battle **1509** (Almeida) → fort **1535** (treaty with Bahadur Shah) → full conquest **1546**.
[152:1:7] - **Churches and forts:** **San Thome** (Mylapore) church over the tomb of **St. Thomas (1523)**; **Bandel** church near Hooghly (**1599**); **Fort Aguada** (Goa) is Portuguese, Geldria Dutch, Fort St. George English.
[152:1:8] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.59, p.65; PMF Modern History Part 1 p.101-104; old app notes row 151 (sub 3), row 152 (sub 4)
## SUB 2 | Cartaz System – Naval Trade Licence
[152:2:0] - **Cartaz** = a **naval trade licence / pass** that Asian ships had to buy from the Portuguese to sail the Indian Ocean; begun by **Vasco da Gama (1502)**, systematised by **Albuquerque**.
[152:2:1] - A ship **without a cartaz was confiscated** and its crew punished; monopoly goods (pepper, horses, ginger, cinnamon …) could not be loaded.
[152:2:2] - Backed by the **cafila** (convoy of local ships under a Portuguese fleet; older app notes wrote "Caes") and **customs duties**.
[152:2:3] - Monopoly and duties caused constant war with the **Zamorin of Calicut**.
[152:2:4] > Distractors in Polytechnic 2020: "Marcent", "Shellback", "Pollywog" are not Portuguese systems.
[152:2:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 1 p.101; Spectrum Modern India p.58
## SUB 3 | Hooghly, Piracy and the Decline
[152:3:0] - **Hooghly** was the **Portuguese** base for **piracy** (with Arakanese pirates) and slave-raiding in the **Bay of Bengal**.
[152:3:1] - **1632:** **Shah Jahan** had Bengal governor **Qasim Khan** besiege and take Hooghly (June-Sept 1632).
[152:3:2] - **Shaista Khan** (Aurangzeb's Bengal governor) took **Sondip and Chittagong** and crushed the Arakanese pirates.
[152:3:3] - **Goa Inquisition** (from 1560): state machinery used for conversions and against religious dissent; Hindus too were persecuted.
[152:3:4] - **Causes of decline:** weak, corrupt successors after Albuquerque; **religious intolerance** and forced conversions (Goa Inquisition); piracy and dishonest trade; **Portugal united with Spain (1580)**; discovery of **Brazil**; Dutch and English competition.
[152:3:5] - **Losses:** Surat 1612 (English); **Hormuz 1622**; Hooghly 1632; **Nagapattinam 1658 and Cochin / Malabar forts 1663** (Dutch); Salsette-Bassein 1739 (Marathas).
[152:3:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.63-66; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.27; PMF Modern History Part 1 p.102, p.106
## SUB 4 | Contributions – Crops, Printing, Francis Xavier
[152:4:0] - **New World crops brought by the Portuguese:** **tobacco, potato, chilli, tomato, pineapple, papaya, guava, sapota, cashew, maize, groundnut**, lady's finger.
[152:4:1] - **Telugu soil:** the **tomato** (an American plant); not banana, apple or orange.
[152:4:2] - **Chilli** came with the Portuguese; opium, coffee and betel leaf did not.
[152:4:3] - **NOT Portuguese introductions:** **tea, coffee, rubber**; **wheat** is not a New World crop.
[152:4:4] - **Calico:** cotton cloth of **Calicut**, so called in Europe.
[152:4:5] - **Printing press:** Goa **1556**; Bible printed in Kannada and Malayalam.
[152:4:6] - **St. Francis Xavier:** a **co-founder of the Jesuit Order (1534)**; reached Goa 1542; **died on Shangchuan island, China (1552)** – not in Goa – but his body lies in the **Basilica of Bom Jesus, Goa**; feast **3 December** every year.
[152:4:7] > UPSC 2021: statements 1 and 3 ✓, "died in Goa" ✗. UPSC 2025: papaya, pineapple and guava – all three Portuguese introductions.
[152:4:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.27; Spectrum Modern India p.59 (tobacco, cashew); old app notes rows 151-152; general knowledge for Xavier's death place (not checked)
## SUB 5 | First to Come, Last to Leave – Goa 1961 and the Andhra Coast
[152:5:0] - **After 15 August 1947** Goa, Daman and Diu stayed **Portuguese**; the freedom struggle continued against **Portugal**.
[152:5:1] - **Operation Vijay, 19 December 1961** freed them; Goa statehood **30 May 1987**.
[152:5:2] - **Estado da India** = the Portuguese state in Asia (HQ Cochin, then Goa).
[152:5:3] - **Telugu name:** "**Budata Keechu**"; **Petapoli** = **Nizampatnam**; the **1669-70 Machilipatnam factory** allowed by **Abdullah Qutb Shah** was **French**.
[152:5:4] - **Andhra coast:** posts at Masulipatnam, Pulicat, San Thome; Pulicat lost to the Dutch (1610); influence faded by the mid-17th century.
[152:5:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.61; PMF Modern History Part 1 p.107; old app notes row 152 (sub 7-8)

=== NOTES 1:154 | English East India Company – Charter of 1600, Surat, Madras, Bombay, Calcutta; Farman of 1717
## SUB 0 | Surat – the First Permanent Factory and the Mughal Court
[154:0:0] - **Surat (1613)** = the English Company's **first permanent factory in India** – on a **farman of Jahangir** (not Akbar, Shah Jahan or Aurangzeb); Pune, Goa, Pondicherry, Bangalore were never its first factory.
[154:0:1] - **Masulipatnam (1611)** came earlier but only as a temporary trading post (permanent factory 1616) – so "first factory in India" = **Surat**, "first in South India / Andhra" = **Machilipatnam**.
[154:0:2] - **Captain William Hawkins** – third voyage, landed at **Surat 1608**, at Jahangir's court (Agra) **1609**; first envoy of **James I**; permission withdrawn under Portuguese pressure.
[154:0:3] - **Battle of Swally (1612)**: **Captain Thomas Best** defeated the **Portuguese** off Surat → Jahangir's farman of **1613** (factory under Thomas Aldworth).
[154:0:4] - **Sir Thomas Roe (1615-19)** = ambassador of **King James I** to **Jahangir**; no commercial treaty, but privileges to set up factories at **Agra, Ahmedabad and Broach**; his chaplain was **Edward Terry**.
[154:0:5] - **Ralph Fitch (1583-86)** = first Englishman to visit **Akbar's** court (Agra, Fatehpur Sikri) – before Hawkins and Roe.
[154:0:6] - **Western Presidency**: seat first at **Surat**, shifted to **Bombay in 1687**.
[154:0:7] - **Factories of the 1st quarter of the 17th century**: **Broach** (yes, Roe's privileges); **Chicacole** and **Trichinopoly** – no (UPSC 2021: 1 only).
[154:0:8] TABLE head: Order | Person | Year | Emperor
  [154:0:8.0] 1 | Ralph Fitch | 1583-86 | Akbar
  [154:0:8.1] 2 | William Hawkins | 1608-11 | Jahangir
  [154:0:8.2] 3 | Thomas Best (Swally) | 1612 | Jahangir
  [154:0:8.3] 4 | Sir Thomas Roe | 1615-19 | Jahangir
[154:0:9] > Company formed under **Akbar** (1600), first factory under **Jahangir** (1613, Surat); Roe was sent by **James I**.
[154:0:10] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.69-73 (book p.37-41); NextGen Modern India L3 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l3-01.txt) p.7-9; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 5 p.31-32; old app notes row 154
## SUB 1 | The Charter of 1600 and the Company's Formation
[154:1:0] - **31 December 1600**: **Queen Elizabeth I** granted the charter → the Company was founded in **1600** (not 1601, 1604 or 1607).
[154:1:1] - Name: "**The Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies**"; promoted by the "**Merchant Adventurers**" (1599).
[154:1:2] - Charter gave only **exclusive trading rights** – a **15-year monopoly** between the **Cape of Good Hope** and the **Straits of Magellan** (made indefinite in 1609); **no territorial governance or legislative power**.
[154:1:3] - **Emperor of India in 1600 = Akbar** (1556-1605), contemporary of **Elizabeth I** (1558-1603).
[154:1:4] - Management: a **Governor + 24-member committee** (later Court of Directors); shareholders = General Court (later Court of Proprietors).
[154:1:5] - **First voyage 1602** under **James Lancaster** (flagship **Red Dragon**, capital £68,000) → factory at **Bantam** (Java), not India.
[154:1:6] - **Levant Company (1592)** traded with the Ottoman lands; the **East India Company** was the first chartered to trade with India; "The English Company trading to the East Indies" was the rival of **1698**.
[154:1:7] TABLE head: Year | Change
  [154:1:7.0] 1657 | Cromwell's charter – permanent joint stock
  [154:1:7.1] Charles II, James II | Coin money, jurisdiction, war and peace with non-Christians
  [154:1:7.2] 1708 | Rival companies merged – United Company of Merchants of England Trading to the East Indies
  [154:1:7.3] 1858 | Company rule ended – Government of India Act, 1858
[154:1:8] - Early objective: **eastern trade** (spices, textiles), paid for with **imported bullion**; secret of later success (UPPCS 1994): absence of nationalism, western-trained army – "all the above".
[154:1:9] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.69-70, 74 (book p.37-38, 42); NextGen Modern India L3 Part 1 p.5-7; general knowledge, not checked (Red Dragon); old app notes row 154
## SUB 2 | Madras – Francis Day and Fort St. George
[154:2:0] - **1639**: **Francis Day** (with **Andrew Cogan**), a member of the Masulipatnam council, got **Madraspatnam** on lease from the **Chandragiri** ruler **Venkatapati Raya III**, through the **Damerla brothers (Venkatadri, Ayyappa)** – not John Child, Roe or Oxenden.
[154:2:1] - **Fort St. George** at Madraspatnam (near **Mylapore**/San Thome): built from 1 March 1640, completed **23 April 1644** (St George's Day) = **first fort built by the English in India** and the **first fortified English settlement** (not Fort William, Mahim or Aguada).
[154:2:2] - **Chennapatnam** named after **Damerla Chennappa**; Madras = chief of east-coast factories (1641), **presidency 1684**, **first municipality in India (1687-88)**.
[154:2:3] - Main business of the early English settlements in Andhra and Fort St. George = **trade in locally woven piece-goods** (not conquest, spices or agriculture).
[154:2:4] - **Mid-18th century populations** of the fortified English settlements: **Madras about 3 lakh**, Calcutta 2 lakh, Bombay 70,000 → **Madras largest**.
[154:2:5] TABLE head: Presidency | Seat
  [154:2:5.0] Madras | Fort St. George
  [154:2:5.1] Bombay | Bombay (replaced Surat, 1687)
  [154:2:5.2] Bengal | Fort William, Calcutta
[154:2:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L3 Part 1 p.13-15; NextGen Modern India L2 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l2-01.txt) p.11; Spectrum Modern India p.71; https://tutorialspoint.com/modern_indian_history/modern_indian_history_east_india_company.htm (populations); old app notes row 154
## SUB 3 | Bengal and Calcutta – Hugli, Job Charnock, Fort William
[154:3:0] - **1651**: **Shah Shuja** (subahdar) let the English trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year → **first English factory in Bengal = Hugli (1651)**, then **Qasim Bazar**, Patna, Rajmahal (earlier Hariharpur and Balasore, 1633, are in **Odisha**).
[154:3:1] - **Job Charnock**, chief of the **Qasim Bazar** factory, returned to **Sutanuti** in **August 1690** → **founder of Calcutta** (not Charles Eyre, Aungier, Norris or John Surman).
[154:3:2] - **1698**: zamindari of **Sutanuti, Gobindapur and Kalikata** bought; **1700**: fortified settlement named **Fort William** – Sir **Charles Eyre** first president.
[154:3:3] - Fort built by the British at Calcutta = **Fort William** (Fort St. David is at Cuddalore; Fort St. George at Madras).
[154:3:4] - Europeans got the best **saltpetre (shora) and opium from Bihar**.
[154:3:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.68, 71-72 (book p.36, 39-40); old app notes row 154
## SUB 4 | Bombay – Dowry, Lease and Gerald Aungier
[154:4:0] - **1661**: Bombay came to **Charles II** as dowry of the **Portuguese** princess **Catherine of Braganza** (married 1662) – taken from the **Portuguese**, not Dutch, French or Danes.
[154:4:1] - **1668**: Charles II gave it to the Company for **£10 a year** (some books 1674/1688 – the lease was 1668).
[154:4:2] - **Gerald Aungier** (President of Surat and Governor of Bombay, 1669-77) made Bombay a major commercial hub – "founding father" of Bombay.
[154:4:3] - Bombay **replaced Surat** as the chief English settlement on the west coast (1687).
[154:4:4] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.70; NextGen Modern India L3 Part 1 p.17; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Aungier; old app notes row 154
## SUB 5 | Chronology, Child's War and the Farman of 1717
[154:5:0] - Order of English centres: **Surat 1613 → Madras 1639 → Bombay 1668 → Calcutta 1690**.
[154:5:1] - **Child's War (1686-90)**: under **Josiah Child** (London) and **Sir John Child** (in India) the Company fought **Aurangzeb**, lost, was pardoned on paying a fine – Aurangzeb demanded Sir John Child's expulsion.
[154:5:2] - **Shivaji** sacked Surat twice (1664, 1670) and threatened the English factory.
[154:5:3] - **Farman of 1717** (mission of **John Surman**, 1715) by **Farrukhsiyar** = "**Magna Carta**" of the Company.
[154:5:4] TABLE head: Region | Privilege (1717)
  [154:5:4.0] Bengal | Duty-free trade for Rs 3,000 a year; dastaks
  [154:5:4.1] Surat | All duties dropped for Rs 10,000 a year
  [154:5:4.2] Bombay | Company coins current in the Mughal empire
[154:5:5] - Misuse of dastaks for private trade drained the Nawab's revenue → Plassey (1757), Buxar (1764) → **Bengal** = first major territorial base.
[154:5:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.72-73 (book p.40-41); NextGen Modern India L3 Part 1 p.17; old app notes row 154

=== NOTES 1:157 | Advent of Europeans in Andhra – Portuguese, Dutch, French and English
## SUB 0 | The English in Andhra – Globe, Machilipatnam and Armagaon
[157:0:0] - **1611**: the ship **Globe** under **Captain (Anthony) Hippon** – not Hawkins – reached **Machilipatnam** (January 1611), with **Peter Floris** (a Dutchman in English service) as merchant.
[157:0:1] - Permission from the Golconda Sultan **Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah** → **first English factory in Andhra / South India / on the east coast = Machilipatnam (1611)** – not Kakinada, Visakhapatnam, Bheemunipatnam or Golconda.
[157:0:2] - A-R (APPSC G2 2025): "Globe under Hawkins" is **false**; "Quli Qutb Shah permitted the factory" is **true** → (A) false, (R) true.
[157:0:3] TABLE head: Year | English settlement | Note
  [157:0:3.0] 1611 | Machilipatnam | 1st
  [157:0:3.1] 1621 | Pulicat (Dutch settlement) | Abandoned – Dutch hostility
  [157:0:3.2] 1626 | Armagaon (Dugarajapatnam), Nellore region, now Tirupati district | Named after Karanam Armugam Mudali; 35 miles north of Pulicat; second English factory in the Andhra region
  [157:0:3.3] 1632 | Golden Farman → back to Machilipatnam | 
  [157:0:3.4] 1639 | Madras | Francis Day
  [157:0:3.5] 1682 | Visakhapatnam | 
[157:0:4] - English factory in **Nellore district** = **1626** (Armagaon); other English posts: Nizampatnam, Narsapur, **Madapollam**, Bheemunipatnam.
[157:0:5] - **Golden Farman** = **1632** (Spectrum, PMF; NextGen Qutb Shahi notes give 1636) from the Sultan of Golconda **Abdullah Qutb Shah**: free trade in **Golconda ports** for **500 pagodas a year** – not from the Mughal emperor.
[157:0:6] - English used **Dadni** advances through **dubashes**; they **paid weavers less** and demanded high quality, so weavers preferred the Dutch, Portuguese and French.
[157:0:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L3 Part 1 p.7, 13; NextGen Modern India L2 Part 1 p.10; NextGen Modern India Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-part1.txt) p.2-3; Spectrum Modern India p.71 (Golden Farman 1632); PMF Modern History Part 2 p.5 (Golden Farman 1632); NextGen Qutb Shahis (src/ap-history/nextgen-11-qutbshahis.txt) p.8 (1636); old app notes row 157
## SUB 1 | First Europeans in Andhra – Order of the Factories
[157:1:0] - **First Europeans to trade with India = Portuguese (1498)**; order of arrival: **Portuguese → Dutch → English → French**.
[157:1:1] - **First trade contacts with the Andhra region = Portuguese** (16th century, from San Thome and Pulicat) – but they opened a factory at Machilipatnam only in **1670**.
[157:1:2] - **First European factory in Andhra = Dutch, Machilipatnam, 1605** (NextGen; Spectrum) – "first factory / trade centre at Machilipatnam" = **Dutch**, not Portuguese.
[157:1:3] TABLE head: Order | Power | Machilipatnam factory | Permission
  [157:1:3.0] 1st | Dutch | 1605 | Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
  [157:1:3.1] 2nd | English | 1611 | Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
  [157:1:3.2] 3rd | French | 1669 | Abdullah Qutb Shah
  [157:1:3.3] 4th | Portuguese | 1670 | Abdullah Qutb Shah
[157:1:4] - Why the Europeans came: coastal Andhra's position on the **Bay of Bengal** for sea trade, its **chintz** and **diamonds**; Hyderabad founded **1591** by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah.
[157:1:5] - **Tavernier** (17th-century French jeweller) visited the Andhra (Golconda) mines for diamonds; **Marco Polo** visited **Motupalli**.
[157:1:6] - **Portuguese** contributions: crops such as **tobacco**, chilli, cashew (to check soil erosion in Goa); Arabian Sea monopoly until the **17th century**; **Blue Water Policy** of **Almeida**.
[157:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 1 p.4-5, 8, 12; Spectrum Modern India p.67 (Dutch first factory Masulipatnam 1605); NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 5 p.27-28; NextGen Qutb Shahis p.12-13 (Tavernier); old app notes row 157
## SUB 2 | The French in Andhra – Machilipatnam to the Northern Circars
[157:2:0] - **French factory in Andhra = Machilipatnam, 1669** (by **Marcara**, permission of **Abdullah Qutb Shah**) – not Motupalli, Narsapur, Visakhapatnam, Yanam or Kakinada.
[157:2:1] - **Yanam** (1723) = the **only French territorial possession / settlement in Andhra**; not Rajahmundry, Hamsaladivi or Ongole.
[157:2:2] - **1753**: **Bussy** got the **Northern Circars** – Mustafanagar (**Kondapalli**), Eluru, Rajahmundry, Chicacole – from **Salabat Jang** to pay for French troops (Nellore was not among them).
[157:2:3] TABLE head: Battle | Year | Fact
  [157:2:3.0] Tumnapalem | 1756 | Bussy + Vijayaramaraju vs Jafar Ali
  [157:2:3.1] Bobbili | 24 Jan 1757 | Vijayaramaraju of Vizianagaram, with Bussy's French, destroyed Bobbili; Ranga Rao killed; queen Mallamma; Tandra Papayya then killed Vijayaramaraju
  [157:2:3.2] Chandurthi (Condore) | Dec 1758 | Col. Forde (sent from Bengal), aided by Ananda Gajapati of Vizianagaram, defeated the French under Conflans
  [157:2:3.3] Fall of Masulipatnam | 1759 | Forde took Machilipatnam; Salabat Jang gave the English Machilipatnam, Nizampatnam, Vakal Mannar, part of Kondapalli
  [157:2:3.4] Wandiwash | 1760 | Eyre Coote beat Count de Lally
[157:2:4] - **Chandurthi** lies in the old **East Godavari** district (now the **Kakinada** region) – not Vizianagaram, Nellore, Chittoor or Kurnool.
[157:2:5] - Chandurthi led to the **expulsion of the French** from the Northern Sarkars; Circars to the English 1765-68, **Guntur 1788**.
[157:2:6] - The **European** traders entered Indian politics when the Nizams of Hyderabad sought their help against rivals.
[157:2:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 1 p.11-13 (Chandurthi 7 Dec 1758); NextGen Modern India Part 1 p.3-4 (gives 1759); https://www.deccanchronicle.com/amp/southern-states/andhra-pradesh/at-26-pusapati-king-drove-away-french-forces-from-north-andhra-1896173 (Chandurthi "now in Kakinada region", 7 Dec 1758); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Condore (9 Dec 1758); Spectrum Modern India p.74; old app notes rows 155, 157
## SUB 3 | The Dutch in Andhra
[157:3:0] TABLE head: Dutch settlement | Year | Note
  [157:3:0.0] Machilipatnam | 1605 | First Dutch (and first European) factory in Andhra; Admiral Van Hagen; they built a fort there
  [157:3:0.1] Nizampatnam (Petapoli) | 1606 | Second Dutch factory on the Coromandel coast
  [157:3:0.2] Pulicat | 1610 | Fort Geldria; Dutch HQ till 1690, then Nagapattinam
  [157:3:0.3] Palakollu | 1613 | Godavari delta
  [157:3:0.4] Draksharama | 1633 | Godavari delta
  [157:3:0.5] Bheemunipatnam, Narasapuram, Jagannayakapuram | 17th century | 
[157:3:1] - APPSC statements: Dutch factories at **Surat, Machilipatnam and Petapoli** (true); settlements at **Nagapattinam, Narasapuram, Bheemunipatnam, Chinsurah** (true); "51 trading centres on the Andhra coast" – not in the sources → **B and C only**.
[157:3:2] - Dutch = first to get the right to **mint coins** in Andhra; traded **without middlemen**; Chinsura (Bengal) was Dutch; defeated at **Bedara/Chinsura (1759)**.
[157:3:3] - Other Dutch factories in India (Spectrum): **Surat (1616)**, Bimlipatam (1641), Karaikal (1645), Chinsura (1653), Nagapatam (1658), Cochin (1663).
[157:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L3 Part 1 p.3; NextGen Modern India Part 1 p.1; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 5 p.29-30; NextGen Modern India L2 Part 1 p.8-10; old app notes row 157
## SUB 4 | Missionaries and Colonial Firsts in Andhra
[157:4:0] - **Christian missionaries** contributed most to education in Andhra; **Rev. Robert Noble** started a school at **Machilipatnam (1843)** → **Noble College**.
[157:4:1] - **Benjamin Schultze** completed the first Telugu Bible translation about **1732** (printed at Halle 1746-47).
[157:4:2] TABLE head: System | Fact
  [157:4:2.0] Ryotwari | First tried in the Baramahals (Madras Presidency)
  [157:4:2.1] Zilla-bandi system | Hyderabad State, 1865, by Salar Jung
  [157:4:2.2] Mulki rules | 1888, under Mir Mahboob Ali Khan
[157:4:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History - APPSC Part 7 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-07.txt) p.6 (Zilla-bandi 1865); Rocket AP History (Zilla-bandi); old app notes row 157

=== NOTES 1:158 | Trade Centres of Coastal Andhra – Masulipatnam, Nizampatnam, Bheemunipatnam, Yanam
## SUB 0 | Machilipatnam – the Great Port of the Qutb Shahis
[158:0:0] - **Machilipatnam (Masulipatnam)** = the **most famous port town for (handloom) textile trade in the 16th-17th centuries** and the **chief trading centre of Andhra with the world before the 19th century** – not Motupalli, Visakhapatnam, Narsapur, Korangi or Bheemunipatnam.
[158:0:1] - Under **Golconda** in the 1600s it was famous for **textiles and diamonds** (also rubies) – not silver, gold or platinum.
[158:0:2] - Principal maritime gateway of the **Qutb Shahis**; passed to the Mughals when **Aurangzeb annexed Golconda (1687)**; **Komatis** were the key merchant community.
[158:0:3] - Ptolemy's **Maisolia (Mysolia)**, the "great market" = Machilipatnam (Kantakossyla = Ghantasala).
[158:0:4] - **First English factory in South India = Masulipatam, 1611** (Vizagapatam came in 1682).
[158:0:5] TABLE head: Export | Centre
  [158:0:5.0] Chintz (glazed, brighter after washing), palampores, kalamkari | Machilipatnam
  [158:0:5.1] Saltpetre | Machilipatnam, Narsapur, Pulicat
  [158:0:5.2] Diamonds, rubies | Golconda mines; Koh-i-Noor from Kollur (Guntur)
  [158:0:5.3] Silk and cotton piece-goods | Bengal
  [158:0:5.4] Indigo | Nagulavancha, Nalgonda
  [158:0:5.5] Salt | Pedaganjam, Chinaganjam
  [158:0:5.6] Cheap calico | Narasapuram
  [158:0:5.7] Taanis | Injaram
  [158:0:5.8] Rumaals (kerchiefs) | Nellore
[158:0:6] - Textiles = dominant industry, second only to diamonds in the Qutb Shahi economy; **pintado** = printed textile; English purchases were financed with **bullion**.
[158:0:7] - Imports: **horses** from Ormuz/Persia, **elephants** from Ceylon, **camphor** from Punjab – credited to the Reddi-period merchant **Avachi Tippaya Setti**.
[158:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L3 Part 1 p.13, 19; NextGen Qutb Shahis p.8; NextGen AP History - APPSC Part 15 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-15.txt) p.22 (Machilipatnam, Narsapur trade lists); old app notes row 158
## SUB 1 | Ports Before the Europeans – Motupalli and Ghantasala
[158:1:0] - **Motupalli (Desiyakondapattanam)**, now in Bapatla district = the **most important seaport of the Kakatiya kingdom** – not Machilipatnam (Qutb Shahi port), Kakinada, Nellore or Dharanikota.
[158:1:1] - **Marco Polo** visited it in **1287** under **Rudrama Devi**; **Ganapatideva's Abhaya Sasanam** protected foreign traders; Reddi minister **Somaya** issued another; **Anavota Reddi** lifted customs duties.
[158:1:2] - **Haravilasam** of **Srinatha**, dedicated to **Avachi Tippaya Setti**, describes the **sea trade of the Reddi period** – not Kashikhandam, Harivamsa or Bhimeswara Purana.
[158:1:3] - **Roman coins** in Andhra: **Bhattiprolu** (NextGen previous-paper key), Nagarjunakonda, Vinukonda, Vijayawada, Attirala, Salihundam; **Ghantasala** (Ptolemy's **Kantakossyla**) and **Koddura** were the Satavahana ports of Indo-Roman trade.
[158:1:4] - **Penugonda** = central trade centre of medieval Andhra.
[158:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Previous Papers (src/ap-history/nextgen-previous-papers.txt) p.39 (Roman coins – Bhattiprolu; Motupalli Abhaya inscription); Rocket AP History (Roman coins at Bhattiprolu and Nagarjunakonda); NextGen AP History - APPSC Part 2 p.10 (Roman coin sites); NextGen Satavahanas p.20 (Kantakasela = Ghantasala); NextGen Post-Kakatiyas (src/ap-history/nextgen-09-post-kakatiyas.txt) p.10 (Haravilasam – trade); old app notes row 158
## SUB 2 | Shipbuilding – Narasapuram
[158:2:0] - **Narasapuram / Narsapur** (West Godavari, Godavari delta) = the **chief shipbuilding centre of coastal Andhra in the 16th-17th centuries** – not Machilipatnam, Kakinada (Cocanada), Nagapattinam, Quilon or Madras.
[158:2:1] - **Methold** described large, strongly built ships there under the Qutb Shahis; good timber and a sheltered river mouth.
[158:2:2] - **Corangi** = a Company-era shipbuilding site; **odaberam** = sea-going ships (Shuka Saptati).
[158:2:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History - APPSC Part 15 p.22 (ships and boats: Narasapuram, Machilipatnam); old app notes row 158
## SUB 3 | Other European Trade Centres – Madapollam, Bheemunipatnam, Yanam
[158:3:0] TABLE head: Centre | Power | Note
  [158:3:0.0] Madhavayapalem (Madapollam), near Narsapur | English (not French) | Cloth factory; gave "madapollam" cloth its name – a leading textile centre of the 17th-18th centuries
  [158:3:0.1] Nizampatnam (Petapoli) | Dutch and English | Early 17th century
  [158:3:0.2] Bheemunipatnam (Bhimili) | Dutch → English | Dutch cemetery tombs from 1661; Dutch fort allowed after Maratha plunder (1754); first municipality in Andhra (1861)
  [158:3:0.3] Vizagapatnam | English | 1682
  [158:3:0.4] Pulicat | Dutch (1610) | Fort Geldria; Nagapattinam = Dutch HQ from 1690
  [158:3:0.5] Yanam | French | 1723; joined India 1954, de jure 1962; now part of the UT of Puducherry
[158:3:1] - Other textile centres: Injaram, Maddepalem, Bandamurlanka, Tuni, Kakinada, Coringa, Gollapalem; Berhampur silks, Srikakulam muslins (**Pochampally** ikat is a later, Telangana centre).
[158:3:2] - Today: new ports at **Machilipatnam, Mulapeta, Ramayapatnam, Kakinada SEZ**; proposed **Nizampatnam and Vodarevu** under the **PPP-BOOT** model.
[158:3:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L3 Part 1 p.19; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madapollam; NextGen Modern India L2 Part 1 p.7, 9; old app notes row 158

=== NOTES 1:162 | Anglo-french Rivalry – the Three Carnatic Wars and the English Ascendancy
## SUB 0 | The Three Carnatic Wars at a Glance
[162:0:0] TABLE head: War | Years | European link | Battle | Treaty | Result
  [162:0:0.0] First | 1746-48 (Spectrum 1740-48) | Austrian War of Succession | St. Thome (Adyar), 1746 | Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) | Madras returned to the English for Louisburg (N. America); no lasting supremacy
  [162:0:0.1] Second | 1749-54 (not 1750-55) | None – Hyderabad and Carnatic successions | Ambur 1749; Arcot 1751 | Pondicherry (1754) | Inconclusive ("undecided"); Dupleix recalled
  [162:0:0.2] Third | 1758-63 (also given 1756-63) | Seven Years' War | Wandiwash 1760 | Paris (1763) | Decisive English victory
[162:0:1] - **Yandabo (1826)** ended the First Anglo-Burmese War – never a Carnatic treaty.
[162:0:2] - **Outcome:** the English emerged supreme – by 1761 their influence was firm at **Arcot** (Muhammad Ali) and at the **Nizam's court**; they became the **kingmakers of South India**; the French were left with trading enclaves.
[162:0:3] - Small disciplined European armies beat far larger Indian armies (lesson of St. Thome).
[162:0:4] - Chronology: capture of Madras (1746) → Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) → Pondicherry (1754) → Paris (1763).
[162:0:5] > First = Aix-la-Chapelle; Second = Pondicherry (inconclusive); Third = Paris (Wandiwash).
[162:0:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 2 p.20 (wars–battles–treaties table); Spectrum Modern India p.76-82, 90; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.18; old app notes row 162
## SUB 1 | First Carnatic War (1746-48)
[162:1:0] - Fought between the **British and the French** companies; an **extension of the Austrian War of Succession**.
[162:1:1] - **Immediate cause:** the English navy under **Barnett** **seized French ships**; France retaliated by seizing **Madras (Fort St. George), 1746** with **La Bourdonnais**'s fleet from Mauritius.
[162:1:2] - La Bourdonnais agreed to **ransom Madras** back to the English, but **Dupleix overruled him** and kept it.
[162:1:3] - **Battle of St. Thome (Adyar), 1746:** **Captain Paradis** with about **930** French beat about **10,000** men of **Nawab Anwaruddin** (under Mahfuz Khan); the Nawab had sided with the English.
[162:1:4] - Ended by **Aix-la-Chapelle (1748)**; did **not** give permanent British supremacy.
[162:1:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.76-77; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.18; old app notes row 162
## SUB 2 | Second Carnatic War (1749-54) – Dupleix, Ambur and Arcot
[162:2:0] TABLE head: Dispute | English candidate | French candidate
  [162:2:0.0] Hyderabad (Nizam-ul-Mulk died 1748) | Nasir Jang (son) | Muzaffar Jang (grandson)
  [162:2:0.1] Carnatic | Anwaruddin, then his son Muhammad Ali | Chanda Sahib
[162:2:1] - **Dupleix** – Governor of Pondicherry (from **1742**; Director-General 1741), first European to interfere in Indian succession politics; originator of the subsidiary-force idea (French army at Hyderabad).
[162:2:2] - **Ambur (near Vellore), 1749:** Muzaffar Jang, Chanda Sahib and the French killed **Anwaruddin**; Muzaffar Jang became Subahdar of the Deccan and **rewarded the French** with grants (Masulipatnam, lands near Pondicherry).
[162:2:3] - **Arcot, 1751:** **Clive** seized it with about **210** men and held it **53 days**; then won **Arni and Kaveripak** over **Raja Sahib and Chanda Sahib**.
[162:2:4] - **Trichinopoly:** **Stringer Lawrence** and Clive forced the French commander **Law** to surrender (1752); Chanda Sahib executed.
[162:2:5] - **Bussy** kept **Salabat Jang** in power at Hyderabad and won the **Northern Circars (1753)** for the French.
[162:2:6] - **Godeheu** replaced Dupleix and signed the **Treaty of Pondicherry (1754)**: no interference in princes' quarrels, each kept its possessions; the **Seven Years' War broke out before it was ratified** → Third war.
[162:2:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.77-81; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.18; old app notes row 162
## SUB 3 | Third War Commanders and French Failures
[162:3:0] TABLE head: Person | Side | Role
  [162:3:0.0] Count de Lally | French | Third war: Fort St. David 1758; lost Wandiwash; surrendered Pondicherry 16 Jan 1761
  [162:3:0.1] Eyre Coote | English | Won Wandiwash (22 Jan 1760)
  [162:3:0.2] Francis Forde | English | Won Condore/Chandurti (1758); took Machilipatnam (1759)
  [162:3:0.3] Pocock | English | Admiral; beat d'Aché's fleet off Pondicherry (naval advantage)
  [162:3:0.4] Bussy | French | Taken prisoner at Wandiwash
[162:3:1] - **French failures:** recall of **Dupleix**, **unpaid troops under Lally**, **withdrawal of Bussy from Hyderabad**.
[162:3:2] - English company = **private body run for profit**; French = **state-controlled** (a statement calling the French company private is wrong).
[162:3:3] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.80-83; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.18; old app notes row 162
## SUB 4 | French Settlements and the Northern Circars
[162:4:0] TABLE head: Place | Year | Feature
  [162:4:0.0] Surat | 1668 | First French factory
  [162:4:0.1] Masulipatnam | 1669 | Second factory; patent from the Sultan of Golconda
  [162:4:0.2] Tumnapalem | 1756 | Bussy with Vijayaramaraju → Treaty of Charmahal
  [162:4:0.3] Chendurthi | 1758 | "Plassey of Andhra" (Malleson) – drove the French out of the Northern Circars
  [162:4:0.4] Yanam | – | Enclave in AP's Godavari delta, part of Puducherry UT
  [162:4:0.5] Karaikal | – | Former French settlement in Tamil Nadu
[162:4:1] - **Pondicherry:** transferred to India **1954**; UT by the **14th Amendment (1962)**; renamed **Puducherry in 2006**.
[162:4:2] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.90 (Pondicherry 1954); old app notes row 162

=== NOTES 1:165 | Dual Government in Bengal and Its Consequences; the Bengal Famine of 1770
## SUB 0 | Dual Government in Bengal (1765-1772)
[165:0:0] - **Introduced by Robert Clive** (second governorship 1765-67) after Buxar and the **First Treaty of Allahabad** (Diwani from **Shah Alam II**, tribute **Rs 26 lakh**).
[165:0:1] - **Period: 1765-1772** – not 1764-72 or 1765-70.
[165:0:2] TABLE head: Diwani (Company) | Nizamat (Nawab)
  [165:0:2.0] Revenue collection and civil justice – real power, no responsibility | Police, criminal justice, law and order – responsibility without power or funds
[165:0:3] - Company got diwani from the emperor and controlled nizamat through its right to nominate the **deputy subahdar**; it collected revenue through **Indian deputies**:
[165:0:4] TABLE head: Naib Diwan | Region
  [165:0:4.0] Mohammad Reza Khan (Deputy Diwan of Murshidabad, appointed by Clive; also deputy nazim) | Bengal
  [165:0:4.1] Raja Shitab Rai | Bihar
[165:0:5] - **Why "dual":** hide the Company's imperial role; avoid British Parliament's scrutiny; other Europeans kept paying duties to the "Nawab" – **not** because the Company had enough British manpower (it lacked it).
[165:0:6] - Criticised as "**power divorced from responsibility**"; conflict of the two sidelined the local nobility and bred resentment.
[165:0:7] - **Abolished 1772 by Warren Hastings** (Court of Directors' decision) – he "tore the mask of Mughal sovereignty"; the Calcutta council acted as Diwan; **treasury Murshidabad → Calcutta**; Reza Khan and Shitab Rai removed.
[165:0:8] - Hastings = **last Governor of Bengal (1772-73)** and **first Governor-General of Bengal (1773)**; **first Governor of Bengal = Clive**.
[165:0:9] - Company debt → government loan (1772) → **Regulating Act, 1773**.
[165:0:10] > Clive introduced (1765), Hastings abolished (1772).
[165:0:11] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.125; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.16-17; old app notes row 165
## SUB 1 | Consequences and the Bengal Famine of 1770
[165:1:0] - In under two decades **Bengal, the richest province**, was reduced to **acute poverty, famines and epidemics**.
[165:1:1] - **Weavers** forced to sell to Company agents at low prices; Company servants misused **dastaks** for private trade (Mir Qasim had abolished internal duties for all in protest).
[165:1:2] - **R.P. Dutt:** Bengal's surplus revenue drained in the **mercantilist phase, 1757-1813**.
[165:1:3] - **Famine of 1770:** first major famine under Company rule; struck **Bengal and Bihar**; about **ten million** died – about **one-third (≈33%)** of Bengal's people.
[165:1:4] - Causes: monsoon failure; **land revenue demanded in cash** kept rising, peasants sold grain; directly linked to the **Dual Government**.
[165:1:5] - Company gave **little or no relief** and **kept collecting revenue**; Governor at the time: **John Cartier** (1769-72), not Hastings.
[165:1:6] - Andhra's **Guntur (Dokkala) famine, 1832-33** is a separate event.
[165:1:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 p.54, 86; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.17, 34; old app notes row 165
## SUB 2 | Sanyasi-Fakir Revolt and Bankim Chandra's Anandamath
[165:2:0] - **Sanyasi (Fakir) Revolt, 1763-1800** (Bengal): causes – **famine of 1770**, Company insensitivity, **restrictions on visits to holy places**; sanyasis raided Company factories and treasuries; subdued by **Warren Hastings**.
[165:2:1] - Leaders: **Majnum Shah**, Chirag Ali, Musa Shah, **Bhawani Pathak**, **Debi Chaudhurani** – not Shah Alam II.
[165:2:2] - **Anandamath (1882)** by **Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay** (not Sarat Chandra) – based on the **Sanyasi revolt**, set in the 1770 famine; contains **Vande Mataram**.
[165:2:3] TABLE head: Work / fact | Detail
  [165:2:3.0] Durgeshnandini (1865) | First Bengali historical novel – Pathan–Mughal conflict in Akbar's reign
  [165:2:3.1] Sitaram (1887) | His last novel (Spectrum calls Rajasimha his finale – its enlarged edition was 1893)
  [165:2:3.2] First graduates of Calcutta University (1858) | Bankim and Jodu Nath Bose
  [165:2:3.3] Birthplace | Naihati (Kanthalpara) – Rail Coach Factory and Museum, Rail Budget 2012-13
[165:2:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.34; Spectrum Modern India p.42, 171-172; newworldencyclopedia.org (Bankim: 1858 graduate, Sitaram 1887); old app notes row 165

=== NOTES 1:166 | Anglo-mysore Wars I–iv – Haidar Ali, Tipu Sultan, Treaty of Mangalore and Srirangapatnam
## SUB 0 | Four Anglo-Mysore Wars at a Glance
[166:0:0] TABLE head: War | Years | Mysore | British head | Treaty / result
  [166:0:0.0] First | 1767-69 | Haidar Ali | Harry Verelst (Governor of Bengal) | Haidar before Madras → Treaty of Madras, 4 April 1769 (mutual restitution, help against third party)
  [166:0:0.1] Second | 1780-84 | Haidar (died 7 Dec 1782), then Tipu | Warren Hastings | Pollilur, Porto Novo; Treaty of Mangalore (March 1784) with Tipu – mutual restitution
  [166:0:0.2] Third | 1790-92 (PMF 1789-92) | Tipu | Lord Cornwallis (led in person) | Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) with Tipu – ended Tipu's supremacy in the south
  [166:0:0.3] Fourth | 1799 | Tipu | Lord Wellesley | Seringapatam fell; Tipu killed 4 May 1799
[166:0:1] - **Correct pairs:** Fourth war – Tipu defeated and killed; First – Haidar **not** defeated; Second – inconclusive; Third – Tipu **lost**.
[166:0:2] - **Dates (match):** death of Haidar **1782**; Treaty of Mangalore **1784**; Treaty of Srirangapatnam **1792**; death of Tipu **1799**.
[166:0:3] > Madras 1769 = Haidar; Mangalore 1784 and Seringapatam 1792 = Tipu.

## SUB 1 | Tipu Sultan – Capital, Embassies, Jacobin Club
[166:1:0] - **Capital: Srirangapatna (Seringapatam)**; born 1750; **"Tiger of Mysore"**; also **Padshah** (1787) and **"Citizen Tipu"** – "Lion of Mysore" is not his title.
[166:1:1] - **Embassies on modern lines:** **France** (three ambassadors in Paris, 1788), **Ottoman Empire**, Oman, Persia, **Afghanistan (Zaman Shah)**, Arabia, Mauritius – not Haidar, Mir Qasim or Shah Alam II.
[166:1:2] - **Navy:** Board of Admiralty (1796), dockyards at Mangalore, Wajedabad, Molidabad.
[166:1:3] - **Jacobin Club** at Seringapatam (**1797**); he became **Citizen Tipu** and **planted the Tree of Liberty**.
[166:1:4] - **Reforms:** new calendar, coinage, weights and measures; sericulture; **war rockets** (pioneer – he did **not** discontinue them).
[166:1:5] TABLE head: Monument (Srirangapatna) | Feature
  [166:1:5.0] Gumbaz | Mausoleum of Haidar Ali and Tipu
  [166:1:5.1] Daria Daulat Bagh | Summer palace with war murals
[166:1:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.130-131; PMF Modern History Part 1 p.79; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.17; old app notes row 166
## SUB 2 | Second War Battles – Pollilur and Porto Novo
[166:2:0] TABLE head: Battle | Date | Result
  [166:2:0.0] Arcot | 1780 | Captured by Haidar
  [166:2:0.1] Pollilur | 10 Sept 1780 | Haidar Ali and Tipu destroyed Col. William Baillie's British force (Spectrum misprints 1781)
  [166:2:0.2] Porto Novo | 1 July 1781 | Sir Eyre Coote defeated Haidar – reversed Pollilur, saved Madras
[166:2:1] - Haidar's anti-English alliance with the **Nizam and the Marathas**; British detached them – the Nizam bought off (Guntur), the Marathas by the **Treaty of Salbai (1782)**.
[166:2:2] - Coote came from Bengal with men and money sent by Hastings; **Thomas Munro** served under **Hector Munro** and **Eyre Coote**.
[166:2:3] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian History part 1 (battles table); PMF Modern History Part 2 p.38-39; Spectrum Modern India p.128-129; old app notes row 166
## SUB 3 | Haidar Ali (1761-82)
[166:3:0] - Rose in the **Wodeyar** army under ministers **Nanjaraj** (sarvadhikari) and **Devaraj** (dalwai), who had made **Chikka Krishnaraja Wodeyar II** a puppet.
[166:3:1] - **Faujdar of Dindigul (1755)** under **Nanjaraja**; set up a **modern arsenal at Dindigul with French help**; trained troops on Western lines; de facto ruler **1761**.
[166:3:2] - **First war diplomacy:** paid the **Marathas** to stay neutral and **won over the Nizam**; appeared before Madras → humiliating **Treaty of Madras (1769)** – the **first South Indian ruler to defeat British armies**.
[166:3:3] - Defeated by Peshwa **Madhav Rao** (1764, 1766, 1771); the English did not help him in 1771 → Second war.
[166:3:4] - **Velu Nachiyar** of Sivaganga recovered her kingdom with Haidar's help – the first queen to fight the British.
[166:3:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.126-128; PMF Modern History Part 1 p.78; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.17, 36; old app notes row 166
## SUB 4 | Third War and the Treaty of Seringapatam (1792)
[166:4:0] - Cause: Tipu attacked **Travancore** (1789/90), a Company ally; Tipu beat **General Meadows (1790)**; **Cornwallis** took **Bangalore (March 1791)** via Ambur and Vellore.
[166:4:1] - **Both the Nizam and the Marathas** joined the British (the grand alliance) – only in the **Third** war.
[166:4:2] - **Treaty of Seringapatam** – with **Tipu Sultan** (not Haidar): about **half his territory** ceded, indemnity **Rs 3 crore** (330 lakh), **two sons as hostages**.
[166:4:3] TABLE head: Gainer | Share
  [166:4:3.0] British | Malabar, Coorg (protectorate), Dindigul, Bara Mahal – Ryotwari began here (Read and Munro)
  [166:4:3.1] Nizam | Krishna to beyond the Pennar – Bellary, Gurramkonda, Gandikota, Kambham, Kadapa
  [166:4:3.2] Marathas | Around the Tungabhadra
[166:4:4] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.129-130; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.19, Part 6 p.18; PMF Modern History Part 2 p.39; old app notes row 166
## SUB 5 | Fourth War (1799) and the Settlement of Mysore
[166:5:0] - Tipu refused the **Subsidiary Alliance**; **Wellesley** declared war (17 April – 4 May 1799); led by **General George Harris**, General Stuart and **Arthur Wellesley**.
[166:5:1] - **Nizam** fought as a subsidiary ally (since 1798); the **Marathas** are listed as allies by NextGen, PMF and Spectrum, but in fact gave **no active help** and refused their share.
[166:5:2] - Wodeyars restored: boy ruler **Krishnaraja Wodeyar III** under a subsidiary alliance; Nizam got **Gooty and Gurramkonda**.
[166:5:3] - The Nizam's Mysore lands were handed to the Company in **1800** = **Ceded Districts** (**Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur, Bellary**).
[166:5:4] - Removed the French-backed threat; brought Mysore and Rayalaseema under the Company; Bentinck took over Mysore 1831, Ripon restored it 1881.
[166:5:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.130-132; PMF Modern History Part 2 p.40-41; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.18; old app notes row 166

=== NOTES 1:167 | The Nizam of Hyderabad, Subsidiary Alliance, and the Cession of the Northern Circars
## SUB 0 | Subsidiary Alliance – Wellesley, Terms, Aims and the Order of States
[167:0:0] # Author and aims
[167:0:1] - **Lord Wellesley (Governor-General 1798-1805)** used it to build the empire; he did **not invent** it – Dupleix first hired out troops, Awadh's **1765** treaty "anticipated" it – but made **cession of territory for the subsidy** the general rule (its final shape).
[167:0:2] - **Aims:** keep the **French** out (fear of **Napoleon**); bring the states into dependence = **British paramountcy** without direct rule; a large army kept **at the states' expense**. A **fixed income** for the Company was **not** an aim (UPSC 2018 ×2: "does not apply" = fixed income).
[167:0:3] - **Rajput states (1818):** the Company's aim = to **establish British sovereignty / paramountcy** (RAS 1992); the Rajputs themselves sought protection from the **Marathas and Pindaris**; treaties negotiated by **Charles Metcalfe** under Lord Hastings.
[167:0:4] # Terms
[167:0:5] - 1. Permanent **subsidiary force** in the state, paid by a subsidy – or, if unpaid, by **ceding territory**.
[167:0:6] - 2. A **British Resident** at the court.
[167:0:7] - 3. **No other Europeans** in service without the Company's consent.
[167:0:8] - 4. **No war or negotiation** with other states without the Governor-General = **foreign affairs surrendered**.
[167:0:9] - 5. In return the Company **defends the ruler** and promises **non-interference** in internal affairs.
[167:0:10] - **Effects:** rulers lost independence and revenue, became weak and irresponsible, subjects exploited; unpaid subsidies → cessions (the **Nizam's Ceded Districts**).
[167:0:11] # Order of acceptance
[167:0:12] TABLE head: State | Year
  [167:0:12.0] Hyderabad (Nizam Ali Khan) | 1 Sep 1798 (and Oct 1800) – the first
  [167:0:12.1] Mysore (restored Wodeyars) | 1799
  [167:0:12.2] Tanjore | Oct 1799
  [167:0:12.3] Awadh | Nov 1801
  [167:0:12.4] Peshwa Baji Rao II (Treaty of Bassein) | 31 Dec 1802 – first Maratha
  [167:0:12.5] Bhonsle (Berar/Nagpur) | Dec 1803
  [167:0:12.6] Sindhia | Feb 1804
  [167:0:12.7] Jodhpur, Jaipur, Bundi, Bharatpur, Holkar | 1818 – Holkar the last Maratha
[167:0:13] - **First state (asked ×9):** **Hyderabad, 1798** – APPSC G2 2002, 2008 ×2, JL 2011, IAS 1994, AP History PYQ; **⚠ APPSC Inspector of Factories key gave Awadh** – Awadh's 1765 defence treaty only anticipated the system and Awadh joined Wellesley's system in **1801**.
[167:0:14] - **Year with the Nizam = 1798** (G2-A 1991); first Maratha sardar = **Peshwa Baji Rao II** (1802).
[167:0:15] - **Not accepted under Wellesley:** **Holkar** of Indore resisted (signed only in 1818 after defeat); **Tipu Sultan** refused → Fourth Mysore War (1799).
[167:0:16] - **Rayalaseema** came to the British **through the Subsidiary Alliance** – ceded by the Nizam on **12 Oct 1800** in lieu of the subsidy.
[167:0:17] # Policies towards the states
[167:0:18] TABLE head: Policy | Author
  [167:0:18.0] Ring-fence – defend neighbours' frontiers (Awadh as buffer shielding Bengal from Marathas and Afghans) | Warren Hastings
  [167:0:18.1] Subsidiary Alliance | Wellesley (1798)
  [167:0:18.2] Subordinate isolation | Lord Hastings (1813-23)
  [167:0:18.3] Doctrine of Lapse – annex states without a natural male heir | Dalhousie
  [167:0:18.4] Subordinate union – princes as "breakwaters to the storm"; right of adoption recognised | Crown, after 1858
[167:0:19] - Other "policy" pairs used as distractors: Dhamma – Ashoka; Blood and Iron – Balban; Market control – Alauddin Khalji; Blue Water – Almeida.
[167:0:20] - **Grounds for intervention** in states: succession disputes, misgovernment, and the need to fulfil their **international commitments**.
[167:0:21] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.152-154 (file pages); PMF Modern History Part 2 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-02.txt) p.41, p.44, p.72; NextGen modern India L2 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l2-01.txt) p.14; old app notes row 167 (sub 4, 5, 7, 8)
## SUB 1 | Asaf Jahi Nizams – Reigns and Firsts
[167:1:0] TABLE head: Nizam | Reign | Key point
  [167:1:0.0] Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan, Nizam-ul-Mulk, Asaf Jah I | from 1724 | independent after defeating Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda; founder (Chin Qilich Khan)
  [167:1:0.1] Nizam Ali Khan (Asaf Jah II) | 1762-1803 | capital Aurangabad → Hyderabad, 1763; Circars leased (1766); Guntur given (1788); first Subsidiary Alliance (1798); Ceded Districts (1800)
  [167:1:0.2] Sikandar Jah (Asaf Jah III) | 1803-29 | Secunderabad cantonment (near Hussain Sagar) named after him
  [167:1:0.3] Nasir-ud-Daula (Asaf Jah IV) | 1829-57 | Wahabi conspiracy 1839 (Mubariz-ud-Daula arrested); Berar Treaty 1853 (Berar, Raichur, Dharashiv/Osmanabad); Salar Jung I made Diwan (1853); died 16 May 1857
  [167:1:0.4] Afzal-ud-Daula (Asaf Jah V) | 1857-69 | Nizam during the 1857 revolt in Hyderabad; loyal → title "Star of India"
  [167:1:0.5] Mir Mahbub Ali Khan (Asaf Jah VI) | 1869-1911 | youngest Asaf Jahi ruler – Nizam as an infant (turned 18 only in 1884); Salar Jung I regent
  [167:1:0.6] Mir Osman Ali Khan (Asaf Jah VII) | 1911-48 | last Nizam; Razakar struggle for an independent Hyderabad → Police Action (Sept 1948)
[167:1:1] - **1763 shift (asked ×2):** **Nizam Ali Khan** moved the Deccan capital from **Aurangabad to Hyderabad** (not Guntur; not 1756/1758/1760).
[167:1:2] - **1857:** the Meerut outbreak (10 May) fell under Nasir-ud-Daula, but the **Hyderabad events** (Aurangabad, June; Residency attack, **17 July 1857**) came under **Afzal-ud-Daula** – the answer for "Nizam during 1857" (APPSC G2 2001, ATWO).
[167:1:3] - **Residency attack:** **Turrebaz (Tura Baz) Khan**, a Rohilla jamedar, with ~5,000 men, to free **Chida Khan**; repulsed by **Col. Davidson**; the Nizam and Salar Jung stayed loyal.
[167:1:4] > Trap: Sikandar Jah = Secunderabad; Mahbub Ali Khan = youngest; Afzal-ud-Daula = 1857 + Star of India; Osman Ali Khan = Razakars.
[167:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen modern India L3 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l3-01.txt) p.55, p.61, p.65; NextGen AP History Part 21 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-21.txt) p.10-12; NextGen modern India L2 Part 2 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l2-02.txt) p.4; NextGen previous papers (src/ap-history/nextgen-previous-papers.txt) p.22 (Chin Qilich Khan); old app notes row 167 (sub 0); 1763 shift and Secunderabad: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 2 | Salar Jung I and the Hyderabad Reforms (1853-1883)
[167:2:0] - **Mir Turab Ali Khan = Salar Jung I**, made **Diwan on 31 May 1853** (after Siraj-ul-Mulk) by **Nasir-ud-Daula** → the **Salar Jung family rose under Nasir-ud-Daula**; served **three Nizams** (Nasir-ud-Daula, Afzal-ud-Daula, Mahbub Ali Khan) till his death in **1883**.
[167:2:1] - **Revenue:** curbed the daftardars; **paid talukdars** replaced the **auctioning of revenue to contractors** = he **abolished revenue farming**; **Zillabandi (1865)** – districts under talukdars; Halisikka rupee, central mint at Hyderabad.
[167:2:2] - **Post-1857 offices (ATWO A-R):** more work in the Minister's **Dar-ul-Insha** → a **Munshi Khana** for correspondence with the **taluqdars**, beside the offices for the restored districts (**Azla-i-Mustarida**).
[167:2:3] # Judiciary
[167:2:4] TABLE head: Court | Role
  [167:2:4.0] Mahkama-i-Sadar | High Court of Hyderabad (controlled munsiffs, mir adils)
  [167:2:4.1] Majlis-i-Murafa | Supreme Court / Court of Appeal above it
  [167:2:4.2] Buzurg and Khurd Diwani Adalat | civil courts (senior, junior)
  [167:2:4.3] Faujdari Adalat | criminal court, chief judge titled Nazim
  [167:2:4.4] Darul Kazi / Mahkama-i-Sadarat | Muhammadan law / religious endowments
[167:2:5] - **Police (1865 on):** Mahkama-i-Kotwali; force = Nizamat; SP = Muhtamim, inspector = Amin, station = chauki.
[167:2:6] - **Education:** Darul-ulum (1855), City High School (1870), Chaderghat (1872), Madrasa-e-Aliya (1873); **Nizam College 1887**.
[167:2:7] - **Railways:** Hyderabad-Wadi line completed **1878** (NextGen; old app notes said 1874).
[167:2:8] - **Chanda Railway Scheme (1883):** the elite under **Dr Aghornath Chattopadhyaya** demanded its details; he was deported on **20 May 1883** → the **beginning of public political awakening** in Hyderabad.
[167:2:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen modern India L3 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l3-01.txt) p.55-63; NextGen modern India L3 Part 4 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l3-04.txt) p.1-5; NextGen AP History Part 7 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-07.txt) p.6 (Zillabandi 1865); Munshi Khana: printed ATWO key, not checked in a source
## SUB 3 | Northern Circars Lease, Kandregula Jogipantulu and Guntur
[167:3:0] TABLE head: Year | Step
  [167:3:0.0] 1759 | Salabat Jang gave the British Machilipatnam, Nizampatnam, Vakal Mannar, part of Kondapalli
  [167:3:0.1] 1765 | Mughal Shah Alam II's farman, received by Clive, granted the five Circars – Nizam Ali refused it at first
  [167:3:0.2] 12 Nov 1766 | Treaty of Hyderabad (envoy Calliaud): Circars leased – ₹9 lakh a year or military aid
  [167:3:0.3] 1768 | Treaty of Masulipatnam: Nizam accepted Shah Alam's grant and resigned the Circars
  [167:3:0.4] 18 Sep 1788 | Guntur handed over by Nizam Ali Khan for ₹7 lakh, after Basalat Jang's death (1782)
[167:3:1] - **Negotiator (asked ×2):** **Kandregula Jogipantulu** – mediator between Nizam Ali and the Company's men at **Machilipatnam**; used the **Gollapudi pay mutiny** to propose a lease at **₹15 lakh** (1766 treaty fixed ₹9 lakh); Nizam made him **Majumdar of Rajamahendravaram**, the British "**Raja Bahadur**". **Col. Forde** took Machilipatnam from the French (1759) – not the negotiator.
[167:3:2] - **Circars of 1766:** Chicacole, Rajahmundry, Ellore, **Mustafanagar (Kondapalli)** – **not Kurnool** (Ceded District, 1800); **Guntur (Murtazanagar / Kondaveedu) = the fifth Circar**, excepted as Basalat Jang's estate.
[167:3:3] - **"Main point of difference between Nizam Ali and the English" (G2 2011 ×2):** **the Northern Sarkars** – the 1765 grant over his head, the 1766-68 treaties (NextGen previous papers). Guntur was the later, narrower dispute (1779 lease from Basalat Jang, handover 1788).
[167:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen modern India L2 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l2-01.txt) p.13-14; NextGen previous papers (src/ap-history/nextgen-previous-papers.txt) p.22; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Circars; old app notes row 167 (sub 2)
## SUB 4 | Road to 1798 – Kharda, Raymond and the Hyderabad Residency
[167:4:0] - Nizam beaten by the Marathas at **Kharda (1795)** → blamed **Sir John Shore's neutrality** → relied on **French battalions under Raymond** → **Wellesley** forced the alliance (1 Sep 1798).
[167:4:1] - **Resident James Kirkpatrick** reported the French battalions; built the Residency ("**Koti**"). The Resident controlled the Nizam's **foreign relations** and the subsidiary force.
[167:4:2] - **Russell Brigade** – reformed Hyderabad force raised by **Resident Henry Russell** (c. 1813).
[167:4:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 2 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-02.txt) p.72; old app notes row 167 (sub 3)
## SUB 5 | Ceded Districts and Andhra Consequences
[167:5:0] - **12 Oct 1800:** the Nizam ceded the lands he had gained from Mysore – **Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur, Bellary** – in lieu of the subsidy = **Dattamandalalu (Ceded Districts)**.
[167:5:1] - Name **Rayalaseema** (1928) proposed by **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** at the **Nandyal Andhra Mahasabha**, presided by **Dr S. Radhakrishnan**.
[167:5:2] - **1801:** Nellore and Chittoor from the Carnatic Nawab → the whole of Andhra under the Company; **Telangana stayed under the Nizam**.
[167:5:3] - **Padmanabham (10 July 1794):** the Company defeated and killed **Chinna Vijayaramaraju** of Vizianagaram.
[167:5:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen modern India L2 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l2-01.txt) p.14-15; NextGen modern India L3 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l3-01.txt) p.23

=== NOTES 1:168 | Andhra Region Under the Company – Machilipatnam, Ceded Districts, Early Administration and Revenue
## SUB 0 | Revenue Systems and Taxes – Moturpha, Peshkash, Zamindari and Ryotwari
[168:0:0] # Revenue terms
[168:0:1] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [168:0:1.0] Moturpha | tax on looms – a tax on trades and occupations (weavers, shops, artisans); not a salt tax; attacked in the Madras Native Association's 1861 petition; abolished 1861
  [168:0:1.1] Peshkash / Peshcush | the share of revenue (land tax / tribute) paid by zamindars to the British
  [168:0:1.2] Korunu | revenue the zamindars collected from the farmers
  [168:0:1.3] Haveli lands | lands under direct British (government) control
  [168:0:1.4] Sunkams / Sayer | land customs, inland transit duties
  [168:0:1.5] Abkari | excise on liquor and toddy
[168:0:2] - **Moturpha (asked ×7):** "tax on looms" (APPSC G2 2011 ×2, AP History PYQ, Asst Social Welfare, BC Welfare); **G2 Mains 2025 statements:** Moturpha a salt tax – **false**; Peshcush = revenue from the zamindars – **true** → "(A) false, (B) true".
[168:0:3] # Three methods of land revenue (both statements true)
[168:0:4] TABLE head: System | Where | Settled with
  [168:0:4.0] Zamindari (Permanent Settlement) | coastal Northern Circars (Uttara Sarkarlu) – Vizianagaram, Bobbili, Pithapuram | zamindar pays peshkash
  [168:0:4.1] Ryotwari | Ceded Districts / Rayalaseema (Datta mandalalu) first (from 1802), later most of Madras (1820, Munro) | the ryot directly
  [168:0:4.2] Mahalwari | Nellore | village headmen
[168:0:5] - **Permanent Settlement:** Cornwallis **1793** ended the auctions and fixed the demand; applied to Andhra in **1802** (Vizianagaram peshcush fixed at ₹6 lakh); zamindars kept 1/10, government 9/10.
[168:0:6] - **Effects:** zamindari → absentee landlords, rack-rented tenants; ryotwari → over-assessment, cash payment, moneylender debt, land alienation.
[168:0:7] - **Zamindari abolished:** Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act **1948**, in force **19 April 1949**.
[168:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen modern India L2 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l2-01.txt) p.16; NextGen modern India L3 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l3-01.txt) p.21, p.25-27, p.47; NextGen previous papers (src/ap-history/nextgen-previous-papers.txt) p.22; old app notes row 168 (sub 8)
## SUB 1 | Ceded Districts – Headquarters and Rayalaseema
[168:1:0] - **Ceded Districts (1800)** = **Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur** (now AP) + **Bellary** (now Karnataka) = present-day **Rayalaseema**; old name **Dattamandalam / Dattamandalalu**.
[168:1:1] - **Headquarters (asked ×3, G2 2011):** one collectorate till **1808** with its **headquarters at Anantapur**; Munro Principal Collector (Nov 1800) with four sub-collectors; divisions Cuddapah, Cumbum, Adoni, Harpanahalli. **Bellary** and **Cuddapah** became district seats only after the **1808** split.
[168:1:2] - **Rayalaseema districts:** Kurnool, Kadapa, Anantapur, Chittoor (and their 2022 offshoots) – **Guntur is coastal**, not Rayalaseema.
[168:1:3] - **Name:** **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao**, Andhra Mahasabha at **Nandyal, Nov 1928**, presided by **S. Radhakrishnan**; resolution moved by Chilukuri Narayana Rao (old app notes).
[168:1:4] > Trap: "Dattamandalam headquarters" = Anantapur (not Bellary); Bellary is now in Karnataka.
[168:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen modern India L2 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l2-01.txt) p.14-15; NextGen modern India L3 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l3-01.txt) p.25, p.33; old app notes row 168 (sub 2)
## SUB 2 | How Andhra Came Under the Company and Its Early Administration
[168:2:0] TABLE head: Region | Year | How
  [168:2:0.0] Machilipatnam and parganas | 1759 | grant of Salabat Jung
  [168:2:0.1] Northern Circars (Godavari etc.) | 1765-66 | Shah Alam II's farman, lease from Nizam Ali
  [168:2:0.2] Guntur Circar | 1788 (18 Sep) | Nizam Ali, ₹7 lakh, after Basalat Jang's death
  [168:2:0.3] Ceded Districts | 1800 | Subsidiary Alliance
  [168:2:0.4] Nellore, Chittoor (Carnatic) | 1801 | Carnatic Treaty with Nawab Azim-ud-Daula (NextGen: 1802); Andhra merged into the Madras Presidency
[168:2:1] - **Guntur:** came under the Company in **1788** and became a Madras district (G2 JA); "finally took possession" = **1788** (not 1768/1775/1782/1789).
[168:2:2] - **Godavari district** came under the Company in **1766**.
[168:2:3] - **Before 1794:** factories and warehouses at **Machilipatnam and Visakhapatnam**; **Chiefs and Councils** (provincial revenue boards) there ran the Circars; "Sarkars came in 1799" is false (1766).
[168:2:4] - **Committee of Circuit (Circuit Committee), 1775:** sent by the Madras Council to inquire into the zamindars' (samsthanams') revenue and abuses; recommended **against the auction system**. ("Union of Circuits" in a G2-A 1984 translation = this committee.)
[168:2:5] - **Madras Board of Revenue:** set up **1786**.
[168:2:6] - **Collector system:** **1794** – district **Collectors replaced the Chiefs and Councils** in the coastal districts (G2-A 1989, G2 2012); **1800** – Munro Collector of the Ceded Districts. 1786 is the Board of Revenue, not the Collectors.
[168:2:7] - **Carnatic districts:** Muhammad Ali installed as Nawab after the Second Carnatic War; annexed in 1801 after his death.
[168:2:8] - Hierarchy: Board of Revenue → Collector → Tahsildar (taluk) → Karanam, Munsab (village); Andhra's own Board of Revenue 1953. Collectors leaned on **dubashis**.
[168:2:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen modern India L2 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l2-01.txt) p.14-16; NextGen modern India L3 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l3-01.txt) p.25, p.49; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Circars; old app notes row 168 (sub 0, 1, 3, 6)
## SUB 3 | Districts and Collectorates
[168:3:0] - **1794:** coastal Andhra had **5 collectorates** – Ganjam, Visakhapatnam, Godavari, Krishna (HQ **Machilipatnam**), Nellore.
[168:3:1] - **By 1856: 8 collectorates** – Ganjam, Visakhapatnam, Godavari, Krishna (Machilipatnam), Nellore, **Bellary, Cuddapah, Kurnool**.
[168:3:2] TABLE head: District | Formed
  [168:3:2.0] Cuddapah, Bellary | 1808 (split of the Ceded Districts)
  [168:3:2.1] Kurnool | 1858
  [168:3:2.2] Godavari, Krishna (renamed) | 1859
  [168:3:2.3] Anantapur | 1882
  [168:3:2.4] Guntur, East Godavari | 1904
  [168:3:2.5] Chittoor | 1911 – took Kadapa's eastern taluks, so Kadapa got its (pre-2022) area in 1911
  [168:3:2.6] West Godavari | 1925
[168:3:3] - **Match (ACF/AEE):** Dutch Masulipatnam **1605** – English Masulipatnam **1611** – Ceded Districts re-divided **1808** – Godavari to the Company **1766** → 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-d.
[168:3:4] - **⚠ Outdated area facts:** the April 2022 reorganisation (26 districts) carved **Annamayya** out of Kadapa and Chittoor and **Sri Sathya Sai** out of Anantapur; more districts (e.g. **Markapuram**, 31 Dec 2025) followed – old "largest district = Anantapur" and "Kadapa's present area = 1911" answers predate this.
